Alimony and Spousal Support in Arvada, CO
You’ve been through the emotional toll of your divorce, and are finally ready to move on with your life. However, the financial implications may have caught you off guard. Adjusting to a new financial reality after being accustomed to a certain standard of living during your marriage can be challenging. The good news is that you have the option to request alimony.
Alimony, or spousal support, was established to assist individuals, regardless of gender, who either didn’t work outside the home during their marriage or earned significantly less than their former partners. The determination of the support amount considers various factors, including the duration of the marriage and income disparities.
At The Drake Law Firm, P.C., we understand the financial challenges that often arise during and after divorce.  If you’re wondering about your eligibility for spousal support or are seeking clarity on the amount you may be entitled to, don’t hesitate to reach out to our experienced alimony and spousal support lawyer in Arvada, CO. Our dedicated team of family law attorneys is here to guide you through the complexities of alimony and spousal support.
Types Of Alimony In Colorado
In Colorado, alimony, also known as spousal support or spousal maintenance can take various forms, each serving a specific purpose:
Temporary Maintenance: Temporary support is provided during the divorce proceedings and helps to meet immediate financial needs.
Rehabilitative Maintenance: This form of support aims to assist the lower-earning spouse in acquiring the skills or education needed to become financially independent. You will receive payments until you achieve financial self-sufficiency. Once you secure a steady job and attain financial independence, the payments will stop.
Reimbursement Maintenance: If one spouse supported the other in obtaining education or professional certifications during the marriage, reimbursement maintenance may be appropriate to compensate the supporting spouse.
Permanent Maintenance: Reserved for unique circumstances, permanent maintenance provides ongoing financial support, typically when one spouse faces health issues or a significant income disparity.
Requirements For Spousal Support
To determine eligibility for spousal support in Colorado, several factors come into play:
Marriage Duration: Typically, marriages lasting three years or more are eligible for spousal support consideration.
Income Disparity: The court considers the income and potential earnings of both parties. If there’s a significant financial gap, spousal support becomes more likely.
Employability: The court evaluates each spouse’s ability to gain employment and support themselves independently.
Property and Assets: The division of property and assets, along with child support arrangements, can influence spousal support decisions.
Health and Age: The physical health and age of both parties can impact the court’s determination of spousal support.
Contribution to the Marriage: The marriage contributions of both spouses, whether financial or non-financial, are taken into account. This covers responsibilities such as maintaining the household, nurturing children, and aiding the career advancement of the other spouse.
In Colorado, alimony determinations are not swayed by marital misbehavior, such as infidelity. The primary focus centers on the financial requirements and capacities of both spouses.

What Is Temporary Maintenance?
Temporary Maintenance is one of the various types of Alimony/Spousal Support available for those getting out of a marriage. Other common types of alimony are:
Rehabilitative maintenance
Reimbursement maintenance
Permanent maintenance
How is Alimony Calculated?
In general, unless specific factors are met, the marriage must have lasted 3 or more years for Alimony to be considered. Your lawyer can either negotiate spousal support or represent you in court if a case goes to trial. In the event that the case goes to court, the judge will evaluate several factors to determine whether you’re eligible for support and the appropriate amount.
The courts look for a few factors when considering alimony. The courts take into account the income of both parties, including potential future earnings. Other considerations include employability, property distribution, child support obligations, and the lifestyle maintained during the marriage. The age and health of both parties are also factors in the decision. One other consideration is related to specific training or education. Courts can look at whether spousal support should be considered if it will be used to gain education or training.

Types of Child Custody in Colorado
Understanding the different types of child custody arrangements is crucial when approaching child custody matters. In Colorado, child custody can be divided into two main categories:
Physical Custody: This refers to where the child primarily resides. Parents living in close proximity often opt for joint physical custody, allowing the child to spend significant time with each parent. However, if parents live further apart or face challenges due to different school districts, a suitable physical custody plan can be devised to ensure the child maintains a meaningful relationship with both parents.
Legal Custody: Legal custody involves decision-making authority for the child’s well-being, including choices related to education, healthcare, and religious upbringing. Joint legal custody is typically preferred, enabling both parents to have a say in important decisions affecting their child’s life, even if one parent has primary physical custody.
Click to check out our video resources on family law and child custody
Can you modify child custody?
Modifying child custody agreements can be challenging due to the courts generally preferring to maintain the existing agreement, unless specific circumstances warrant a change.
There are situations where modifications may be possible. For example, if the other parent has a history of abuse or has been convicted of criminal activity, it may be possible to seek a modification. Similarly, if one parent relocates a significant distance away or becomes unable to provide proper care for the child due to illness, a modification might be considered. It is important to consult with an experienced family law attorney to evaluate your unique circumstances and determine the feasibility of seeking a modification in your child custody agreement.
If you believe that the existing child custody arrangement is no longer in your child’s best interests, our Arvada child custody attorneys can assist you in seeking a modification.
Contact Us Today
If you are facing child custody challenges in Arvada, CO, The Drake Law Firm is here to provide you with reliable legal support. Our compassionate child custody attorneys have the expertise and commitment to guide you through the process, protect your parental rights, and prioritize your child’s well-being. Contact us today to schedule a consultation.

What issues are typically addressed in divorce cases?
Your divorce attorney in Arvada, CO, has the ability to engage in negotiations with the opposing party to resolve the matters at hand. While it’s possible to reach an agreement without court intervention, it’s not guaranteed. Regardless of whether the case is settled in or out of court, we can provide assistance with all aspects of the divorce, which may include child support orders, child custody provisions, and alimony/spousal support.
In Colorado, you can file for divorce without having to prove the other party’s wrongdoing since it is a no-fault divorce state. The grounds for divorce are based on the irretrievable breakdown of the marriage. However, you must first establish a domicile in Colorado for at least 90 days to meet the state’s residency requirement. Once this requirement is met, your divorce lawyer in Arvada, CO can proceed with filing the petition.
There are two options for filing for divorce: a co-petition with the other party or a solo petition. If you choose to file the petition on your own, the other party will be informed. Following notification, you could receive your divorce decree in as few as 91 days. Alternatively, if you and your spouse file together, the 91-day period starts from the date of filing.
Contact our firm today to learn how settling matters beforehand can help you move through the divorce process quickly. Our Colorado divorce lawyer will employ non-adversarial negotiation strategies in an effort to reach an agreement prior to filing for divorce.

Grounds for Filing for Visitation
Our Golden, CO, grandparents’ rights lawyer can help you petition for visitation if one or more of the following has occurred:
The parents are legally divorced.
The parents are legally separated.
The marriage is not valid.
The child is not living with either parent.
The grandparent’s child, the legal parent, has passed away.

Common-Law Marriage in Golden, CO
Do you cohabit with another person you consider your husband or wife, even though you aren’t legally married? If the other party also considers you to be his or her spouse, you are in a common-law marriage. Common-law marriages are legally recognized, and you can obtain a divorce if you’re ready for the relationship to end. However, the divorce process isn’t nearly as straightforward since you don’t have legal marriage documents.
Our Golden, CO, common-law marriage lawyer is experienced in these relationships. We can gather evidence to prove the marriage and then negotiate or litigate the divorce. We can also help you determine if you’re eligible for child support, alimony, and more. Contact us for a consultation today.
Requirements for Common Law Marriage in Colorado
Common-law marriage has been legal in Colorado since 1877, and the requirements are fundamental. Your relationship is recognized as a common-law marriage in Colorado base on a number of factors, including but no limited to:
Open a joint back account
Use the term “spouse” or “wife” or “husband” in public
Wear wedding rings
Use the same last name
Share the expenses and household duties
File Joint Tax Returns
Put the other person in the relationship on your health insurance
Consent to the marriage
Tell friends and family you are married
Are 18 years or older, or have received consent if 16 or 17 years of age
Are unmarried
Evidence To Prove Common-Law Marriage
Your Golden, CO, common-law marriage lawyer will need to gather evidence to prove the marriage exists before you obtain a divorce. Numerous pieces of evidence are required for these cases. Some possible evidence includes proof of cohabitation, shared bills, joint tax returns, joint bank accounts, and jointly-owned property. In addition, your attorney can show that you celebrate anniversaries and refer to each other as husband or wife in public.
If you held a commitment ceremony, you could also use that as evidence. In addition, your attorney might interview friends and family to prove that you acted as a married couple. If your lawyer can prove that you were in a common-law marriage, you can then take steps to end the marriage.

## Spousal Support Lawyer in Boulder County Colorado

Alimony and Spousal Support in Golden, CO
You were prepared for the emotional impact of your divorce, but the financial impact might have taken you by surprise. You’ve become accustomed to a certain standard of living while married, and now, you’re having a hard time making ends meet. Fortunately, you can file a petition for alimony or request a modification for spousal maintenance.
Spousal support was created to help men and women who didn’t work outside of the home during the marriage or who make significantly less money than their former partners. Numerous factors go into the size of the support payment, including the length of the marriage and the income disparity. Contact our Golden alimony and spousal support lawyers to find out if you’re eligible. We can also calculate the amount of money that the other party owes you in spousal support.
Types of Alimony in Colorado
Our Golden alimony and spousal support lawyers can help you apply for:
Temporary maintenance
Rehabilitative maintenance
Reimbursement maintenance
Permanent maintenance
Consult with us today to learn more about your options for alimony.
Straight Shooters – You’ve made an important decision in your life. We respect you for that. You can count on us to give you the honest (sometimes hard) truth about what to expect on the road ahead so that you can be prepared in every way possible.
Because Your Family and Happiness Are at Stake – The smoother and fairer this process goes, the better the post-divorce interactions tend to be. This is better for everyone involved.
Aspects of Maintenance We Assist You With
If you are currently going through a divorce, your Golden alimony and spousal support lawyer can help you get temporary support. These payments can continue through the divorce. When the divorce is finalized, you can transition to another alimony type. Often, the transition is made to rehabilitative support payments. If you receive rehabilitative support, you’ll continue to get payments until you become financially independent. Thus, once you get a stable job, the payments will end.
Reimbursement support is also an option. The judge might grant this if you paid for professional certificates or education expenses. This alimony allows the other party to pay you back and will end once you’re paid in full.
Finally, there is permanent alimony. As the name suggests, this goes on forever. However, it’s only granted in exceptional circumstances. For instance, if you have a chronic illness or disability, you might qualify for permanent support.
Consult with a Golden alimony and spousal support lawyer if you want to modify the agreement. The attorney can review your case to see if you’re eligible for a modification. If you are, your attorney can file the necessary paperwork.
Calculating Spousal Support In Colorado
Your Golden, CO, alimony, and spousal support lawyer can negotiate maintenance payments for you or represent you in court. If the case goes to court, the judge will consider various factors to determine your eligibility and the amount of the support order. First, you must have been married for a minimum of three years unless you meet specific requirements.
Then, the judge will consider the income of both parties, including the potential income. Other factors include employability, property distribution, child support payments, and lifestyle during the marriage. In addition, both parties’ age and health factor into the decision. Finally, the judge will determine if one spouse should provide support so the other could get an education and work.

When to Get a Prenuptial or Postnuptial Agreement
A prenuptial agreement is a contract between two people who plan to marry. Many people hesitate to discuss this planning tool with their future spouses for fear of offending them before marriage. However, an open discussion about assets and what each person expects in the event of a breakup and divorce can lead to a trust-filled relationship.
So you got married without a prenuptial agreement? You can still enter into a postnuptial agreement to document how you have agreed to divide property in the event of a divorce.
The main benefit of a postnuptial agreement is to keep any property you owned before the marriage as non-marital and separate from property acquired during the marriage. Over time, assets tend to shift around and get commingled, and the postnuptial agreement will help document the non-marital assets.
Highly Reviewed & Rated – Superb rating by respected legal website Avvo, and highly rated on Google. See some of our client reviews below.
Straight Shooters –Creating an enforceable marital agreement is critical. If it isn’t enforceable, the judge can throw it out when the marriage ends. Thus, your agreement must be in writing, and both parties must voluntarily sign it. In addition, both sides must exchange financial disclosures and have the ability to discuss the document with a prenup or postnuptial agreements lawyer. You can count on us to give you the honest (sometimes hard) truth about what to expect on the road ahead so that you can be prepared in every way possible.

However, you also realize that life can change in an instant, and there might come a time when you decide to part ways. If that happens, you want it to be as easy as possible. That’s where a prenup or postnuptial agreement can help. These marriage agreements allow you to protect your property and interests in the case of divorce. Then, you can feel secure in your marriage.
Prenuptial and Postnuptial Agreements
There are specific requirements that must be adhered to for executing the prenuptial agreement before the wedding date for the agreement to be valid. These requirements are set forth in Colorado’s Uniform Premarital Agreement Act. Our family law attorneys will help you create a document tailored to your specific situation that can save time and legal fees in the event of a divorce.
Items that our family law attorneys may suggest to include in a postnuptial agreement are:
Alimony award limitations or exclusions to prevent expensive litigation in the event of a divorce
Penalties and attorney’s fees awards in the event the agreement is challenged by the spouse
Specific asset distributions to avoid a judge dividing assets unsatisfactorily
Assets earmarked for children, especially from a prior marriage
Division of assets in the event of separation with no divorce
We understand that people in different situations have different needs and concerns, and we help them find their way.
Creating, or even discussing, a postnuptial agreement with your spouse is not an admission that your marriage will end in divorce. However, knowing that divorce is a reality for over fifty (50) percent of married couples can help the two of you come to the table in a reasonable, professional manner to consider such an agreement. Perhaps you have precious non-marital assets that need protecting. Maybe you just want to hammer out a fair deal on alimony while you and your spouse are both of rational minds.
Divorces involving individuals with high net worth can be more complicated than most, which is why you should retain a Colorado family law attorney with experience in representing business owners, public figures, and other higher-income clients. ## Child Custody Attorneys​ – Lakewood, CO

Child Custody Attorneys in Lakewood, CO
Our Lakewood, CO Family Law Attorneys are here for your Divorce and Child Custody needs.
Child Custody Attorneys in Lakewood, CO
The issue of child custody holds significant weight in a divorce, and it often becomes a matter of contention between parents who strive to secure their parental rights and involvement in their child’s life. At our law firm in Lakewood, CO, our child custody attorney comprehends the legal and emotional complexities involved in such cases. We can support you in surmounting obstacles and achieving an outcome that prioritizes your child’s welfare.
Our initial approach involves collaborating with the other parent to draft a custody agreement. However, if required, we are prepared to take the case to court. To explore your options, please reach out to our Lakewood child custody lawyers today.
Consider Joint Custody: Is it the Right Choice for You and Your Child?
When it comes to child custody, parents commonly receive joint physical and legal custody, which entails shared responsibility for the child’s physical and emotional well-being. However, this option is ideal for parents who can work together amicably, make decisions jointly, create a supportive environment for the child, communicate effectively, and maintain open lines of communication between the child and the other parent at all times.
In Colorado, child custody typically falls into two categories. Firstly, there is physical custody, which pertains to where the child primarily resides. When parents live close to each other, physical custody is often split, allowing the child to move between homes. However, if parents live far apart, dividing custody can pose challenges, particularly when they are in different school districts. In such situations our child custody lawyers can assist in devising a physical custody plan that enables both parents to spend time with their child without adding undue stress to the situation.
Legal custody also refers to the parent authorized to make decisions for the child, such as selecting their school and medical treatments. Joint legal custody is the most common arrangement, even if one parent has physical custody more frequently than the other.
If you’re facing a custody dispute, it’s crucial to seek legal advice from an experienced child custody lawyer who can assess your unique circumstances and provide guidance on the most appropriate course of action. Our Lakewood, Colorado child custody lawyers are well-versed in joint custody and other custody options and can help you determine the best approach for your family. Contact us today to schedule a consultation.

## Child Custody Modifications – Arvada CO
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/child-custody-modifications-arvada-co/

Child Custody Modification in Arvada, CO
The Drake Law Firm, P.C. Guides Parents in Navigating the Complex Landscape of Child Custody Modifications, Advocating for Fair and Equitable Solutions in the Best Interests of the Children.
Child Custody Modification in Arvada, CO.
Our custody modification attorneys in Arvada, CO, are skilled in assisting parents with modifying existing child custody and parenting time agreements. Our firm possesses a thorough understanding of Colorado’s laws and regulations concerning child custody and the legal intricacies of making such modifications. We offer valuable guidance and representation to parents in Arvada who are looking to revise the terms of their current custody arrangements.
Our custody modification attorney can support a range of issues, from applying to change the primary residence of the child to seeking increased parenting time, or adjusting the terms of an existing parenting plan. We provide assistance in navigating the legal system, which includes preparing and filing necessary documents, negotiating with the other parent or their legal counsel, and advocating for clients in court settings. Discover more about legal custody and visitation modifications in Colorado, including:
How to change child custody agreements
Child custody orders can be modified if circumstances change, even after an initial arrangement is set following a separation or divorce. This can happen anytime before the child turns 19, unless the child goes away to college or is otherwise emancipated. To initiate a modification, one parent must request it through the court, often with the assistance of a family law attorney.
Requesting Legal Custody Modifications:
A judge will consider modifying the custody order if some conditions are met:
The parents have come to a mutual agreement regarding the situation.
The child has become a fully integrated member of the moving party’s family, with the consent of the other parent.
The primary residential parent intends to move with the child.
The child’s present environment is detrimental to their physical health or emotional development, and the advantages of changing their environment outweigh the potential harm of such a change.
Parenting Time Modifications:
Visitation modifications don’t always require a “change in circumstances,” unlike child support adjustments. The primary criteria for altering parenting time is the “best interest of the child” standard. This means the court can make changes if it believes they serve the children’s best interests. However, to modify the actual residential custody of a child, the criteria is typically an “endangerment” standard, addressing either physical or emotional harm.
As children approach 15 or 16 years old, courts tend to give more consideration to their preferences regarding visitation modifications, but not always. These adjustments to visitation or custody can be made until the child reaches the age of 19, goes away to college or is otherwise emancipated.
Children aging and their evolving preferences regarding time spent with each parent
Alterations in the circumstances or relationships of the parents
Desire of either parent to spend more time with the children
Ineffectiveness of the current schedule, whether because of logistical challenges or issues with one of the parents, like substance abuse, mental health concerns, or other environmental factors that negatively impact the children
If these conditions are satisfied and the judge agrees, they have the authority to modify the child custody order. This process underscores the flexibility of child custody arrangements to adapt to changing life situations, ensuring the child’s needs and well-being remain a priority.
Emergency Child Custody Modifications:
According to C.R.S. § 14-10-129(4), a parent can file an emergency motion to limit the other parent’s time with their child if there’s an immediate risk of danger. This kind of motion is serious and should be used only when absolutely necessary. It’s crucial to work with a lawyer who understands what the court considers an immediate danger, as using this motion inappropriately can harm your reputation in court.
For the motion to succeed, you must demonstrate that the child is in imminent physical or emotional danger. The court has the authority to decide whether the other parent’s actions genuinely pose a risk to the child. A hearing will be held within 14 days of filing the motion, where both parents can present their evidence and arguments. After this, the court will determine whether to approve, modify, or reject the motion.

## Child Support – Lakewood, CO
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/child-support-attorneys-lakewood/

Child Support in Colorado
Most parents dealing with a separation or dissolution of marriage proceedings quickly encounter a system built around one central question: what financial support does the child need, and who pays it? Under Colorado law, child support is not discretionary. Both parents are legally obligated to support their child in proportion to their respective incomes, regardless of marital status. Understanding how that obligation is calculated — and what happens when circumstances change — is where to start.
Talk to a Child Support Lawyer Now
Colorado governs child support through C.R.S. § 14-10-115, which establishes the Income Shares Model as the mandatory calculation framework. This statute, along with the Colorado Child Support Guidelines periodically updated by the Colorado Child Support Commission, defines which income sources count, what adjustments are allowed, and when a court may depart from the standard formula. Significant updates to the guidelines took effect March 1, 2026, under House Bill 25-1159, and apply to all orders entered or modified on or after that date.
Colorado's Legal Framework for Child Support
The primary statute governing child support in Colorado is C.R.S. § 14-10-115. It establishes mandatory calculation worksheets, defines which income sources are included, identifies allowable adjustments, and sets out when courts may deviate from the guideline amount. Child support cases are handled in the district courts of each county and may arise in several contexts:
As part of a dissolution of marriage proceeding
As part of a legal separation
Within an Allocation of Parental Responsibilities (APR) case
As a standalone action through Colorado Child Support Services (CSS), an agency within the Colorado Department of Human Services
Before a support order can be entered against a legal father, legal paternity establishment is a prerequisite before child support can be ordered. The Drake Law Firm, PC handles paternity matters as part of its family law practice.
Statutory Definitions of Income
Colorado defines gross income broadly under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(5)(a). Includable income sources encompass wages, salaries, commissions, bonuses, dividends, severance pay, pensions, interest, trust income, Social Security benefits (including disability), workers’ compensation, unemployment insurance, and income from self-employment or operation of a business. Non-recurring or extraordinary income — such as a one-time capital gain — may be treated differently by the court depending on whether it reflects the parent’s ongoing financial capacity.
Income imputation rules apply when a parent is voluntarily unemployed or underemployed. In these situations, the court may attribute income based on the parent’s historical earnings, occupational qualifications, and the prevailing job market.
Certain items are excluded from the gross income calculation, including means-tested public assistance (such as TANF and SSI), child support received for children from other relationships, and income of the parent’s new spouse or partner.
How Child Support Is Calculated: The Income Shares Model
Colorado uses the Income Shares Model, which is based on the principle that a child should receive the same proportion of parental income as if the parents lived together. The calculation follows a structured worksheet process using the state’s official Child Support Schedule — a table of presumed combined support obligations based on combined adjusted gross income and number of children.
Step 1 — Determine Each Parent’s Gross Monthly Income
The court starts with each parent’s gross monthly income from all sources. For W-2 employees this is straightforward. For self-employed parents, net business income after ordinary and necessary business expenses (but before personal tax deductions) is used. For parents with variable income, courts often average the prior 12 to 36 months of earnings.
Step 2 — Calculate Combined Adjusted Gross Income
The two parents’ gross incomes are added together to arrive at the Combined Adjusted Gross Income (CAGI). Adjustments may include amounts paid for health insurance premiums for the child and child support obligations for children from prior relationships.
Step 3 — Look Up the Basic Child Support Obligation
The CAGI and the number of children are entered into the Colorado Child Support Schedule to determine the Basic Child Support Obligation (BCSO). This schedule is codified in C.R.S. § 14-10-115(7)(b) and reflects estimated expenditures on children at various income levels based on economic research. The 2026 updated schedule covers combined monthly adjusted gross incomes of up to $40,000 — increased from the prior $30,000 cap — and reflects current costs of raising a child based on the Betson-Rothbarth Study and 2023 Bureau of Labor Statistics data. For combined incomes above $40,000, courts retain discretion in determining the appropriate amount.
Step 4 — Add Work-Related Child Care and Health Insurance
Work-related child care costs and the cost of the child’s health insurance premium are added to the BCSO to produce the Total Child Support Obligation. The health insurance figure used is the cost of the child’s portion of the premium only — not the total family premium. Coverage through public programs such as Medicaid or CHP+ is also accounted for under this step. These are actual, documented costs — not estimates.
Step 5 — Apportion Between Parents
Each parent’s share of the Total Child Support Obligation is proportional to their contribution to the CAGI. For example, if Parent A earns 60% of the combined income, Parent A is responsible for 60% of the obligation. The residential parent is presumed to spend their share directly; the non-residential parent’s share is the payment amount.
Parenting Time and Child Support
For orders entered or modified on or after March 1, 2026, Colorado has eliminated the previous “93-overnight cliff” under the updated C.R.S. § 14-10-115(8). Prior law only recognized shared parenting time for child support purposes once a parent reached 93 or more overnights per year — meaning a parent with 90 overnights received the same credit as a parent with zero. That threshold no longer applies.
Under the 2026 framework, every overnight is formally recognized through a graduated Parenting Time Table. A parent receives incremental credit for parenting time expenses starting from the first overnight, scaled proportionally across the full range of parenting time. The prior dual-worksheet structure (Worksheet A for sole custody, Worksheet B for shared custody) has been replaced by a unified calculation: the basic support obligation is drawn from the standard schedule, allocated between parents in proportion to their adjusted gross incomes, and then each parent receives a parenting time credit based on their share of overnights as listed in the Parenting Time Table. The annual overnight count comes directly from the parenting schedule established in a parenting plan or custody order, making accurate documentation of that schedule essential.
At equal parenting time (182 or more overnights each), the parenting time credit is maximized, though a support obligation may still exist if there is a meaningful income disparity between the parents.
For very low-income parents, the Self-Support Reserve (SSR) and Low-Income Adjustment provisions may affect the final obligation. The SSR is calculated at 29 hours per week at the state minimum wage multiplied by 50 weeks and divided by 12 — a figure that adjusts as Colorado’s minimum wage changes. Parents whose income falls between $650 per month and the SSR are subject to a revised low-income schedule, and those whose income exceeds the SSR but remains near minimum wage have their total support obligation capped as a percentage of income.
Deviation from the Guidelines
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(3)(b), a court may deviate from the guideline amount if application of the formula would be inequitable, unjust, or inappropriate in a specific case. Grounds for deviation include:
Extraordinary medical needs of the child
Educational costs of the child
Special needs of the child
Financial resources of the child
Travel expenses for parenting time
Any deviation must be supported by written findings stating the amount that would have been ordered under the guidelines and why deviation serves the child’s best interests.
Establishing a Child Support Order in Colorado
Through Divorce or Allocation of Parental Responsibilities
When parents divorce or legal separation involves minor children, the court will enter a child support order as part of the final decree. The parties must file a completed Child Support Worksheet along with sworn financial disclosures. Colorado Rule of Civil Procedure 16.2 requires both parties to exchange mandatory financial disclosures, including three years of tax returns, two months of pay stubs, and documentation of all assets and debts. Working with Colorado child support attorneys during this stage helps ensure disclosures are complete and the worksheet accurately reflects each parent’s financial circumstances.
Through Colorado Child Support Services
Colorado Child Support Services (CSS), administered at the county level through local Child Support Units, provides services to establish, collect, and enforce child support orders. Services are available to any parent regardless of income and are required for families receiving TANF benefits. CSS can establish paternity, locate the other parent, establish a support order through the courts or through an administrative process, and collect payments through the Colorado Family Support Registry (CFSR).
During a pending divorce or APR case, either party may request temporary child support via a motion and financial affidavit. Temporary orders remain in effect until the court enters a final order at the permanent hearing. The temporary amount is calculated using the same guideline formula.
Payment, Collection, and the Colorado Family Support Registry
All child support payments ordered by Colorado courts are made through the Colorado Family Support Registry (CFSR), administered by the Colorado Department of Human Services. Direct payments between parents are not recognized as satisfying a court-ordered support obligation unless the order specifically authorizes them — paying directly to the other parent risks having those payments treated as gifts in any subsequent enforcement action.
Income Withholding Orders (IWO) are issued automatically in most cases under C.R.S. § 14-14-111.5. The IWO directs the paying parent’s employer to deduct support from wages and remit directly to the CFSR. IWOs can also be served on unemployment benefits and some other income sources. Parents who are self-employed or have variable income may be required to make direct payments to the CFSR on a scheduled basis.
Enforcement of Child Support in Colorado
When a parent fails to pay court-ordered child support, Colorado law provides a broad array of enforcement tools. Enforcement actions can be initiated by the receiving parent, by their attorney, or by Colorado Child Support Services.
Administrative Enforcement Remedies
C.R.S. § 26-13-122 and related statutes authorize CSS to take the following administrative actions without a court hearing:
License suspension: driver’s licenses, professional licenses, recreational licenses (hunting, fishing), and business licenses
Tax intercept: federal and Colorado state income tax refunds
Credit bureau reporting: delinquent support reported to consumer credit agencies once arrears exceed a threshold
Bank account seizure (FIDM): CSS can freeze and seize funds in bank accounts through the Financial Institution Data Match program
Lottery and gambling intercept: winnings above the statutory threshold are intercepted
Passport denial: the federal Office of Child Support Enforcement (OCSE) denies or revokes passports when arrears exceed $2,500
Judicial Enforcement Remedies
A party or CSS may also seek judicial enforcement through a motion for contempt of court (C.R.C.P. 107). If the court finds a parent in contempt for willful non-payment, remedies include fines, a remedial or punitive jail sentence, and entry of a judgment for arrears. Judgments for unpaid child support bear interest at the statutory rate. In egregious cases, criminal prosecution under C.R.S. § 14-14-104 (criminal nonsupport) may apply.
Interstate Enforcement — UIFSA
Colorado has adopted the Uniform Interstate Family Support Act (UIFSA), codified at C.R.S. § 14-5-101 et seq. Under UIFSA, a Colorado order can be registered and enforced in any other state, and orders from other states can be registered in Colorado. The issuing state retains continuing exclusive jurisdiction over the support order as long as a party or the child remains in that state.
Modifying Child Support in Colorado
A child support order may be modified when there has been a substantial and continuing change of circumstances that results in at least a 10% change in the monthly support amount under C.R.S. § 14-10-122(1)(a). This 10% threshold is the operative standard — a court will not grant a modification unless the recalculated amount reflects that change. The passage of time alone is generally not sufficient grounds for a judicial modification without a corresponding shift in financial circumstances or parenting time.
For cases managed by Colorado Child Support Services, CSS conducts an administrative review every three years. However, even in those reviews, a modification will only be entered if the recalculation produces at least a 10% change in the obligation amount.
What Constitutes a Substantial Change
Examples of changes that may support a modification petition include:
Significant increase or decrease in either parent’s income (including job loss, promotion, or career change)
A change in the number of overnights the child spends with each parent
The child gaining or losing health insurance coverage through a parent’s employer
Substantial changes in work-related child care costs
The child developing significant medical or educational needs not previously ordered • Emancipation of one child in a multi-child order, requiring recalculation for remaining children
The Modification Process
The requesting parent files a Motion to Modify Child Support along with an updated Child Support Worksheet and updated financial disclosures. If the parties agree on the new amount, a Stipulation and Proposed Order can be submitted for the court’s approval. If not, the matter proceeds to a hearing where both parties present current financial information.
The modification is effective from the date of filing of the motion — not the date of the hearing — so prompt filing is important. Until a court enters a modified order, the original obligation remains in full force. A parent experiencing sudden financial hardship, such as a layoff, should file the modification motion immediately rather than waiting to see if circumstances improve.
Duration and Termination of Child Support in Colorado
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(13), child support in Colorado terminates by operation of law when the last or only child covered by the order turns 19. No court motion is required for termination in that circumstance. However, if the order covers multiple children and only one reaches age 19, the obligation does not automatically reduce — the paying parent must file a motion to modify so the court can recalculate the amount for the remaining children.
Additional exceptions that may extend support beyond age 19 include:
The child has not yet graduated from high school at age 19 — support continues until graduation or age 21, whichever occurs first
The child is mentally or physically disabled — the court may order support beyond age 19 upon a showing of need
The parties have agreed in writing to extend support for post-secondary education or other purposes — Colorado courts cannot order a parent to pay college expenses over their objection, but such provisions are enforceable as contract terms if voluntarily agreed upon and incorporated into the court order
Support also terminates upon the child’s emancipation before age 19, which may occur through marriage, military enlistment, or a court order.
Tax Considerations
Child support payments are tax-neutral under both federal and Colorado state law. The paying parent may not deduct child support payments, and the receiving parent does not report them as taxable income. For divorce decrees entered after December 31, 2018, Colorado spousal maintenance is also tax-neutral at both the federal and state level under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act — the payer may not deduct it and the recipient does not report it as income. Both obligations are treated the same way for tax purposes under current law.
By default, the parent with the majority of overnights has the right to claim the child as a dependent for purposes of the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit. However, parents may agree — or the court may order — that the non-residential parent claim the child in alternating years or under other arrangements, formalized through IRS Form 8332.
Child Support and Paternity in Colorado
Before a child support order can be entered against a legal father, Colorado paternity law governs how legal fatherhood is determined. In Colorado, paternity is established in one of three ways:
The parents are married at the time of birth (the marital presumption under C.R.S. § 19-4-105)
Both parents sign a Voluntary Acknowledgment of Paternity (VAP) at the hospital or through the Colorado Vital Records office
A court or administrative order following genetic testing adjudicates paternity
Once legal paternity determination is complete, either parent may seek a child support order. The Colorado Child Support Services program provides administrative paternity establishment services at no cost to the applicant.
Frequently Asked Questions About Child Support
Is child support taxable in Colorado?
No, child support is tax-neutral. The parent receiving the payments does not report them as taxable income, and the parent paying support cannot claim them as a tax deduction on their state or federal return.
Does child support count as income?
For tax purposes, child support does not count as income. However, lenders may consider it as income when you apply for a mortgage or car loan, and state agencies may count it when determining eligibility for certain public assistance programs.
How is child support calculated in Colorado?
Colorado uses the Income Shares Model, which estimates the amount parents would have spent on the child if they were still together. The court inputs both parents’ gross monthly incomes, the number of overnight visits, and expenses like health insurance and childcare into a statutory formula to determine the final amount.
How to apply for child support?
You can apply directly through the Colorado Child Support Services (CSS) website or your county’s Department of Human Services. Alternatively, if you are going through a divorce or custody case, a Colorado child support lawyer at The Drake Law Firm, PC can file the necessary motions with the court to establish an order as part of your case.
What happens if a parent doesn't pay child support in Colorado?
Colorado takes non-payment seriously, and enforcement measures can include wage garnishment, interception of tax refunds, and suspension of driver’s or professional licenses. In severe cases, a motion for contempt of court may result in fines or jail time for the non-paying parent.
How The Drake Law Firm, PC Can Help with Child Support in Colorado
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents clients in child support matters at all stages — from initial establishment through modification and enforcement.
The firm’s attorneys bring direct experience with Colorado’s Income Shares Model, the financial disclosure requirements of C.R.C.P. 16.2, and the practical realities of income withholding, CSS enforcement actions, and post-decree modifications in Jefferson County and the surrounding district courts served by our family law offices in Colorado. The firm offers both non-adversarial resolution strategies and courtroom advocacy when litigation is required.
Taking the Next Steps for Your Children
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents parents in child support matters throughout Colorado. Whether you are establishing a support order for the first time, seeking support modification after a change in income or parenting time, or enforcing an order that isn’t being followed, our attorneys work to protect your child’s financial security and your rights under Colorado law.

## Adoption in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/adoption/

Adoption in Colorado
Are you ready to add to your family through adoption? Once the process is finalized, you’ll be the child’s legal parent, meaning you’ll have the same rights and responsibilities as a biological parent. You are excited to get to that point but also afraid of the complicated adoption process. That’s where our Colorado adoption lawyer can help. We are experienced in international, private domestic, stepparent, and foster care adoptions and can assist you with the case.
Our firm enjoys helping families grow through adoption, and we won’t rest until your family is whole. Contact us to consult about your adoption case.
Types of Adoptions in Colorado
Our adoption lawyer can assist with all types of adoptions. These include:
Foster care adoption
Stepparent adoption
Contact us today if you are interested in completing your family through adoption.
Adoption From Foster Care
With hundreds of children in foster care waiting for homes, adoption from foster care is a popular choice for Colorado families. First, you have to become a foster parent. In addition, you have to pass a background check and a home study. The state also requires that you undergo training before you can take in a foster child.
After becoming a foster parent, you can begin the adoption process. At this point, it’s wise to consult with an adoption lawyer. Your lawyer can prepare the paperwork and strategize for any hurdles you might encounter during the process.
Stepparent Adoption
Have you relished in your role as a stepparent and want to formalize the bond by adopting the child? You might be eligible for a stepparent adoption if the biological parent has refused to pay child support for at least a year. Also, you can file for a stepparent adoption if the parent abandoned the child or passed away. Finally, the other parent can agree to the adoption and terminate his or her parental rights.
Your stepchild must consent to the adoption if he or she is over 12 years old. In addition, your spouse will need to agree to the adoption for it to move forward. Finally, you will need consent from the other parent, or you’ll have to prove that the court should terminate the parental rights and grant the adoption.
Your Colorado adoption lawyer can assist with this process. Our firm will gather evidence to support your petition for adoption and represent you during the hearing. Contact us today to learn more about stepparent adoption in Colorado.
Can Single People Adopt Children?
Both single individuals and married couples can adopt in Colorado. If you are married, you and your spouse must both be on the petition to adopt. Otherwise, the petition will not be granted. While these are the general rules, various adoption agencies can set their own guidelines. For instance, some agencies require that couples are married for a minimum of two years before petitioning for adoption. Your adoption lawyer from The Drake Law Firm, P.C. can go over the conditions for various agencies to help you choose one that fits your situation.
Will a Criminal Record Prevent You From Adopting?
You will have to undergo a home study and background check during the adoption process. If your background check brings up a history of child abuse, domestic violence, assault, felony-drug convictions, or sexual crimes, your petition will likely be denied. However, you can still get approved if you are a one-time non-violent offender, and the crime didn’t include a child. Contact a adoption lawyer to review your criminal history to see if you’re likely to get approved.
Colorado Adoption FAQs
Can I adopt my grandchild without a lawyer?
Adopting a grandchild involves permanently terminating the biological parents’ rights, a legal standard that is difficult to meet without professional help. We strongly advise against “DIY” efforts in these cases; a mistake in the paperwork can result in the adoption being denied or challenged years later.
How much does an adoption lawyer cost?
Legal fees depend heavily on whether the adoption is contested by a biological parent or if it is a streamlined, uncontested process. Contact The Drake Law Firm, PC to schedule a consultation for an accurate quote based on your specific family situation.
What does an adoption lawyer do?
An adoption lawyer manages the complex filings required to terminate biological parental rights and finalize the adoption decree. We specifically handle background checks, consent hearings, and ensure that the “chain of custody” is legally secure so the adoption cannot be overturned in the future.
Do I need a lawyer to adopt my stepchild in Colorado?
While you technically can attempt a stepparent adoption without a lawyer, strict background checks and the termination of the biological parent’s rights make the process complex. A single filing error can restart the entire timeline, so legal counsel is highly recommended to ensure the process is smooth and permanent.

## Colorado Spousal Support
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/alimony/

Alimony in Colorado
The Drake Law Firm, P.C. helps men and women petition to receive temporary, rehabilitative, reimbursement, and permanent alimony.
Colorado law uses the term spousal maintenance — not alimony or spousal support — to describe court-ordered financial support paid by one spouse to the other following a dissolution of marriage. All three terms refer to the same legal obligation and are used interchangeably in practice. The governing statute is C.R.S. § 14-10-114.
Spousal maintenance is not awarded automatically. A spouse seeking maintenance must request it, and the court must find that the requesting spouse lacks sufficient property to meet their reasonable needs and is either unable to support themselves through appropriate employment or is the primary caregiver of a child whose circumstances make outside employment inappropriate.
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents both maintenance-seeking and maintenance-paying spouses throughout Jefferson County, Denver, and the greater Front Range — handling maintenance determinations as part of broader divorce proceedings and as standalone post-decree modification matters.
Eligibility for Spousal Maintenance in Colorado
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-114(3), a court may award maintenance only after finding that the requesting spouse:
Lacks sufficient property, including any share of marital property awarded in the decree, to provide for their reasonable needs; and
Is unable to support themselves through appropriate employment, or is the primary caregiver of a child whose age or condition makes outside employment inappropriate.
Both conditions must be satisfied before the court will consider the amount or duration of a maintenance award. If the requesting spouse has sufficient property or is capable of self-support, the court will not reach the advisory guidelines.
The Colorado spousal maintenance attorneys at The Drake Law Firm, PC represent clients on both sides of this threshold determination — both establishing eligibility and contesting claims where the statutory conditions are not met.
Factors courts consider when determining maintenance amount and duration (C.R.S. § 14-10-114(3)(b)):
The financial resources of the requesting spouse, including property awarded in the divorce
The requesting spouse’s ability to meet their needs independently
The paying spouse’s ability to meet their own needs while paying maintenance
The marital standard of living
The length of the marriage
The age, physical condition, and financial condition of each spouse
The time and expense necessary for the requesting spouse to acquire education or training
Significant economic disparity created by either spouse’s contributions to the marriage, including homemaking
Types of Spousal Maintenance in Colorado
Colorado courts may award spousal maintenance in different forms depending on the stage of the proceedings and the circumstances of the parties. The nature, amount, and duration of each type is governed by C.R.S. § 14-10-114 and, for post-decree orders, the advisory guidelines tied to marriage length and income.
Temporary Spousal Maintenance
Temporary maintenance is awarded during the pendency of the dissolution proceedings before a final order is entered. It addresses the immediate financial disruption caused by separation — covering housing, living expenses, and related costs while the case is active. Temporary maintenance terminates automatically upon entry of the final decree.
Long-Term Spousal Maintenance
Post-decree maintenance is awarded as part of the final dissolution order and runs for a defined term scaled to the length of the marriage under the advisory guidelines, or for an indefinite period in marriages of 20 years or longer where the court finds an ongoing support need. Long-term maintenance is the form most directly governed by the C.R.S. § 14-10-114 formula and duration table.
High-Income Spousal Maintenance Disputes
When combined household income exceeds $240,000 per year, the advisory guidelines do not apply and the court exercises full discretion. These cases turn heavily on competing expert analysis, business income documentation, and the parties’ respective standards of living during the marriage
Spousal Maintenance in Long-Term Marriages
Marriages of 20 years or longer fall outside the standard advisory duration caps and open the door to indefinite maintenance awards. Courts in these cases give significant weight to the economic disparity created by the marriage, each spouse’s age and employability, and the standard of living the parties maintained.
How Spousal Maintenance Is Calculated in Colorado
For couples with a combined adjusted gross income of $240,000 or less per year, Colorado courts apply statutory advisory guidelines under C.R.S. § 14-10-114(3)(b)(I). The guidelines produce a monthly maintenance amount based on both parties’ adjusted gross incomes and are designed to create a predictable baseline — though courts retain discretion to deviate based on the statutory factors above.
For couples with combined income exceeding $240,000 per year, the advisory guidelines do not apply and the court exercises full discretion based on the factors in C.R.S. § 14-10-114(3)(b).
For a full breakdown of the guideline formula and how it applies to specific income scenarios, see Colorado spousal maintenance calculator.
Duration of Spousal Maintenance in Colorado
The advisory duration guidelines under C.R.S. § 14-10-114(3)(b)(II) scale maintenance length to the length of the marriage. The advisory duration begins at 31% of the marriage length for a 3-year marriage and scales up gradually, capping at 50% for marriages of 12.5 years or longer.
Length of Marriage
Advisory Duration (% of marriage length)

Court discretion — may be indefinite
These are advisory, not mandatory. Courts may deviate based on the statutory factors, and parties may agree to a different term in a separation agreement.
Maintenance and property division are determined separately but are financially interconnected. A substantial property award to one spouse may reduce or eliminate the need for ongoing maintenance, and Colorado courts consider the marital property each spouse receives before determining whether a maintenance award is appropriate. The Drake Law Firm, PC serves clients across Colorado with family law offices throughout Jefferson County, Denver, and the greater Front Range.
For a full explanation of how Colorado divides marital assets, see equitable distribution of marital assets.
Modification and Termination of Spousal Maintenance
Modification
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-122, a maintenance order may be modified upon a showing of a substantial and continuing change in circumstances that makes the existing order unfair. Common grounds include a significant change in either party’s income, job loss, disability, or retirement.
Modification is not available if the original separation agreement expressly waived the right to seek modification.
Automatic Termination
Maintenance terminates automatically upon:
The death of either party
The remarriage of the recipient spouse (C.R.S. § 14-10-122(2))
The date specified in the order
Cohabitation
Colorado does not provide for automatic termination upon cohabitation. However, cohabitation that results in reduced financial need may be grounds to seek modification under the substantial change standard.
How is spousal maintenance calculated in Colorado?
Colorado applies advisory guidelines under C.R.S. § 14-10-114 to couples with combined adjusted gross income of $240,000 or less per year. The guidelines produce a monthly maintenance figure based on both parties’ adjusted gross incomes. For couples above that threshold, the court exercises full discretion based on the statutory factors. For a detailed breakdown of how the formula works, see Colorado spousal maintenance calculator.
How long does alimony last?
The duration is typically determined by the length of the marriage. Colorado guidelines suggest a term ranging from 31% of the marriage length (for a 3-year marriage) up to 50% (for a 20-year marriage). For marriages lasting longer than 20 years, the court may award support for an indefinite period.
How long does spousal maintenance last in Colorado?
Advisory durations are scaled to the length of the marriage under C.R.S. § 14-10-114(3)(b)(II), beginning at 31% at three years and increasing by 0.165% per month of marriage, up to a cap of 50% at approximately 12.5 years. For marriages of 20 years or longer, the court has discretion to award maintenance for an indefinite period. These durations are advisory — courts may deviate based on the circumstances of each case.
How long does a marriage have to last to qualify for maintenance?
Colorado’s advisory guidelines generally apply to marriages of at least three years. For marriages shorter than three years, maintenance is rarely awarded unless exceptional circumstances prevent a spouse from achieving self-sufficiency — such as a disabling medical condition or the need to care for a young child.
What qualifies a spouse for spousal maintenance in Colorado?
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-114(3), the requesting spouse must demonstrate two things: first, that they lack sufficient property to meet their reasonable needs; and second, that they are either unable to support themselves through appropriate employment or are the primary caregiver of a child whose circumstances make outside employment inappropriate. Both conditions must be met before a court will enter a maintenance award.
What disqualifies a spouse from receiving maintenance?
A spouse will not qualify for maintenance if they have sufficient property — including any share of marital property awarded in the divorce — to meet their reasonable needs, or if they are capable of self-support through appropriate employment and have no caregiving barrier. A spouse who voluntarily leaves the workforce without necessity, or who holds significant separate assets, is unlikely to meet the threshold for an award.
Can either spouse receive spousal maintenance regardless of gender?
Yes. Spousal maintenance under C.R.S. § 14-10-114 is gender-neutral. Either spouse may seek or be ordered to pay maintenance based solely on the financial circumstances of each party and the factors listed in the statute. The higher-earning spouse pays; the lower-earning spouse receives — regardless of gender.
Is spousal maintenance taxable income in Colorado?
For divorces and separation agreements finalized on or after January 1, 2019, spousal maintenance is not taxable income to the recipient and not tax-deductible for the payer under federal law. This is the result of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, which eliminated the prior deductibility rules for agreements executed after December 31, 2018. For divorces finalized before that date, the prior tax treatment — deductible for the payer, taxable to the recipient — may still apply unless the agreement has been modified to adopt the new rules.
Can a spousal maintenance order be modified after the divorce?
Yes. Under C.R.S. § 14-10-122, either party may petition for modification upon demonstrating a substantial and continuing change in circumstances that makes the existing order unfair. Significant income changes for either party — including job loss, promotion, disability, or retirement — are common grounds. Modification is not available if the original order or separation agreement expressly waived that right.
Speak With a Spousal Maintenance Attorney
Spousal maintenance determinations in Colorado turn on financial documentation, marriage history, and how each party’s circumstances are presented under C.R.S. § 14-10-114. Whether you are pursuing a maintenance award or responding to one, the strength of your financial record and legal positioning before the first hearing shapes the range of outcomes available at every stage that follows. To discuss your situation with a member of our team, contact The Drake Law Firm, PC to schedule a case assessment.

## Child Custody in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/child-custody/

Child Custody in Colorado
Most parents searching for custody information in Colorado quickly discover that the state does not use the word ‘custody’ in its family law statutes at all. If you are trying to understand how parenting time or decision-making authority works in Colorado, this is where to start.
Colorado governs these decisions through a framework called the Allocation of Parental Responsibilities (APR), which replaces the traditional terms “custody” and “visitation” with two distinct legal concepts: decision-making responsibility and parenting time. These two components are evaluated and allocated independently under Colorado Revised Statutes Title 14, Article 10.
APR proceedings arise in two primary contexts: as part of a divorce and dissolution of marriage under C.R.S. § 14-10-106, or as a standalone action when parents were never married. In the latter case, establishing paternity in Colorado is typically a prerequisite before APR can be formally addressed by the court.
Decision-Making Responsibility
Decision-making responsibility governs which parent—or both parents jointly—holds the legal authority to make major decisions affecting the child’s life during and after a divorce. While Colorado statute covers various areas, these typically center around the “Big Three”: medical care, education, and religious upbringing. It also frequently addresses the child’s involvement in extracurricular activities.
Joint Decision-Making
Under joint decision-making, both parents share equal authority over major decisions and must confer before implementing significant changes in the child’s life. Joint decision-making is the statutory presumption in Colorado. It does not dictate the parenting time schedule and is evaluated independently of where the child physically resides.
C.R.S. § 14-10-124(1.5) permits the court to allocate decision-making independently across categories. For example, one parent may be granted sole authority over educational decisions while the parties retain joint authority over healthcare.
Sole Decision-Making
Sole decision-making grants one parent exclusive authority without requiring consultation with the other. Courts award it when joint decision-making would endanger the child’s physical health or significantly impair emotional development. Statutory grounds include:
A history of domestic violence or child abuse (C.R.S. § 14-10-124(4)(a))
Substance abuse that impairs parenting capacity
A documented inability of the parties to cooperate without conflict
Even where sole decision-making is ordered, the non-custodial parent generally retains parenting time unless that contact would also endanger the child.
Parenting Time
Parenting time defines the physical schedule under which the child resides with and is cared for by each parent. It is determined independently of decision-making responsibility.
Equal Parenting Time (50/50)
Colorado courts have moved toward equal parenting time as a general preference when both parents are fit and geographically proximate. Common schedules include the 2-2-3 rotation and alternating week arrangements. Equal parenting time does not eliminate child support obligations—support is calculated based on income differential and number of overnights regardless of schedule symmetry (see managing child support in Colorado for how the Income Shares model applies to equal-time arrangements).
Majority Parenting Time
In majority parenting time arrangements, the child resides primarily with one parent and spends designated time with the other. This structure is common when parents reside in different school districts or when a parent’s employment schedule makes equal time impractical.
Supervised Parenting Time
When the court finds that unsupervised parenting time would endanger the child’s physical or emotional health, it may order supervised parenting time under C.R.S. § 14-10-129. Supervision may be conducted by a designated family member or a professional agency and is typically a transitional arrangement subject to review upon demonstrated behavioral change.
The Best Interests Standard: C.R.S. § 14-10-124
All APR determinations in Colorado are governed by the best interests of the child standard codified at C.R.S. § 14-10-124. Colorado courts do not apply a maternal or paternal preference. The statute enumerates specific factors the court must consider.
Parenting history and caretaking function: The court examines which parent has historically performed caretaking functions—medical appointments, school involvement, daily care routines—and the quality of the parent-child relationship with each parent.
Physical and emotional safety: Any history of child abuse, domestic violence (C.R.S. § 14-10-124(1.5)(b)), neglect, or substance abuse is weighted heavily. A documented history of domestic violence triggers mandatory statutory consideration and may result in restricted or supervised parenting time.
Ability to encourage the other parent’s relationship: Courts explicitly consider which parent is more likely to facilitate frequent and continuing contact between the child and the other parent. A parent who attempts to limit or obstruct the child’s relationship with the other parent—absent legitimate safety concerns—may receive an unfavorable allocation.
Geographic proximity: The physical distance between parents’ residences affects the practical viability of equal time schedules and informs the court’s analysis of what arrangement best supports the child’s routine and schooling. The Drake Law Firm handles APR cases across Colorado’s judicial districts, including cases where parents reside in different counties or regions.
The child’s adjustment: The court considers the child’s adjustment to home, school, and community, and the degree of disruption a particular allocation would cause.
The child’s wishes: A child’s preference is a statutory factor under C.R.S. § 14-10-124(1)(b)(III). There is no fixed age at which preference becomes controlling. Courts weigh preference against the child’s age and maturity, but the judge retains final decision-making authority.
The APR Legal Process in Colorado
Initiating the Case
APR proceedings are initiated by filing a Petition for Allocation of Parental Responsibilities in the district court of the county where the child has resided for at least six months, establishing jurisdiction under the UCCJEA (C.R.S. § 14-13-201). If filed as part of a dissolution proceeding, APR is addressed within that case. The petitioner must submit a proposed parenting plan outlining both decision-making allocation and a parenting time schedule, along with required financial disclosures. The Colorado child custody attorneys at The Drake Law Firm can help ensure your petition and proposed parenting plan are properly prepared from the outset.
Initial Status Conference
Following service, the court schedules an Initial Status Conference to establish the case timeline and procedural deadlines. Where a party demonstrates urgency—such as one parent denying the other access to the child—a temporary orders hearing may be requested at or prior to the ISC.
Temporary orders establish the interim parenting schedule while the case is pending. Courts are reluctant to disrupt arrangements that appear to be working, so temporary orders often carry weight through the final hearing. They address both parenting time and, where applicable, interim decision-making authority.
Mandatory Mediation
Colorado courts require parties to attempt mediation before proceeding to a final orders hearing. C.R.S. § 13-22-311 governs court-ordered mediation. The mediator is a neutral third party; attorneys may attend. Agreements reached in mediation are typically incorporated into stipulated orders and entered as a final judgment.
Parenting Education
Most Colorado judicial districts require both parents to complete a court-approved parenting education course before final orders are entered. Completion is a prerequisite to finalizing the case in most districts
Child and Family Investigators (CFIs)
When contested issues require independent fact-finding, the court may appoint a Child and Family Investigator (CFI) under C.R.S. § 14-10-116.5. The CFI conducts interviews with both parents, the child, and relevant third parties; reviews records; and submits a written report with recommendations to the court. CFI recommendations are not binding, but they are given substantial weight by the judge.
Final Orders Hearing
If mediation does not resolve all issues, the case proceeds to a final orders hearing. The court hears testimony, reviews evidence, and may receive the CFI’s report. The judge issues permanent orders governing decision-making and parenting time, which remain in effect until modified by subsequent court order or until the child reaches the age of majority.
Parenting Plans
A parenting plan is a written document required by Colorado courts that specifies the parenting time schedule, holiday allocations, and decision-making protocols. Required elements include:
The regular parenting time schedule (school year and summer)
Holiday, school break, and vacation schedules
Transportation responsibilities and exchange locations
Communication protocols between parents
Process for resolving future disputes
Colorado courts encourage parents to submit an agreed parenting plan. If no agreement is reached, the court issues its own plan based on the evidence presented.
Modifying an APR Order
An existing APR order may be modified under C.R.S. § 14-10-129. The threshold showing depends on what is being modified.
Decision-making modification requires a showing of a substantial and continuing change in circumstances and that modification is in the child’s best interests. The statute imposes a two-year waiting period after entry of final orders before a decision-making modification may be sought, absent specified emergency circumstances.
Parenting time modification (non-majority) may be sought upon showing the modification serves the child’s best interests, without the two-year waiting period.
Majority parenting time modification requires both the substantial change in circumstances showing and a best-interests analysis. Courts apply greater scrutiny to these modifications due to the disruption they cause to the child’s stability.
Emergency Restrictions on Parenting Time
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-129(4), a party may file a Motion to Restrict Parenting Time when the child is in imminent physical or emotional danger. Upon filing, the court must schedule a hearing within 14 days. This is a high-threshold remedy; filing without adequate factual support can damage credibility with the court and lead to sanctions.
Colorado Child Custody FAQs
How to get custody of a child in Colorado?
To obtain legal custody, formally known as the “Allocation of Parental Responsibilities,” you must file a petition with the district court in the county where the child has resided for at least the last 182 days. The court determines custody based on the “best interests of the child,” so submitting a comprehensive parenting plan is essential for a favorable outcome.
Who claims a child on taxes with 50/50 custody?
Technically, the IRS allows the parent with the higher number of overnight stays to claim the child, but in 50/50 scenarios, parents often rotate the tax deduction every other year. A Colorado child custody lawyer can help draft a specific provision in your parenting plan to ensure this agreement is legally binding and clearly understood by both parties.
What not to say in child custody mediation?
You should avoid badmouthing the other parent, making threats, or focusing solely on money rather than the child’s well-being. Comments that suggest you are using the child to punish your ex can backfire, as mediators look for parents willing to facilitate a positive relationship between the child and the other parent.
How to get full custody of a child?
Because Colorado courts presume that shared parenting is in a child’s best interest, obtaining “full custody”—which usually implies both primary parenting time and sole decision-making authority—is a high legal bar. You typically must prove that shared responsibility would endanger the child physically or emotionally. Since this requires presenting substantial evidence to the court, it is vital to work with an experienced child custody attorney to build your case.
How much does it cost to file for full custody in Colorado?
The court requires a filing fee to open the case, usually over $200, excluding additional costs for serving papers or mandatory mediation. However, if you are seeking full custody in a contested battle, total legal costs can vary widely depending on the complexity of litigation and the evidence required.
Contact The Drake Law Firm, PC
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents parents in Allocation of Parental Responsibilities proceedings throughout Colorado. Whether you are establishing a parenting plan for the first time, seeking to modify an existing order, or navigating a high-conflict custody dispute, our attorneys work to protect your parental rights and your child’s best interests under Colorado law.
Unfit Parents
Sadly, some parents are unfit to raise children. If a parent is an alcoholic, abusive, neglectful, or mentally ill, he or she might be deemed unfit. Then, the other parent can receive sole physical and legal custody. If you think the other parent is unfit, speak to your  child custody lawyer. Your child’s safety and well-being are at risk, so you need to move forward and take action quickly.
Unmarried Fathers
In Colorado, if a child is born to parents who are not married, the mother is automatically granted both full legal and physical custody of the child. The father does not have any custody or visitation rights unless a court order is obtained or if the parents reach an agreement. It’s important to note that the birth of a child does not immediately establish a legal parent-child relationship in this situation.
Can The Child Decide Where To Live?
While the child cannot choose the custody arrangement, the court will consider his or her opinion. First, the judge will assess the child’s maturity. If the judge believes he or she is mature enough to understand the situation, the child can then provide an opinion. The child’s opinion is just one of many factors that go into developing custody agreements.

Fathers’ Rights in Colorado
Fathers’ Rights in Golden, CO
Legally, mothers and fathers have the same rights regarding divorces, child custody, and child support. However, many men find that the law doesn’t protect them as it should. While they have the same rights on paper, they lose out on parenting time and sometimes get cut out of the decision-making process. Your children are important to you, and they need their father in their lives. Thus, hire a Golden, CO, fathers’ rights lawyer to ensure that your interests are represented.
Our firm has defended fathers against false claims and helped numerous men receive favorable child custody and support agreements. Fair child custody agreements
Access to child support
Fair child support payments
It can feel like the law is against you, but that isn’t the case. Instead, you just need an advocate by your side. Contact our fathers’ rights lawyer today for a consultation.
Child Custody And Fathers’ Rights
Both men and women have equal rights regarding child custody in Colorado. Often, custody can be determined without going to court. Our Golden, CO, fathers’ rights lawyer will sit down with the other side and work out an agreement. In most cases, parents agree to share both physical and legal custody since it’s often in the child’s best interests.
Unfortunately, sometimes, one parent is not fit to raise a child. If the child’s mother isn’t up to the task, we can petition the court for sole custody.
