Even though the child support formula is based on the income share model, it’s still quite complicated. Your Golden, CO, fathers’ rights lawyer can review your income and assets, as well as those of the other parent. False Allegations And Fathers’ Rights

You don’t need to be married to have parental rights. However, you might have to establish paternity. ## Grandparents’ Rights in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/child-custody/grandparents-rights/

Grandparents’ Rights in Colorado
Grandparents’ Rights in Golden, CO
Most people agree that it takes a village to raise a child. Still, some parents attempt to keep their children away from their grandparents. The relationship between grandparents and grandchildren is vital to the children’s overall well-being. Thus, Colorado recognizes that grandparents have the right to see their grandchildren, even if one parent fights against it during a contentious divorce.
Our Golden, CO, grandparents’ rights lawyer can help you petition for visitation. We can also assist in filing for an allocation of parental responsibilities if your grandchild does not currently live with his or her parents.
Grounds for Filing for Visitation
Our Golden, CO, grandparents’ rights lawyer can help you petition for visitation if one or more of the following has occurred:
The parents are legally divorced.
The parents are legally separated.
The marriage is not valid.
The child is not living with either parent.
The grandparent’s child, who is the legal parent, has passed away.
Requesting Visitation
If you meet the criteria, you can file for visitation to see your grandchildren. Our Golden, CO, grandparents’ rights lawyer can negotiate with the other side to attempt to set a visitation schedule. However, these cases sometimes must be tried in front of a judge.
The judge will evaluate the evidence to see if regular visits are in the best interests of the child. If they are, the judge can then set a visitation schedule. Because these cases are up to the judge’s discretion, it’s wise to have an attorney by your side. Your lawyer will present evidence and advocate for your rights as a grandparent.
Child Custody And Grandparents’ Rights
In most cases, grandparents just want visitation with their grandchildren. However, in some circumstances, grandparents request custody to protect and care for the child. You can file for custody of your grandchild if he or she is no longer under the care of his or her parents. For example, if law enforcement removed your grandchild from the family home due to substance abuse issues, you can petition for custody. Then, your grandchild can avoid going into foster care.
You can also petition for custody of your grandchild if he or she has been living with you for at least six months. You must file for custody within six months of your grandchild moving out, if applicable.
Our Golden, CO, grandparents’ rights lawyer can go over your case to see if you qualify for custody. If you don’t, we can explore other options that can help you and your grandchild.
Evidence For Visitation And Custody
Your Golden, CO, grandparents’ rights lawyer will gather evidence to support your right to visitation or custody. This might include evidence that the parents are deceased, incarcerated, or suffer from substance abuse problems. It could also be evidence of your close relationship with your grandchild and how he or she will be negatively impacted if the bond is severed. Because these cases require a great deal of evidence, it’s important to get started as soon as possible. Then, your lawyer can prepare everything and file a legal claim so you can assert your rights as a grandparent.
Terminating And Modifying Visitation Agreements
Visitation agreements can be modified or even terminated. In order for this to happen, something substantial must have changed. For instance, if the child is adopted or the grandparent’s child loses his or her parental rights, the agreement can be terminated or modified. Also, the court will evaluate the child’s changing needs to see if the agreement is still in his or her best interests.

## Colorado Child Custody Modification
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/child-custody/modification/

Colorado Child Custody Modification
A parenting order that made sense at the time of your original case may not fit your life today. When circumstances change, Colorado courts allow either parent to request a modification to an existing divorce-related parenting time and parenting responsibilities order or an allocation of parental responsibilities (APR) order where parties were never married. But the process has a real legal threshold, a defined procedure, and a timeline that rewards acting sooner rather than later.
Waiting is not neutral. Living under an order that no longer works while the other parent digs in deeper is a cost. The Drake Law Firm helps Colorado parents navigate the modification process without the drama, and with a plan.
This page explains how the process works, what courts require, and what you should realistically expect. If you already know you need to move forward, call us now. If you are still assessing your options, read on.
Ready to talk through your situation? Call (303) 261-8111
or schedule a consultation online.
What Custody Modification Means in Colorado
Colorado statutes do not use the word “custody.” What most people mean by custody is formally called an order regarding parenting responsibilities and parenting time in a divorce or an order regarding allocation of parental responsibilities (APR) if parties were never married. Both modifications fall under C.R.S. 14-10-129
[1]. Parenting time and parenting responsibilities have two components: decision-making responsibility (who makes major calls about education, healthcare, and religion) and parenting time (the schedule for when the child is with each parent). A modification can target either component, both, or emergency provisions, depending on what has changed.
When you say you want to “change custody,” you likely mean more parenting time, a change in decision-making authority, or both. The legal standard that applies depends on the scope of what you are asking the court to do.
The Legal Standard: Two Tiers Depending on What You Are Asking For
Colorado does not apply a single modification standard to every request. The applicable threshold depends on the scope of the change you are seeking.
Tier 1: Best interests only. If you are seeking a change to parenting time that does not alter the majority residential parent, the court applies the best-interests standard under C.R.S. 14-10-129(1)(a)(I) [1]. The court may modify parenting time whenever doing so would serve the child’s best interests.
Tier 2: Substantial change plus endangerment. If you are seeking a modification that substantially changes parenting time and changes which parent the child lives with the majority of the time, the standard is higher. Under C.R.S. 14-10-129(2)
[1], the court will not grant that modification unless it finds, based on facts that arose after or were unknown at the time of the prior order, that a change has occurred in the circumstances of the child or the majority-time parent, and that modification is necessary to serve the child’s best interests.
Within that higher tier, the endangerment exception applies: under C.R.S. 14-10-129(2)(d)
[1], a court may modify a prior order when the child’s present environment endangers the child’s physical health or significantly impairs the child’s emotional development, and the harm from continuing the arrangement is outweighed by the advantage of changing it.
In plain terms: the more significant the change you are seeking, the harder the court looks. Knowing which tier applies to your situation is the first strategic question.
What Courts Recognize as a Changed Circumstance
Before a court will consider a Tier 2 modification, you must establish that circumstances have changed since the prior order. Courts that have addressed this include circumstances such as:
Relocation by either parent, particularly when it significantly impacts the child’s access to the other parent
A child’s changed developmental needs, such as new special education requirements, a significant medical diagnosis, or a major schooling change
A parent’s major life change, including remarriage, job loss, incarceration, or a serious health issue affecting parenting capacity
Evidence of endangerment or abuse, including domestic violence, substance abuse, or documented neglect
Consistent parenting-time violations, where one parent is repeatedly interfering with the other’s court-ordered time
A child’s stated preferences, depending on the child’s age and maturity (courts weigh this, but it is not determinative on its own)
What does not clear the threshold: normal life transitions, general frustration with the schedule, or short-term disruptions that are not ongoing. Courts are designed to discourage repeated filings over temporary friction. The change must be real, material, and continuing.
When Your Child's Safety Is the Issue
The endangerment standard under C.R.S. 14-10-129(2)(d) requires a three-part showing: first, that the prior order shall be presumed to stand; second, that the child’s present environment endangers the child’s physical health or significantly impairs emotional development, and that the harm from a change is outweighed by the advantage of changing; third, that the proposed modification is in the child’s best interests.
This standard is demanding even though it allows modification without showing a broader change in circumstances. Accusations alone do not carry cases. Police reports, medical records, school records, therapist notes, and witness statements all build the evidentiary record courts actually examine.
If your child is in immediate danger right now, a standard modification petition is not the right tool. Emergency motions to restrict parenting time are heard within 14 days of filing. Call us before you make any move.
The Colorado Modification Process, Step by Step
Modification cases are filed in the same Colorado district court that entered the original parenting order. Jefferson County cases are handled at the Jefferson County Combined Court (1st Judicial District). Here is what the process looks like:
File a Motion to Modify Parental Responsibilities and Parenting Time. You or your attorney file in the originating district court. The motion must identify the specific relief requested and the grounds for the modification. This document sets the framework for everything that follows.
Serve the other parent. Proper service is required under the Colorado Rules of Civil Procedure. The other parent has the opportunity to respond, object, or file a counter-motion. The response deadline runs from the date of service.
Initial case management and mediation. Courts frequently require mediation before setting a hearing. Colorado policy favors parents resolving post-decree disputes without judicial intervention when possible. In many cases, mediation is not optional.
Evaluation, if ordered. In contested cases, the court may appoint a Child and Family Investigator (CFI) or Parental Responsibilities Evaluator (PRE) to assess the situation and make recommendations. This step adds meaningful time and cost.
Evidentiary hearing. If no agreement is reached, the case proceeds to hearing where both parents present evidence and testimony. The judge applies the best-interests factors under C.R.S. 14-10-124 [2].
Court order. The judge enters a written Order modifying the current Parenting Responsibilities and Parenting Time Order if it is post-divorce or a written Order Modifying modified the current APR order if parties were never married. That new order controls until a future modification is sought and granted.
Timeline matters. Uncontested modifications can resolve in a few months once paperwork is processed. Contested modifications involving a CFI or PRE commonly take six months to over a year. Do not underestimate the timeline when planning school enrollment, childcare, or relocation decisions.
Ready to talk through your situation? Call (303) 261-8111 or schedule a consultation online. You can also visit our physical Colorado offices.
What Colorado Courts Look At: The Best-Interests Factors
Once the court clears the applicable threshold, the analysis shifts to whether the proposed modification serves the child’s best interests. C.R.S. 14-10-124
[2] sets out the factors the court must consider. The full list includes:
The wishes of each parent as to parenting time
The wishes of the child, if the child is mature enough to express reasoned and independent preferences
The child’s relationship with each parent, siblings, and others who significantly affect the child’s interests
The child’s adjustment to home, school, and community
The mental and physical health of all individuals involved (disability alone is not a basis to restrict parenting time)
Each parent’s ability to encourage sharing of love, affection, and contact with the other parent (protecting a child from witnessing abuse is not held against the protective parent)
Whether the past pattern of involvement of each parent reflects a system of values, time commitment, and mutual support
The physical proximity of the parents as it relates to the practical logistics of parenting time
The ability of each parent to place the child’s needs ahead of their own
This list is not exhaustive. Courts consider all relevant factors. The weight given to each factor depends on the specific facts of your case.
Colorado courts do not disrupt stable arrangements without compelling reason. If your child is adjusted and thriving, the bar for modification is higher. That is not a reason to give up. It is a signal to build a stronger record. We help you do that.
Your Parenting Plan Will Need to Be Updated
Any modification to parenting time or decision-making requires an updated Colorado parenting plan that reflects the new arrangement in writing. A well-drafted parenting plan specifies the schedule, holidays, school breaks, communication rules, and how future disagreements get resolved. It is not a formality. It is the document you and your co-parent will live by, and getting it right the first time prevents the disputes that bring people back to court.
When Parents Agree vs. When They Do Not
If both parents agree to the modification, the process is far simpler. You submit a written stipulation to the court, the judge reviews it against the best-interests standard, and an order enters. You bypass the evidentiary hearing entirely.
One thing cannot be shortcut: the stipulation must be properly drafted. An informal text-message agreement is not legally enforceable. It creates problems later.
When the other parent contests the modification, the process is more involved, more expensive, and harder on everyone, including your child. That is not a reason to back down if the change is warranted. It means you need a strategy before you file: what evidence to gather, whether mediation is worth pursuing first, whether a CFI appointment helps or hurts your position, and what the realistic range of outcomes looks like at hearing.
We prefer resolving cases without trial. If the other parent is cooperative, we push hard for agreement. If they are not, if they are violating the current order, blocking your access, or creating real risk for your child, we will not hesitate to litigate. No Drama Divorce does not mean no spine.
Custody Changes Often Affect Child Support
Significant shifts in parenting time, particularly changes in overnight stays, typically affect the child support calculation under Colorado’s income shares guidelines. If your modification results in a substantially different time allocation, a child support modification should be addressed in the same proceeding or immediately after. Addressing both together is more efficient and prevents stale support orders that no longer reflect the actual arrangement.

How long does a custody modification take in Colorado?
Uncontested modifications can resolve in a few months once the court processes the stipulation. Contested cases involving a CFI evaluation or evidentiary hearing typically take six months to over a year. The timeline depends on the court’s docket, whether the parties can agree, and whether an evaluator is appointed.
Can I modify custody without going to court?
If both parents agree, you can submit a written stipulation for court approval without a full hearing. You still need a signed court order. A verbal agreement or a text exchange is not legally enforceable and sets up problems down the road. The process is much simpler with agreement, but the court must still enter the modified order.
What if my child is in danger right now?
Do not file a standard modification petition. Colorado courts can enter emergency orders restricting or suspending parenting time when there is credible, documented evidence of immediate risk. Emergency motions under C.R.S. 14-10-129(4) are heard within 14 days. Call us immediately.
How often can custody be modified in Colorado?
There is no statutory cap on the number of modifications. But courts are not interested in repeated filings based on the same facts. Each new motion petition requires a new and continuing substantial change. Filing too soon after a prior modification, without genuinely new grounds, risks dismissal and can affect your standing with the court going forward.
Do I need an attorney for a custody modification?
You are not legally required to have one. But the two-tier standard, the evidentiary requirements, the procedural rules, and the nuances of what actually moves Jefferson County judges are not things you want to figure out as you go. A wrong move on the threshold analysis or a poorly drafted stipulation is harder and more expensive to fix than getting it right the first time. We give you a straight read from the first call, whether or not that leads to hiring us.

## Child Support in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/child-support/

Child Support in Colorado
Most parents dealing with a separation or dissolution of marriage proceedings quickly encounter a system built around one central question: what financial support does the child need, and who pays it? Under Colorado law, child support is not discretionary. Both parents are legally obligated to support their child in proportion to their respective incomes, regardless of marital status. Understanding how that obligation is calculated — and what happens when circumstances change — is where to start.
Talk to a Child Support Lawyer Now
Colorado governs child support through C.R.S. § 14-10-115, which establishes the Income Shares Model as the mandatory calculation framework. This statute, along with the Colorado Child Support Guidelines periodically updated by the Colorado Child Support Commission, defines which income sources count, what adjustments are allowed, and when a court may depart from the standard formula. Significant updates to the guidelines took effect March 1, 2026, under House Bill 25-1159, and apply to all orders entered or modified on or after that date.
Colorado's Legal Framework for Child Support
The primary statute governing child support in Colorado is C.R.S. § 14-10-115. It establishes mandatory calculation worksheets, defines which income sources are included, identifies allowable adjustments, and sets out when courts may deviate from the guideline amount. Child support cases are handled in the district courts of each county and may arise in several contexts:
As part of a dissolution of marriage proceeding
As part of a legal separation
Within an Allocation of Parental Responsibilities (APR) case
As a standalone action through Colorado Child Support Services (CSS), an agency within the Colorado Department of Human Services
Before a support order can be entered against a legal father, legal paternity establishment is a prerequisite before child support can be ordered. The Drake Law Firm, PC handles paternity matters as part of its family law practice.
Statutory Definitions of Income
Colorado defines gross income broadly under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(5)(a). Includable income sources encompass wages, salaries, commissions, bonuses, dividends, severance pay, pensions, interest, trust income, Social Security benefits (including disability), workers’ compensation, unemployment insurance, and income from self-employment or operation of a business. Non-recurring or extraordinary income — such as a one-time capital gain — may be treated differently by the court depending on whether it reflects the parent’s ongoing financial capacity.
Income imputation rules apply when a parent is voluntarily unemployed or underemployed. In these situations, the court may attribute income based on the parent’s historical earnings, occupational qualifications, and the prevailing job market.
Certain items are excluded from the gross income calculation, including means-tested public assistance (such as TANF and SSI), child support received for children from other relationships, and income of the parent’s new spouse or partner.
How Child Support Is Calculated: The Income Shares Model
Colorado uses the Income Shares Model, which is based on the principle that a child should receive the same proportion of parental income as if the parents lived together. The calculation follows a structured worksheet process using the state’s official Child Support Schedule — a table of presumed combined support obligations based on combined adjusted gross income and number of children.
Step 1 — Determine Each Parent’s Gross Monthly Income
The court starts with each parent’s gross monthly income from all sources. For W-2 employees this is straightforward. For self-employed parents, net business income after ordinary and necessary business expenses (but before personal tax deductions) is used. For parents with variable income, courts often average the prior 12 to 36 months of earnings.
Step 2 — Calculate Combined Adjusted Gross Income
The two parents’ gross incomes are added together to arrive at the Combined Adjusted Gross Income (CAGI). Adjustments may include amounts paid for health insurance premiums for the child and child support obligations for children from prior relationships.
Step 3 — Look Up the Basic Child Support Obligation
The CAGI and the number of children are entered into the Colorado Child Support Schedule to determine the Basic Child Support Obligation (BCSO). This schedule is codified in C.R.S. § 14-10-115(7)(b) and reflects estimated expenditures on children at various income levels based on economic research. The 2026 updated schedule covers combined monthly adjusted gross incomes of up to $40,000 — increased from the prior $30,000 cap — and reflects current costs of raising a child based on the Betson-Rothbarth Study and 2023 Bureau of Labor Statistics data. For combined incomes above $40,000, courts retain discretion in determining the appropriate amount.
Step 4 — Add Work-Related Child Care and Health Insurance
Work-related child care costs and the cost of the child’s health insurance premium are added to the BCSO to produce the Total Child Support Obligation. The health insurance figure used is the cost of the child’s portion of the premium only — not the total family premium. Coverage through public programs such as Medicaid or CHP+ is also accounted for under this step. These are actual, documented costs — not estimates.
Step 5 — Apportion Between Parents
Each parent’s share of the Total Child Support Obligation is proportional to their contribution to the CAGI. For example, if Parent A earns 60% of the combined income, Parent A is responsible for 60% of the obligation. The residential parent is presumed to spend their share directly; the non-residential parent’s share is the payment amount.
Parenting Time and Child Support
For orders entered or modified on or after March 1, 2026, Colorado has eliminated the previous “93-overnight cliff” under the updated C.R.S. § 14-10-115(8). Prior law only recognized shared parenting time for child support purposes once a parent reached 93 or more overnights per year — meaning a parent with 90 overnights received the same credit as a parent with zero. That threshold no longer applies.
Under the 2026 framework, every overnight is formally recognized through a graduated Parenting Time Table. A parent receives incremental credit for parenting time expenses starting from the first overnight, scaled proportionally across the full range of parenting time. The prior dual-worksheet structure (Worksheet A for sole custody, Worksheet B for shared custody) has been replaced by a unified calculation: the basic support obligation is drawn from the standard schedule, allocated between parents in proportion to their adjusted gross incomes, and then each parent receives a parenting time credit based on their share of overnights as listed in the Parenting Time Table. The annual overnight count comes directly from the parenting schedule established in a parenting plan or custody order, making accurate documentation of that schedule essential.
At equal parenting time (182 or more overnights each), the parenting time credit is maximized, though a support obligation may still exist if there is a meaningful income disparity between the parents.
For very low-income parents, the Self-Support Reserve (SSR) and Low-Income Adjustment provisions may affect the final obligation. The SSR is calculated at 29 hours per week at the state minimum wage multiplied by 50 weeks and divided by 12 — a figure that adjusts as Colorado’s minimum wage changes. Parents whose income falls between $650 per month and the SSR are subject to a revised low-income schedule, and those whose income exceeds the SSR but remains near minimum wage have their total support obligation capped as a percentage of income.
Deviation from the Guidelines
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(3)(b), a court may deviate from the guideline amount if application of the formula would be inequitable, unjust, or inappropriate in a specific case. Grounds for deviation include:
Extraordinary medical needs of the child
Educational costs of the child
Special needs of the child
Financial resources of the child
Travel expenses for parenting time
Any deviation must be supported by written findings stating the amount that would have been ordered under the guidelines and why deviation serves the child’s best interests.
Establishing a Child Support Order in Colorado
Through Divorce or Allocation of Parental Responsibilities
When parents divorce or legal separation involves minor children, the court will enter a child support order as part of the final decree. The parties must file a completed Child Support Worksheet along with sworn financial disclosures. Colorado Rule of Civil Procedure 16.2 requires both parties to exchange mandatory financial disclosures, including three years of tax returns, two months of pay stubs, and documentation of all assets and debts. Working with Colorado child support attorneys during this stage helps ensure disclosures are complete and the worksheet accurately reflects each parent’s financial circumstances.
Through Colorado Child Support Services
Colorado Child Support Services (CSS), administered at the county level through local Child Support Units, provides services to establish, collect, and enforce child support orders. Services are available to any parent regardless of income and are required for families receiving TANF benefits. CSS can establish paternity, locate the other parent, establish a support order through the courts or through an administrative process, and collect payments through the Colorado Family Support Registry (CFSR).
During a pending divorce or APR case, either party may request temporary child support via a motion and financial affidavit. Temporary orders remain in effect until the court enters a final order at the permanent hearing. The temporary amount is calculated using the same guideline formula.
Payment, Collection, and the Colorado Family Support Registry
All child support payments ordered by Colorado courts are made through the Colorado Family Support Registry (CFSR), administered by the Colorado Department of Human Services. Direct payments between parents are not recognized as satisfying a court-ordered support obligation unless the order specifically authorizes them — paying directly to the other parent risks having those payments treated as gifts in any subsequent enforcement action.
Income Withholding Orders (IWO) are issued automatically in most cases under C.R.S. § 14-14-111.5. The IWO directs the paying parent’s employer to deduct support from wages and remit directly to the CFSR. IWOs can also be served on unemployment benefits and some other income sources. Parents who are self-employed or have variable income may be required to make direct payments to the CFSR on a scheduled basis.
Enforcement of Child Support in Colorado
When a parent fails to pay court-ordered child support, Colorado law provides a broad array of enforcement tools. Enforcement actions can be initiated by the receiving parent, by their attorney, or by Colorado Child Support Services.
Administrative Enforcement Remedies
C.R.S. § 26-13-122 and related statutes authorize CSS to take the following administrative actions without a court hearing:
License suspension: driver’s licenses, professional licenses, recreational licenses (hunting, fishing), and business licenses
Tax intercept: federal and Colorado state income tax refunds
Credit bureau reporting: delinquent support reported to consumer credit agencies once arrears exceed a threshold
Bank account seizure (FIDM): CSS can freeze and seize funds in bank accounts through the Financial Institution Data Match program
Lottery and gambling intercept: winnings above the statutory threshold are intercepted
Passport denial: the federal Office of Child Support Enforcement (OCSE) denies or revokes passports when arrears exceed $2,500
Judicial Enforcement Remedies
A party or CSS may also seek judicial enforcement through a motion for contempt of court (C.R.C.P. 107). If the court finds a parent in contempt for willful non-payment, remedies include fines, a remedial or punitive jail sentence, and entry of a judgment for arrears. Judgments for unpaid child support bear interest at the statutory rate. In egregious cases, criminal prosecution under C.R.S. § 14-14-104 (criminal nonsupport) may apply.
Interstate Enforcement — UIFSA
Colorado has adopted the Uniform Interstate Family Support Act (UIFSA), codified at C.R.S. § 14-5-101 et seq. Under UIFSA, a Colorado order can be registered and enforced in any other state, and orders from other states can be registered in Colorado. The issuing state retains continuing exclusive jurisdiction over the support order as long as a party or the child remains in that state.
Modifying Child Support in Colorado
A child support order may be modified when there has been a substantial and continuing change of circumstances that results in at least a 10% change in the monthly support amount under C.R.S. § 14-10-122(1)(a). This 10% threshold is the operative standard — a court will not grant a modification unless the recalculated amount reflects that change. The passage of time alone is generally not sufficient grounds for a judicial modification without a corresponding shift in financial circumstances or parenting time.
For cases managed by Colorado Child Support Services, CSS conducts an administrative review every three years. However, even in those reviews, a modification will only be entered if the recalculation produces at least a 10% change in the obligation amount.
What Constitutes a Substantial Change
Examples of changes that may support a modification petition include:
Significant increase or decrease in either parent’s income (including job loss, promotion, or career change)
A change in the number of overnights the child spends with each parent
The child gaining or losing health insurance coverage through a parent’s employer
Substantial changes in work-related child care costs
The child developing significant medical or educational needs not previously ordered • Emancipation of one child in a multi-child order, requiring recalculation for remaining children
The Modification Process
The requesting parent files a Motion to Modify Child Support along with an updated Child Support Worksheet and updated financial disclosures. If the parties agree on the new amount, a Stipulation and Proposed Order can be submitted for the court’s approval. If not, the matter proceeds to a hearing where both parties present current financial information.
The modification is effective from the date of filing of the motion — not the date of the hearing — so prompt filing is important. Until a court enters a modified order, the original obligation remains in full force. A parent experiencing sudden financial hardship, such as a layoff, should file the modification motion immediately rather than waiting to see if circumstances improve.
Duration and Termination of Child Support in Colorado
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(13), child support in Colorado terminates by operation of law when the last or only child covered by the order turns 19. No court motion is required for termination in that circumstance. However, if the order covers multiple children and only one reaches age 19, the obligation does not automatically reduce — the paying parent must file a motion to modify so the court can recalculate the amount for the remaining children.
Additional exceptions that may extend support beyond age 19 include:
The child has not yet graduated from high school at age 19 — support continues until graduation or age 21, whichever occurs first
The child is mentally or physically disabled — the court may order support beyond age 19 upon a showing of need
The parties have agreed in writing to extend support for post-secondary education or other purposes — Colorado courts cannot order a parent to pay college expenses over their objection, but such provisions are enforceable as contract terms if voluntarily agreed upon and incorporated into the court order
Support also terminates upon the child’s emancipation before age 19, which may occur through marriage, military enlistment, or a court order.
Tax Considerations
Child support payments are tax-neutral under both federal and Colorado state law. The paying parent may not deduct child support payments, and the receiving parent does not report them as taxable income. For divorce decrees entered after December 31, 2018, Colorado spousal maintenance is also tax-neutral at both the federal and state level under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act — the payer may not deduct it and the recipient does not report it as income. Both obligations are treated the same way for tax purposes under current law.
By default, the parent with the majority of overnights has the right to claim the child as a dependent for purposes of the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit. However, parents may agree — or the court may order — that the non-residential parent claim the child in alternating years or under other arrangements, formalized through IRS Form 8332.
Child Support and Paternity in Colorado
Before a child support order can be entered against a legal father, Colorado paternity law governs how legal fatherhood is determined. In Colorado, paternity is established in one of three ways:
The parents are married at the time of birth (the marital presumption under C.R.S. § 19-4-105)
Both parents sign a Voluntary Acknowledgment of Paternity (VAP) at the hospital or through the Colorado Vital Records office
A court or administrative order following genetic testing adjudicates paternity
Once legal paternity determination is complete, either parent may seek a child support order. The Colorado Child Support Services program provides administrative paternity establishment services at no cost to the applicant.
Frequently Asked Questions About Child Support
Is child support taxable in Colorado?
No, child support is tax-neutral. The parent receiving the payments does not report them as taxable income, and the parent paying support cannot claim them as a tax deduction on their state or federal return.
Does child support count as income?
For tax purposes, child support does not count as income. However, lenders may consider it as income when you apply for a mortgage or car loan, and state agencies may count it when determining eligibility for certain public assistance programs.
How is child support calculated in Colorado?
Colorado uses the Income Shares Model, which estimates the amount parents would have spent on the child if they were still together. The court inputs both parents’ gross monthly incomes, the number of overnight visits, and expenses like health insurance and childcare into a statutory formula to determine the final amount.
How to apply for child support?
You can apply directly through the Colorado Child Support Services (CSS) website or your county’s Department of Human Services. Alternatively, if you are going through a divorce or custody case, a Colorado child support lawyer at The Drake Law Firm, PC can file the necessary motions with the court to establish an order as part of your case.
What happens if a parent doesn't pay child support in Colorado?
Colorado takes non-payment seriously, and enforcement measures can include wage garnishment, interception of tax refunds, and suspension of driver’s or professional licenses. In severe cases, a motion for contempt of court may result in fines or jail time for the non-paying parent.
How The Drake Law Firm, PC Can Help with Child Support in Colorado
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents clients in child support matters at all stages — from initial establishment through modification and enforcement.
The firm’s attorneys bring direct experience with Colorado’s Income Shares Model, the financial disclosure requirements of C.R.C.P. 16.2, and the practical realities of income withholding, CSS enforcement actions, and post-decree modifications in Jefferson County and the surrounding district courts served by our family law offices in Colorado. The firm offers both non-adversarial resolution strategies and courtroom advocacy when litigation is required.
Taking the Next Steps for Your Children
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents parents in child support matters throughout Colorado. Whether you are establishing a support order for the first time, seeking support modification after a change in income or parenting time, or enforcing an order that isn’t being followed, our attorneys work to protect your child’s financial security and your rights under Colorado law.

## Colorado Child Support Modification
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/child-support/modification/

Colorado Child Support Modification
2026 LAW UPDATE: Colorado’s child support guidelines changed significantly on March 1, 2026 under HB 25-1159. The 93-overnight threshold has been eliminated, the income cap raised, and support schedules updated for the first time since 2014. If your order predates March 1, 2026, the new formula may produce a materially different result. This page reflects current law.
Child support orders are not permanent. When income changes, parenting time shifts, or a child’s financial needs evolve, the order that made sense at the time of your original case may no longer reflect reality. Colorado law lets either parent request a modification. There is a defined threshold, a formula-driven calculation, and a timeline that matters. The Drake Law Firm helps Colorado parents navigate that process without the drama and with a plan.
Whether you are paying more than your income supports, receiving less than your child needs, or living under an order that predates the 2026 guideline update, the question is the same: does your current order still hold up? This page explains how to find out and what to do about it.
Ready to talk through your situation? Call (303) 261-8111
or schedule a consultation online.
Phone and Zoom consults available, including Saturdays by request.
The Legal Standard: Substantial and Continuing Change
Colorado child support may be modified only upon a showing of changed circumstances that are substantial and continuing, under C.R.S. 14-10-122(1)(a) [1]. Both conditions must be met. Substantial means the change is large enough to produce a meaningful difference in the calculated support amount. Continuing means the change is not temporary.
The statute provides a concrete benchmark: under C.R.S. 14-10-122(1)(b) [1], a change is deemed substantial when applying the current child support guidelines to the new circumstances would produce a difference of at least 10% in the monthly support obligation, up or down.
What this means in practice: if you can run the current guidelines with updated income figures and parenting time, and the result differs from your existing order by 10% or more, you have a statutory basis for modification. If the difference is less than 10%, the change is not considered substantial, and the court will not modify the order on that basis alone.
The continuity requirement matters just as much. A temporary job loss, a short-term deployment, or a brief increase in overtime income is unlikely to qualify. The change must represent your actual ongoing financial reality, not a snapshot of one difficult month.
What Changed in 2026: HB 25-1159 and Why It Matters for Your Order
On March 1, 2026, Colorado’s most significant child support reform in over a decade took effect. House Bill 25-1159, signed by Governor Polis in May 2025, amended C.R.S. 14-10-115 [2] and changed how support is calculated in three important ways. The three major changes:The 93-overnight threshold is eliminated. Under the prior law, parenting time below 93 overnights per year received no credit in the calculation. Every overnight now reduces the paying parent’s obligation proportionally, through a graduated formula. The financial incentive to fight over the 93-overnight line no longer exists.
The combined income cap increased from $30,000 to $40,000 per month. For higher-income families, support is now calculated on a wider schedule range before judicial discretion is required.
Support schedules updated for the first time since 2014. The prior schedule was based on 2010 economic data. The new schedule reflects 2023 cost-of-living data, which means recalculated amounts will often be higher than existing orders, even without a change in income or parenting time.
The law is not retroactive. An existing order does not change automatically. But if you file a motion to modify and the new guidelines produce a result that differs from your current order by 10% or more, you have grounds for modification. For parents with orders entered before March 1, 2026, this is worth calculating immediately.
If your order predates March 1, 2026, call us. We can run the updated numbers with you and tell you whether you have grounds to file. (303) 261-8111 or schedule a consultation online.
Common Reasons Colorado Parents Seek a Child Support Modification
Any of the following can be the basis for a modification when the resulting support difference meets the 10% threshold:Significant income change, including job loss, a raise, a new job at a different salary, or a move from employment to self-employment
Change in parenting time, particularly when the number of overnights changes materially from the arrangement reflected in the original order
Changes in the child’s financial needs, such as new medical expenses, changes in childcare costs, or significant educational expenses
Health insurance changes, including a parent gaining or losing coverage, or the cost of coverage changing substantially
A parent becoming voluntarily underemployed or unemployed, in which case the court may impute income based on earning capacity under C.R.S. 14-10-115(5)(b.5) [2]
The child reaches a milestone that affects the order, such as an older child turning 19 (when Colorado child support terminates for that child), which may require recalculating for remaining children
A prior order that predates the March 2026 guideline update, which alone may produce a 10% or greater difference when recalculated under the new schedule
What does not qualify: minor fluctuations in income that are temporary, routine cost-of-living adjustments not tied to a change in income, and disagreements about how existing support is being spent. The change must be real, measurable, and ongoing.
How Colorado Calculates Child Support Under the 2026 Guidelines
Colorado uses an income shares model under C.R.S. 14-10-115 [2]. The model estimates what an intact household at the combined income level would spend on children, then allocates that cost between parents in proportion to each parent’s share of combined adjusted gross income. The 2026 guidelines also introduced a self-support reserve. This is a floor amount of income a paying parent keeps before support is calculated, set at approximately $1,790 per month in 2026 based on Colorado’s minimum wage. Parents earning at or below $650 per month pay a flat $10 regardless of the number of children. This protects lower-income parents from orders that would leave them below subsistence level. The inputs that drive the calculation:Both parents’ adjusted gross incomes, including wages, salary, self-employment income, bonuses, investment income, rental income, and other sources. The court looks at actual earning capacity, not just what a parent chooses to earn.
Parenting time, measured in overnights per year. Under the 2026 guidelines, every overnight a child spends with the paying parent reduces that parent’s obligation proportionally.
Work-related childcare costs, divided between parents in proportion to adjusted gross income.
Health insurance premiums for the children, with the cost allocated proportionally.
Extraordinary medical expenses exceeding $250 per child per year, split proportionally based on income.
The calculation runs through a court-approved worksheet. Courts do not guess at the number. The formula produces a presumptive amount, which courts are expected to follow. Deviation is allowed but requires written findings explaining the basis. Income is not always straightforward. Bonuses, commission income, stock vesting, and self-employment earnings all require analysis. If a parent is voluntarily earning less than their capacity, the court can impute income based on what they could earn at full-time employment. Getting the income figure right on both sides is one of the most consequential parts of a modification case.
The Child Support Modification Process in Colorado
Modifications are filed in the district court that entered the original order. Jefferson County cases are handled at Jefferson County Combined Court (1st Judicial District). Here is how the process works:
Calculate whether you have grounds. Before filing, run the current guidelines with updated income figures and parenting time. If the result differs from your existing order by 10% or more, you have a statutory basis. An attorney can help you do this accurately and spot issues with income imputation before you file.
File a Motion to Modify Child Support. The motion is filed in the originating district court and must identify the grounds for modification. Under C.R.S. 14-10-122(1)(a) [1], modifications only apply to installments accruing after the date of filing. Filing sooner preserves more retroactive benefit.
Serve the other parent and exchange financial disclosures. Both parents are required to provide updated financial information: income verification, tax returns, pay stubs, and documentation of childcare and insurance costs. The numbers on both sides drive the outcome.
Attempt agreement or proceed to hearing. Many modifications resolve by stipulation once both parents exchange accurate financial information. If the other parent disputes the figures or contests the modification, the case proceeds to a hearing where a judge applies the guidelines to the facts.
Court enters a modified order. The new order becomes effective and replaces the prior one. It controls until another modification is sought and granted.
Timeline: uncontested modifications with a stipulation can resolve in a few months. Contested cases, particularly those involving disputed income or imputation arguments, take longer. Do not wait to file. Every month you delay is a month the old order continues.
Timing is not neutral. A modification only goes back to the date you file. Call (303) 261-8111 or schedule a consultation online now and do not leave money on the table.
One Rule That Catches People Off Guard: Retroactivity
Colorado courts cannot modify child support retroactively before the date the motion was filed, under C.R.S. 14-10-122(1)(d) [1]. This rule has real financial consequences. If your income dropped significantly six months ago but you have not yet filed, you cannot go back and recapture the overpayment for those six months.
The same applies in the other direction. If you are receiving support that should have been higher for the past year, you cannot collect the difference for months that predated the filing. The modification only runs forward from when you act.
There is one exception: under C.R.S. 14-10-122(5), if both parents have mutually agreed to a change in physical care and the child has already been living under that new arrangement, the court may modify support retroactively to the date the physical care actually changed, not just the filing date. This exception only applies to agreed changes in care, not to disputed modifications. There is also a hard cap: the court cannot modify support under this exception for any period more than five years before the motion was filed. If you changed custody arrangements informally six or seven years ago and never updated the support order, the first five years of that gap is locked. The last five are potentially recoverable.
This is one of the clearest reasons not to wait. Every month without a filed motion is a month that is locked in under the old order, regardless of how much circumstances have changed.
When Both Parents Agree vs. When They Do Not
If both parents agree on the modification, you can submit a written stipulation to the court. The judge reviews it, confirms it reflects the correct guideline calculation, and enters the new order without a hearing. You skip the contested process entirely. No hearing prep, no financial disclosure disputes, no waiting for a court date. You get the order and move on.
When the other parent disagrees or disputes the income figures, the modification becomes contested. The most common flashpoints: one parent claims the other is voluntarily underemployed, one parent disputes the accuracy of the other’s income documentation, or the parties disagree on what counts as a qualifying change. These disputes require a hearing and, often, careful preparation of financial evidence.
We work toward agreement wherever it is achievable. If the numbers are clear and the other parent is reasonable, a stipulation is the most efficient outcome for everyone, including your child. If the other parent is hiding income, improperly reducing their earnings, or refusing to provide accurate financials, we are prepared to litigate. Protecting your child’s financial support is not optional.
Child Support and Parenting Time Are Connected
Under the 2026 guidelines, every overnight a child spends with the paying parent affects the support calculation. This means that a child custody modification that changes the parenting schedule will almost always warrant a simultaneous support recalculation. Filing both in the same proceeding is more efficient than handling them separately and avoids the problem of an outdated support order that does not reflect the actual parenting arrangement.
If you are pursuing a parenting time modification, ask about support at the same time. If you are pursuing a support modification, bring your current parenting schedule. The two calculations are linked.

Getting the numbers right matters. So does knowing when to push for a hearing and when a well-structured stipulation serves your child better.

How much does income need to change to modify child support in Colorado?
Colorado statute defines substantial change as a change that produces a difference of at least 10% in the monthly support obligation when current guidelines are applied to the updated circumstances. Under C.R.S. 14-10-122(1)(b), a change producing less than a 10% difference is not considered substantial. The change also must be continuing, meaning it reflects your actual ongoing financial situation, not a temporary fluctuation.
Can I modify child support if my parenting time changed?
Yes. Under the 2026 guidelines, parenting time is directly factored into the support calculation for every overnight. If the number of overnights you have with your child has changed materially since the original order was entered, that change will affect the calculated support amount. If the resulting difference meets the 10% threshold, it is a basis for modification.
Does child support end when a child turns 18 in Colorado?
No. Colorado child support continues until the child turns 19 or graduates from high school, whichever is later, but not beyond age 21. This is a common misconception. If you are paying or receiving support and a child is approaching 19, you will need to file a motion to modify the order to reflect the reduced obligation for remaining children.
How far back can a modification go?
Modifications only apply to installments that accrue after the date the motion was filed. Courts cannot modify support retroactively for periods before the filing date, under C.R.S. 14-10-122(1)(d). There is a narrow exception for undue hardship or substantial injustice, but this rarely applies. The practical implication: file sooner rather than later.
What if the other parent is hiding income or underreporting earnings?
Colorado courts can impute income to a parent who is voluntarily unemployed or underemployed, based on their actual earning capacity. Under C.R.S. 14-10-115(5)(b.5), the court considers factors including employment history, education, job market conditions, and local prevailing wages. If you believe the other parent is deliberately suppressing income to reduce their support obligation, we can help you build the evidentiary case for imputation.
Do I need an attorney to modify child support?
You are not legally required to have one. But income disputes, imputation arguments, the 2026 guideline changes, and the retroactivity rules all create real traps for people who navigate this process without legal guidance. A motion filed incorrectly or at the wrong time can cost you months of the correct support amount. We give you a straight read from the first call on whether filing makes sense and what the realistic outcome looks like. That conversation costs you nothing. Getting it wrong does.
