## Divorce in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/divorce/

Divorce in Colorado
Ending a marriage is rarely a sudden decision. It is often the result of months or even years of trying to make things work, followed by the difficult realization that moving forward requires letting go. Colorado courts address four primary issues in a dissolution proceeding: allocation of parental responsibilities, parenting time, division of marital property and debt, and spousal maintenance. Each is governed by its own statutory framework and evaluated independently.
At The Drake Law Firm, PC, we understand that divorce is not just a legal transaction; it is a profound life transition. Our family law and divorce lawyers operate with a philosophy of compassionate strength. We are here to help you close this chapter with dignity and clarity, dedicated to securing the protection you need to build a stable, successful future.
Get A Divorce Lawyer Now
Types of Divorce in Colorado
Colorado is a no-fault state under C.R.S. § 14-10-106 — the only legal ground for dissolution is that the marriage is irretrievably broken. Neither party is required to prove fault, misconduct, or wrongdoing. The path a case takes depends on the degree of agreement between the parties and the complexity of the issues involved.
An uncontested divorce occurs when both spouses reach full agreement on every issue before or shortly after filing — including the division of all marital property and debt, spousal maintenance, and all parenting matters. Because no disputes require court resolution, uncontested cases move through the system significantly faster and at lower cost than contested proceedings.
When a complete agreement is in place, parties may file a Decree upon Affidavit under C.R.S. § 14-10-120.3, which allows the judge to review and sign the decree without requiring either party to appear in court. The agreement must still satisfy the court’s review — a judge will not approve a Separation Agreement that is unconscionable or that fails to adequately address the interests of any minor children.
The mandatory 91-day waiting period under C.R.S. § 14-10-106 applies regardless of how quickly the parties agree. No decree can be entered before that period expires from the date of service or joint filing. For couples with straightforward finances and no children, an uncontested case finalized shortly after the waiting period represents the most efficient resolution available under the law.
A contested divorce does not require hostility — it simply means that at least one issue remains unresolved between the parties. Common disputed issues include the characterization or valuation of marital assets, the division of a business or retirement accounts, the amount or duration of spousal maintenance, and the allocation of parental responsibilities or parenting time.
When disputes cannot be resolved through negotiation, Colorado courts use a structured litigation process to reach resolution. Every divorce, contested or not, includes mandatory financial disclosure under C.R.C.P. 16.2, an Initial Status Conference to establish deadlines, discovery if needed, and in most jurisdictions, mandatory mediation before any trial will be scheduled. More often than not, the parties begin negotiating with one another or through their attorneys once they have exchanged mandatory financial disclosures. If mediation does not resolve all issues, the case proceeds to a Permanent Orders Hearing where a District Court judge makes final binding determinations on every unresolved matter.
Colorado courts applying equitable distribution under C.R.S. § 14-10-113 have broad discretion in how they divide marital property. Similarly, Best Interests of the Child determinations under C.R.S. § 14-10-124 give judges significant latitude in parenting matters. The outcome of a contested hearing is therefore much less predictable than a negotiated settlement, which is why resolution short of trial — through negotiation or mediation — is generally preferable when achievable.
Legal Separation
Legal separation in Colorado is a distinct legal proceeding governed by C.R.S. § 14-10-107. It produces a court order that resolves all the same issues as a divorce — property division, debt allocation, spousal maintenance, and parental responsibilities — but does not legally terminate the marriage. The parties remain legally married after a decree of legal separation.
Legal separation is used in circumstances where the parties choose not to divorce for religious, financial, or personal reasons, but require the legal structure of a court order to govern their separated lives. Common reasons include preserving eligibility for a spouse’s health insurance coverage, maintaining certain federal benefits tied to length of marriage, or satisfying religious constraints on divorce.
Either party may file a motion under C.R.S. § 14-10-107(5) requesting the court convert a decree of legal separation into a decree of dissolution of marriage after six months have elapsed. The court applies the same statutory standards to legal separation proceedings as it does to dissolution — including the Best Interests standard for parenting matters and the equitable distribution framework for marital property division.
Collaborative divorce is a structured, non-adversarial resolution process in which both parties and their attorneys sign a Participation Agreement committing to resolve all issues outside of court. The collaborative process typically involves a team of professionals beyond the two attorneys — including a neutral financial specialist who analyzes the marital estate, and a divorce coach or mental health professional who helps manage communication between the parties.
The defining feature of the collaborative process is the withdrawal obligation: if either party terminates the collaborative process and elects to proceed to litigation, both collaborative attorneys must withdraw entirely. The parties must then retain new litigation counsel. This provision creates a strong structural incentive for all participants to work toward resolution, since abandoning the process is costly for both sides.
Collaborative divorce is best suited to cases where both parties are committed to a cooperative resolution and where the financial or parenting issues are sufficiently complex to benefit from neutral professional input. It is generally not appropriate where there is a significant power imbalance, a history of domestic violence, or reason to believe one party is withholding financial information.
Mediation is a structured negotiation process in which a neutral third-party mediator facilitates discussion between the parties to help them reach agreement on contested issues. The mediator does not represent either party, does not provide legal advice, and cannot impose a resolution — their role is to create conditions under which the parties can negotiate effectively.  Mediation in Colorado is almost always conducted remotely, often on Zoom.
In Colorado, mediation is not optional in most contested cases. Courts in Denver and across the state’s judicial districts require parties to attempt mediation before a Permanent Orders Hearing can be scheduled. In Jefferson County though, a Permanent Orders Hearing will be set but it will not occur if the parties have not mediated or attempted to mediate prior to the trial date. This mediation requirement is built into the case management process as detailed in the Case Management Order issued shortly after the Petition for Dissolution is filed and then further established, if necessary, at the Initial Status Conference. Failure to participate in good faith can result in sanctions.
If mediation produces a full agreement, the terms are memorialized in a mediator-drafted agreement called a Memorandum of Understanding or, in a written Separation Agreement and Parenting Plan, which are submitted to the court for approval as part of the final decree. If mediation resolves only some issues, the remaining disputes proceed to a hearing. Mediation can occur at any point in the process — many cases settle in mediation after discovery is complete and both parties have a clear picture of the financial landscape.
Which Process Applies to Your Situation
The appropriate process depends on the level of agreement between the parties, the complexity of the marital estate, and whether children are involved. Uncontested proceedings are available only when full agreement is reached on every issue. Contested proceedings apply when any dispute remains unresolved. Collaborative divorce and mediation are tools for reaching resolution — they are not separate types of divorce but alternative paths to the same court-approved outcome.
Legal separation is a distinct proceeding with specific eligibility requirements that differ substantially from dissolution. Colorado courts handle all of these proceedings in the District Court of the county where either spouse is domiciled.
The Colorado Divorce Process
The state’s legal system follows a specific statutory roadmap governed by the Colorado Revised Statutes and the Colorado Rules of Civil Procedure.
Step 1 — File the Petition. The process begins with the filing of a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage (JDF 1101). Once filed and served, a mandatory 91-day statutory waiting period begins under C.R.S. § 14-10-106. The divorce cannot be finalized until at least 91 days have passed from the date of service or joint filing.
Step 2 — Mandatory Financial Disclosures. Colorado law (C.R.C.P. 16.2) requires full financial transparency from both parties. Within 42 days of service, both parties must exchange mandatory financial disclosures (Form 35.1), including pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements, and credit card bills. Failure to disclose assets fully can result in severe penalties and reopening of the case.
Step 3 — Initial Status Conference (ISC). Shortly after filing, the court schedules an Initial Status Conference with a Court Facilitator or Magistrate. This sets the case timeline, including deadlines for expert disclosure, mediation, and hearings.
Step 4 —Mandatory Mediation. Colorado courts require mediation in all divorce cases, often before the court will even set a final hearing. Mediation is a necessary process, and a mediator can help parties, including parties with counsel, reach a facilitated agreement or partial agreement, which saves time, money and appearances before a judge.
Step 5 — Resolution or Trial. If the parties reach a full agreement, a Separation Agreement and Parenting Plan are drafted and submitted for court approval. If disputes remain unresolved, the case proceeds to a Permanent Orders Hearing where the judge issues a final Decree of Dissolution of Marriage.
Colorado law no longer uses the term “custody.” Under C.R.S. § 14-10-124, courts determine the Allocation of Parental Responsibilities (APR) under Colorado child custody and parenting time law. APR is divided into two components:
Parenting Time — The actual schedule of overnights the child spends with each parent.
Decision-Making Responsibility — Who decides major issues regarding education, religion, and non-emergency medical care (Sole vs. Joint).
The court’s only standard is the best interests of the child. Colorado does not presume that equal parenting time is automatically in the child’s best interests — the court evaluates the specific circumstances of each family. When parenting matters are contested, child support obligations are calculated in conjunction with the parenting time schedule under C.R.S. § 14-10-115.
Equitable Division of Assets
Colorado is an equitable distribution state, not a community property state. Under Colorado’s equitable property division statute, C.R.S. § 14-10-113, the court divides marital property equitably — meaning fairly, not necessarily equally. Factors include:
Each spouse’s contribution to the acquisition of marital property, including homemaking contributions.
The economic circumstances of each spouse at the time of division.
Whether property is marital (acquired during the marriage) or separate (owned prior to marriage or received by inheritance or gift).
Marital property subject to division includes real estate, bank and investment accounts, retirement accounts, business interests, and debt accumulated during the marriage. Separate property — assets owned before the marriage or received as individual gifts or inheritance — is generally excluded from division, though commingling with marital assets often affects that characterization because placing separate property into joint ownership means that property is a presumed gift to the marriage.
Spousal Maintenance
Under Colorado spousal maintenance law, C.R.S. § 14-10-114, maintenance is not automatic. Courts apply advisory guidelines for couples with combined gross incomes under $240,000 per year. The formula calculates maintenance as approximately 40% of the higher earner’s monthly adjusted gross income minus 50% of the lower earner’s monthly adjusted gross income. The duration of maintenance is also guideline-based, scaled to the length of the marriage. Courts retain discretion to deviate from the guidelines based on the specific circumstances of each case.
Colorado Divorce FAQs
How to get a divorce in Colorado?
To obtain a divorce, at least one spouse must be a resident for 91 days before filing a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage. The process involves serving your spouse and waiting a mandatory 91-day “cooling-off” period, during which financial disclosures are exchanged. Hiring a Colorado divorce lawyer at The Drake Law Firm, PC can streamline this process and ensure all legal requirements are met.
How much does a divorce cost in Colorado?
The court charges a standard filing fee to initiate the case, which is $230 as of January 1, 2026 within Colorado. However, the total cost depends heavily on whether the divorce is contested or uncontested. An uncontested divorce is significantly less expensive, whereas a contested case involving a divorce attorney can range from $10,000 to $50,000 or more depending on litigation needs.
How long does divorce take?
Colorado law mandates a minimum 91-day waiting period after the petition is filed and served before a court can issue a final decree. While uncontested divorces can be wrapped up in approximately 4 months, complex cases often take at least a year to resolve.
Are divorce records public?
Yes, certain divorce records are generally public and accessible to anyone after the decree is finalized; however sworn financial statements, supporting financial schedules, child support worksheets and parenting plans are commonly suppressed.  In addition, parties can request that the court seal or redact sensitive documents to protect their privacy, but those requests are not automatically granted.
Is Colorado a no-fault state for divorce?
Yes, Colorado is strictly a “no-fault” divorce state. You do not need to prove marital misconduct such as adultery; you only need to demonstrate to the court that the marriage is “irretrievably broken.
Is Colorado a 50/50 split in divorce?
Colorado is an “equitable distribution” state rather than a community property state, so assets are not automatically split 50/50. Instead, the court divides property in a manner it deems fair and equitable based on the contributions and economic circumstances of each spouse.
What is a spouse entitled to in a divorce in Colorado?
A spouse is entitled to an equitable portion of the marital property and, in certain cases, spousal maintenance (alimony) if he or she earns significantly less than his or her spouse. Navigating these entitlements can be complex, so consulting a Colorado divorce lawyer is highly encouraged to protect your family’s financial future.
Ready to Take the First Step?
You do not have to face this uncertainty alone. Whether you are ready to file or just need to understand your rights, we are here to help. Contact The Drake Law Firm, P.C and talk about your situation so we can map out a clear path forward.

## Common Law Marriage
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/divorce/common-law-marriage/

Understanding Colorado's Common Law Marriage Laws
The Drake Law Firm, P.C. helps couples in common law marriages obtain legal divorces.
Common Law Marriage in Golden, CO
Do you cohabit with another person that you consider your husband or wife, even though you aren’t legally married? If the other party also considers you to be his or her spouse, you are in a common law marriage. Common law marriages are legally recognized, and you can obtain a divorce if you’re ready for the relationship to end. However, the divorce process isn’t nearly as straightforward since you don’t have legal marriage documents.
Our Golden, CO, common law marriage lawyer is experienced in these relationships. We can gather evidence to prove the marriage and then negotiate or litigate the divorce. We can also help you determine if you’re eligible for child support, alimony, and more. Contact us for a consultation today.
Requirements for Common Law Marriage in Colorado
Common law marriage has been legal in Colorado since 1877, and the requirements are very basic. Your relationship is recognized as a common law marriage if both parties:
Consent to the marriage
Present themselves as married
Are 18 years or older, or have received consent if 16 or 17 years of age
Are unmarried
Evidence To Prove Common Law Marriage
Your Golden, CO, common law marriage lawyer will need to gather evidence to prove the marriage exists before you obtain a divorce. There are numerous pieces of evidence needed for these cases. Some possible evidence includes proof of cohabitation, shared bills, joint tax returns, joint bank accounts, and jointly-owned property. In addition, your attorney can show that you celebrate anniversaries and refer to each other as husband or wife in public.
If you held a commitment ceremony, you could also use that as evidence. In addition, your attorney might interview friends and family to prove that you acted as a married couple. If your lawyer can prove that you were in a common law marriage, you can then take steps to end the marriage.
Common Law Marriage And Divorce
If the court decides that you are in a common law marriage, you can move forward with a divorce. The divorce process is the same for common law and standard marriages with one caveat. You’re only obligated to divide marital property when divorcing in Colorado. However, determining the start date of a common law marriage can be difficult. The other party might claim that property was acquired during the marriage when it was actually purchased beforehand. Your Golden, CO, common law marriage lawyer can provide evidence to help determine the start date of the marriage.
Along with dividing property, you will also decide on matters such as debts, child support, child custody, and alimony. Your attorney will represent you each step of the way, so you can reach a desirable outcome when the divorce is finalized.
What If You Weren’t In A Common Law Marriage?
Were you served with divorce papers, but you don’t believe you were married? You cannot enter into a common law marriage unless you agree to do so. Our Golden, CO, common law marriage lawyer can help you prove your case in court. First, we must show that you are not married to the other party. Then, we will work on dismissing the divorce case, so you won’t have to divide your assets or worry about spousal support. Contact us today for a consultation so we can begin building your case.
Legally Prohibited Marriages In Colorado
If you or the other party is already married, you cannot enter into a common law marriage. The court will not recognize your marriage, so you cannot obtain a divorce. However, if you share children with the other party, you still might be eligible for child support. In addition, you will need to work out child custody. A Golden, CO, common law marriage lawyer can help you handle the legalities involved in the dissolution of your relationship.

## Contested Divorce in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/divorce/contested-divorce/

Contested Divorce in Colorado
A contested divorce in Colorado means you and your spouse cannot agree on one or more issues the court must decide to end your marriage. That can include parenting time, decision-making, child support, spousal maintenance, property, debt, or any combination of those. When agreement is out of reach, a judge ends up making the call.
A contested divorce is a slower process, more expensive, and more emotionally taxing than an uncontested one. It also requires a different strategy. You need a clear picture of what is worth fighting for, what you are willing to fight for, where you can find common ground, and what the court is likely to order if you cannot .
What Makes a Divorce Contested in Colorado
Colorado is a no-fault divorce state. The only legal ground for ending a marriage is that the relationship is irretrievably broken. [1]
No one has to prove infidelity, abandonment, or any other wrongdoing for the dissolution itself to move forward.
What makes a divorce contested is disagreement about what happens next, not the reason for ending the marriage. If you and your spouse cannot agree on one or more of the issues below, the case is contested.
Parenting time and decision-making. Colorado replaced the term ‘custody’ with allocation of parental responsibilities, often shortened to APR. Disputes cover where the children live, how time is divided, and who makes major decisions about education, health care, and religion.
Child support. Colorado uses an income-shares model based on both parents’ gross income, the number of overnights with each parent, health insurance costs, and work-related child care.
Spousal maintenance. Colorado calls alimony “spousal maintenance” although it’s often still called alimony in everyday conversation. Disputes are usually about whether maintenance is owed, how much, whether it’s actually needed, and for how long.
Property and debt division. Colorado is a fair and equitable distribution of property state. Assets and debts acquired during the marriage are divided fairly, which does not always mean equally, but it often does.
Other contested issues. Hidden assets, business valuation, retirement account division, separate property claims, and tax filing for the year of divorce all show up regularly.
Even one open issue makes the divorce contested. Many cases start contested and become uncontested as disclosures, mediation, and negotiation work through the conflict.
The Contested Divorce Process in Colorado
Colorado dissolution cases follow a defined sequence under the Uniform Dissolution of Marriage Act and the civil rules for domestic relations cases. Here is how a contested divorce typically moves through the system.
Petition and response. One spouse files a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage in the district court of the county where either party lives. The other spouse is served unless they sign a waiver of service, and then has 21 days to file a Response, or 35 days if served outside Colorado.
Residency check. At least one party must have been domiciled in Colorado for 91 days before the petition was filed
Mandatory financial disclosures. Both parties must exchange specific financial information under C.R.C.P. Rule 16.2 [2],including a Sworn Financial Statement, 3 years of tax returns, 3 months of pay stubs, the most recent account statements for bank accounts, investment accounts, retirement accounts, credit cards and other debt records. Initial disclosures are due within 42 days of service.
Initial Status Conference. The court typically schedules an Initial Status Conference within about 40 days of filing. Deadlines get set here, mediation is usually ordered to be set and completed within a certain time frame, experts are discussed (such as appraisers, business valuators, child and family investigators, etc.) and procedural questions get sorted out.
Temporary orders. If you need decisions in place while the case is pending, you can request a temporary orders hearing. Common temporary issues include who lives in the house, how bills get paid, and the parenting schedule prior to the divorce being finalized.  Often though, courts will require mediation prior to setting the temporary orders hearing.
Discovery and experts. Contested cases often require additional discovery beyond mandatory disclosures, including written questions, document requests, depositions, business valuations, real estate appraisals, custody evaluations, or vocational assessments.
Mediation. Most Colorado courts require mediation before a final hearing. In Jefferson County, mediation is standard procedure in contested family law cases, and many cases resolve at this stage.
Permanent Orders Hearing. If the case does not settle, the court holds a trial called the Permanent Orders Hearing. Both sides present evidence, call witnesses, and argue their positions, and the judge then enters final orders on every open issue, but not necessarily at the conclusion of the hearing.  More and more, judges will issue the final orders within a few weeks of the actual hearing.
Decree of Dissolution. A final decree cannot be entered until 91 days have passed since service of the petition or the respondent’s first appearance. In contested cases, the decree is usually issued after the Permanent Orders Hearing concludes.
How Long a Contested Divorce Takes in Colorado
Colorado law sets a minimum of 91 days from service of the petition before a decree can be entered. In a contested case, the practical timeline is usually much longer.
Most contested divorces in Colorado finish six to eighteen months after filing. The length depends on several factors.
Complexity of the issues. A case with a contested parenting plan, a business to value, and disputed maintenance moves slower than one with a single open issue.
Court calendar. Trial dates in busy districts like Jefferson County are often booked months out.
Cooperation level. Cases where both sides exchange disclosures on time and engage in good-faith negotiation finish faster.
Discovery scope. Depositions, expert witnesses, and custody evaluations each add weeks or months to the timeline.
If you want a faster outcome, the path is usually to participate in a negotiated settlement, not a faster trial date. That is why we push hard on resolution of any issues that can be resolved equitably, whether that resolution occurs in mediation or outside of it.  Litigation is the right tool when it is the only one that works, and it is rarely the fastest one.
How The Drake Law Firm Helps With Contested Divorce
At The Drake Law Firm, contested cases sit inside our broader Colorado divorce practice, which also covers uncontested filings, legal separation, mediation, and collaborative options. We represent clients across Jefferson County, the Denver metro, and the Front Range.
We do not believe a contested divorce has to be a war. Many cases that start with high conflict end in a negotiated settlement, once both sides have full financial information and time to think. Our job is to make sure you walk into every step informed, protected, and represented by someone who knows how Colorado divorce actually works.
What we do:
Push for resolution where resolution is possible. Most contested cases settle. Preparation is what makes settlement happen on terms you can live with.
File and respond on time. Petitions, responses, motions, disclosures, and discovery requests, filed inside the deadlines that govern Colorado dissolution cases.
Bring in the right experts. Business valuators, custody evaluators, vocational experts, and forensic accountants when the case actually needs them.
Litigate when settlement fails. If the other side refuses to engage in good faith, we are ready to take the case to the Permanent Orders Hearing and present your position to the judge.
Tell you when a fight is not worth it. A win on paper that costs you another year and tens of thousands in fees is not always a win. We will say so.

What we do not do:
Take cases driven by punishment. If the goal is to punish the other parent, drag out the process for leverage, or weaponize the children, we are not the firm for you.
Frank, Honest Advice. We will tell you that directly in the first meeting. A contested divorce is hard enough without making it harder than it has to be.
What Issues Get Contested
Most Colorado contested divorces center on one or more of the following. The longer the marriage and the more complicated the finances, the more issues tend to be in dispute at the same time.
Parenting time and decision-making. Colorado courts decide parental responsibilities under a best-interests-of-the-child standard. Factors include each parent’s relationship with the child, the child’s adjustment to home and community, and the ability of the parents to cooperate.
Child support. Colorado calculates child support using a statutory formula that considers both parents’ gross income, the number of overnights with each parent, health insurance costs, and work-related child care.
Spousal maintenance. Maintenance disputes are usually about whether the lower-earning spouse needs ongoing support, how much, and for how long. Colorado has advisory guidelines that apply to marriages of three years or longer.
Property and debt. Equitable distribution divides marital property and debt fairly between spouses. Separate property generally stays with the spouse who owned it before the marriage, though commingling and appreciation can complicate the analysis.
Business valuation. When one or both spouses own a business, valuing it accurately and deciding what happens to it is often the largest line item in the case.
Hidden assets and financial misconduct. When one spouse suspects the other is concealing income, undervaluing property, or moving money, formal discovery tools become essential.
Do I have to live in Colorado to file for divorce here?
Yes, at least one spouse must have been domiciled in Colorado for 91 days before the petition is filed. The case is filed in the district court of the county where one party lives.
How much does a contested divorce cost in Colorado?
The total cost depends on how much of the case actually gets contested. Hourly billing means the time and complexity of your specific issues drive the bill. A case involving a business valuation, custody evaluation, and multi-day trial costs significantly more than one with a single open issue.
Can a contested divorce become uncontested?
Yes, and it often does. Many cases start contested simply because the parties have not yet exchanged full financial information or had a structured conversation about the open issues. Once disclosures are complete and mediation has taken place, settlement becomes possible in cases that initially looked stuck.
Do we have to go to trial?
Not usually. Most contested divorces in Colorado settle before the Permanent Orders Hearing. We prepare every case as if it could go to trial, because that preparation strengthens settlement leverage.
What happens if my spouse refuses to participate?
The case still moves forward. If a respondent fails to file a Response within the deadline, the petitioner can request a default. The court can issue orders on parenting time, support, and property division without the non-participating spouse’s input.

## Uncontested Divorce in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/divorce/uncontested-divorce/

Uncontested Divorce in Colorado
An uncontested divorce in Colorado is one where you and your spouse agree on every issue the court would otherwise have to decide. That includes parenting time, decision-making, child support, spousal maintenance, property division, and debt. When the agreement is written, signed by the parties and submitted to the court,t, the court approves it, signs a decree of dissolution and the marriage ends.
Uncontested is the fastest, least expensive, and least adversarial path through a Colorado divorce. It is also the path where small mistakes have the biggest consequences. A bad property valuation, a vague parenting plan, or a missed disclosure can lock in a result you will spend years trying to fix.
What Makes a Divorce Uncontested in Colorado
A divorce is uncontested when both spouses sign an agreement covering every issue in the case before the court has to rule on it. The agreement may be filed with the court along with the divorce petition, supporting documents and required financial disclosures. Or the settlement may be filed after the case has been going on for a period of time but prior to any final hearing. If even one issue is left open, the case is contested, not uncontested.
Issues that must be fully resolved:
Parenting time and decision-making. Colorado uses allocation of parental responsibilities instead of custody. The parenting plan must cover where the children live, how time is divided, and who decides major issues about school, health care, and religion.
Child support. Both parents’ incomes, parenting time, health insurance, and child care costs feed into the Colorado guideline formula. The agreed support amount has to fall within what a court would approve.
Spousal maintenance. Whether maintenance is paid, the amount, and the duration must be agreed in writing. The court will review whether the terms are fair and consistent with Colorado law.
Property and debt. Every marital asset and debt has to be identified, valued, and divided in the agreement. That covers the house, retirement accounts, vehicles, credit cards, and loans.
Separate property claims. If either party owned property before the marriage or received gifts or inheritance during it, those claims must be documented in the agreement.
Uncontested does not mean unprepared. Both spouses still owe each other full financial disclosure, and the court still has to approve the agreement before entering a decree.
The Uncontested Divorce Process in Colorado
The Colorado dissolution process follows the same statutory framework whether the case is contested or uncontested. Uncontested cases have fewer disputes and finish faster. Here is how an uncontested divorce typically moves through the system.
Decide how to file. Spouses can file a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage as co-petitioners, or one spouse can file the Petition and the other can sign a waiver of service. Joint filing is cleaner when both sides are in agreement on every issue.
Residency check. At least one party must have been domiciled in Colorado for 91 days before the petition is filed.[1]
Mandatory financial disclosures. Both parties exchange Sworn Financial Statements and supporting documentation under C.R.C.P. Rule 16.2[2]. This step is required even when the divorce is uncontested, and it is the foundation for a defensible settlement.
Initial Status Conference. Most Colorado district courts hold an Initial Status Conference within roughly 40 days of filing. In some counties, the ISC can be waived if the case is filed jointly with a complete settlement agreement attached.
Parenting class. If you have minor children, both parents must complete a court-approved parenting class. The certificate of completion of that class is filed with the court.
Draft and sign the Separation Agreement and Parenting Plan. These are  the documents that capture your full agreement on property, debt, support, and, if children are involved, parenting time and decision-making. Both spouses sign before filing.
91-day waiting period. Colorado law sets a minimum of 91 days from service of the petition, the respondent’s first appearance, or the date of joint filing before a decree can be entered.
Submit final paperwork. After the waiting period, the parties submit the final documents for court approval. The package includes the Decree of Dissolution, support order, parenting plan, and Separation Agreement.
Decree of Dissolution. Many Colorado courts enter the decree on the paperwork alone, often called a Decree on Affidavit, when the agreement is complete. Cases with children may require a brief non-contested hearing instead.
How Long an Uncontested Divorce Takes in Colorado
Colorado law sets a minimum of 91 days from filing or service before a decree can be entered. Most uncontested divorces in Colorado finish three to six months from filing.
The timeline depends on several factors.
Whether you have children. Cases with minor children usually take longer because parenting class certificates must be filed and a brief non-contested hearing is often required.
Court calendar and procedure. Some counties process Decrees on Affidavit quickly. Others require scheduling a non-contested hearing, which adds weeks to the timeline.
Disclosure completeness. If financial disclosures are partial or late, the case stalls. Clean, complete disclosures filed on time keep the case moving.
Agreement quality. A vague or incomplete Separation Agreement gets sent back for revisions, which restarts the clock on signing and filing.
If both sides are ready at filing and have already negotiated the Separation Agreement, the 91-day waiting period is usually the longest single delay. Cases without children, with complete disclosures and clear agreements, can be wrapped up shortly after that window closes.
When an Uncontested Divorce Becomes Contested
Cases shift from uncontested to contested more often than people expect. The most common triggers are predictable.
New financial information. Once the actual financial picture is on paper, prior verbal agreements sometimes fall apart.
Changed parenting positions. What sounded reasonable in conversation can feel different once it is written into a binding plan.
Tax consequences. Real estate transfers, retirement account splits, and dependency claims have tax implications that change the math.
Valuation disputes. A house, a business, or a retirement account can be valued multiple ways. If the parties cannot agree on the number, they cannot agree on the division.
New facts. A new job, a new relationship, or a planned move can change what either side is willing to accept.
If your case shifts mid-process, you have not failed at divorce. You have learned what was actually in dispute. The path forward usually moves into a Colorado contested divorce, which has a different process, timeline, and strategy.
Do You Still Need a Lawyer for an Uncontested Divorce?
You are not required to hire an attorney for an uncontested divorce in Colorado. Many people file pro se (not represented by an attorney) using the JDF forms published by the Colorado Judicial Branch.
What an attorney brings to an uncontested case:
Disclosure accuracy. Mandatory disclosures are the legal foundation of the agreement. Missing a retirement account or undervaluing a business can void parts of the settlement later.
Agreement drafting. Separation Agreements need precise language on enforcement, modification, and tax treatment. Template agreements fail in predictable ways.
Parenting plan structure. Vague schedules and decision-making provisions create conflict the day after the decree is signed.
Procedural compliance. Different counties have different filing quirks. A rejected filing pushes the case back weeks.
If your case is genuinely simple, with a short marriage, no children, no real estate, no retirement, and no maintenance, pro se may work. The closer you get to any of those variables, the more an attorney is worth the cost compared to fixing the same problem in a post-decree modification.
How The Drake Law Firm Helps With Uncontested Divorce
At The Drake Law Firm, uncontested cases sit inside our broader Colorado divorce practice, which also covers contested cases, legal separation, mediation, and collaborative options. We represent clients across Jefferson County, the Denver metro, and the Front Range.
Our job in an uncontested case is to make sure your agreement actually does what you want it to do, ten years from now. That means we treat the documents seriously even when the relationship is friendly.
What we do:
Run the finances. Complete mandatory disclosures, ensure accurate valuations, and generally there are no surprises later.
Draft the Separation Agreement and Parenting Plan. Language built to hold up to enforcement and/or modification, depending on the issue.
File so the court accepts it the first time. County-specific procedural quirks handled.
Flag what looks off. An undervalued asset, a parenting schedule that will collapse in six months, or a tax treatment that hurts one spouse.
Tell you when not to sign. If we cannot recommend the agreement as drafted, we will tell you that, and tell you why.
How we work:
Offices in Golden and Lakewood. Serving Jefferson County, the Denver Metro Area, and the Front Range.
Hourly billing. Uncontested cases take a fraction of the time a contested case requires.
Discounted $200 initial consultation. The right place to get a rough sense of cost.
Flexible access. In-person, phone and Zoom consultations available. Saturday appointments by request.
Can we file jointly if neither of us has a lawyer?
Yes. Colorado allows spouses to file a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage as co-petitioners without attorneys. The court still requires complete financial disclosures, a Separation Agreement, and a Parenting Plan if there are children.
How fast can an uncontested divorce in Colorado finish?
The minimum is 91 days after the petition is filed or served. In practice, three to six months from filing is typical, depending on whether you have children and how quickly the court processes the final paperwork.
Do both spouses still need to file financial disclosures if the divorce is uncontested?
Yes. C.R.C.P. Rule 16.2 requires mandatory financial disclosures in every Colorado dissolution case, including uncontested ones. Skipping or shortcutting disclosures can void parts of the agreement later if one side claims surprise.
What happens if we sign the agreement and one of us changes their mind?
A signed Separation Agreement is binding once the court enters the decree. Before that, either party can ask the court to set the agreement aside for cause. After the decree, most provisions can only be modified for reasons defined by Colorado law, such as a substantial change in circumstances for support.
Do we both need to appear in court?
Not always. Many Colorado courts will enter a Decree of Dissolution based on the paperwork alone, called a Decree on Affidavit, if all documents are complete. Cases with children sometimes require a brief non-contested hearing where the court verifies the agreement.
Sources:
[1] C.R.S. § 14-10-106. Dissolution of marriage and legal separation; jurisdiction and grounds; residency and waiting period. | https://colorado.public.law/statutes/crs_14-10-106
[2] C.R.C.P. Rule 16.2. Court Facilitated Management of Domestic Relations Cases and General Provisions Governing Duty of Disclosure (Colorado Judicial Branch). | https://www.coloradojudicial.gov/sites/default/files/2024-06/Supplement%209_23_22.pdf

## Colorado Guardianship
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/guardianship/

Colorado Guardianship
Understanding how caregivers can petition for emergency, temporary, and permanent guardianship to secure legal authority and protect the best interests of children under Colorado law.
When a family reaches a breaking point, the priority is always the safety and stability of the children involved. Whether a parent is facing addiction, a serious illness, incarceration, or has abandoned the home, relatives or loved ones often step in to provide care. Unfortunately, doing the right thing does not automatically grant you the legal authority you need.
Without a court order, you may be unable to enroll the child in school, consent to medical treatment, or protect the child from being removed from a potentially unsafe situation. These challenges create unnecessary stress at an already difficult time.
At The Drake Law Firm, PC, we help caregivers turn temporary arrangements into legally protected solutions—so the child in your care has stability, and you have the authority to act in their best interests.
Important Scope Notice:
This page addresses minor guardianship (children under 18) under Colorado law. Guardianship of an incapacitated adult or aging parent follows a different probate process and requires additional medical evidence.
What Is Guardianship?
Guardianship is a court-supervised legal arrangement in which a judge grants a qualified adult the authority to make personal, medical, and educational decisions for a child. In legal terms, a guardian assumes the powers and responsibilities of a parent, while biological parents’ rights are temporarily limited or suspended by court order.
Colorado courts do not grant guardianship lightly. The court’s guiding standard in every case is the best interests of the child.
When Is Legal Guardianship Necessary?
Biological parents have fundamental constitutional rights. However, guardianship may be appropriate when a parent is unable or unwilling to provide adequate care and supervision.
Colorado courts commonly consider guardianship in situations involving:
Parental Incapacity: Serious illness, mental health crises, or long-term rehabilitation
Unsafe Living Conditions: Domestic violence, chronic neglect, or substance abuse
Abandonment: A child left with relatives without ongoing parental support
Incarceration: When a parent cannot fulfill daily caregiving responsibilities
Each case is fact-specific, and no outcome is guaranteed without court approval.
Guardianship vs. Adoption
The difference between guardianship and adoption is critical.
Guardianship is typically temporary or reversible. Parental rights are not terminated; instead, they are limited while the guardianship remains in place.
Adoption permanently terminates the biological parents’ rights and establishes a new legal parent-child relationship.
Families often pursue guardianship when there is hope a parent may eventually regain the ability to care for the child, or when preserving family ties is important.
Types of Guardianship in Colorado​
Colorado law allows different forms of guardianship depending on the child’s needs:
Emergency Guardianship
Granted only when a child faces immediate danger. Emergency authority is strictly limited and generally lasts up to 60 days, allowing time for further court review.
Temporary Guardianship
Often used when a parent is temporarily unable to provide care, such as during medical treatment or rehabilitation. Temporary guardianships typically last up to six months.
Permanent (Plenary) Guardianship
A longer-term solution that generally remains in effect until the child turns 18 or the court determines the guardianship is no longer necessary.
Guardianship vs. Conservatorship
In Colorado:
A guardian is responsible for the child’s personal well-being, including medical care, education, and daily living decisions.
A conservator manages a child’s financial assets.
If a child receives significant assets—such as an inheritance, settlement, or insurance proceeds—the court may require a separate conservatorship to protect those funds until adulthood. Whether a conservatorship is required depends on the amount and circumstances involved.
The Guardianship Process in Colorado
While each case is unique, uncontested guardianship matters often proceed more quickly. Emergency orders may be available when immediate harm is present.
Step 1: Filing the Petition
A guardianship petition (Form JDF 824) is filed in the county where the child resides. Supporting evidence must demonstrate why the guardianship serves the child’s best interests.
Court Filing Fees: Fees are set by statute and may vary by county. Additional costs can apply in contested cases.
Step 2: Meeting Eligibility Requirements
In most cases, a guardian must be a competent adult age 21 or older. The court typically requires:
A name-based Colorado Bureau of Investigation (CBI) background check
A current credit report
A valid government-issued photo ID
Step 3: Notice to Interested Parties
Biological parents must receive legal notice. If a parent cannot be located, the court may allow service by publication. Children age 12 or older are also entitled to notice and may express consent or objection.
Step 4: The Guardianship Hearing
A judge reviews the evidence and testimony. If all parties consent, the process is generally streamlined. If objections are raised, the court may require additional proof, evaluations, or the appointment of a court visitor.
Rights and Responsibilities of a Guardian
Once appointed, a guardian may be authorized to:
Consent to medical care, including treatment and procedures
Enroll the child in school and make educational decisions
Determine the child’s residence and provide daily care
Guardians are required to file an Annual Guardian’s Report (Form JDF 834) with the court to document the child’s well-being and living situation.
The Role of a Guardianship Attorney in Colorado
Stepping into the role of a guardian is an act of care and responsibility. Understanding Colorado’s guardianship laws is an important step in ensuring the child in your care receives lasting legal protection.
If you are caring for a child who is not your own, a verbal agreement is not enough.
Consulting with a qualified Colorado family law attorney can help ensure the arrangement is legally sound and sustainable for everyone involved.
How The Drake Law Firm, PC Supports Families
Stepping into the role of a guardian is an act of care and responsibility. Navigating Colorado’s guardianship laws should not add to the burden.
As your guardianship attorney, The Drake Law Firm, PC helps by:
Preparing and filing court-ready petitions
Managing background checks and service requirements
Addressing contested hearings and objections
Advocating for stability and long-term protection for the child
Our goal is to create a legally sound, sustainable arrangement that protects the child and provides peace of mind for your family.
If you are caring for a child who is not your own, a verbal agreement is not enough. Legal protection matters.
Contact The Drake Law Firm, PC today to discuss your Guardianship options

Golden Family Law Attorney FAQs
How can a Golden family law attorney help me with divorce or custody?
A Golden family law attorney assists clients with legal matters that affect their families, including divorce, child custody, parenting plans, child support, and dividing property. At The Drake Law Firm, we work closely with clients to understand their goals and take practical steps to protect their future. Whether you’re starting a divorce, adjusting custody arrangements, or handling support issues, a family lawyer guides you through your rights, paperwork, and agreements.
Will I need to appear in court for a family law case in Golden?
Not every family law case in Golden requires an in-person court appearance. Most cases start with a virtual Initial Status Conference. Many matters, such as custody schedules, support agreements, or property division, can often be resolved through negotiation or mediation. If both parties cooperate, your Golden family law attorney can help create legally binding agreements without stepping into a courtroom. If disputes arise, your lawyer is ready to represent you at hearings to protect your interests.
What is the timeline for getting a divorce in Colorado?
Colorado requires a 91-day waiting period before a divorce can be finalized, beginning after your spouse is served or immediately if you file jointly. Beyond this mandatory period, the divorce timeline depends on how quickly you and your spouse reach agreements on issues like child custody, support, and property division. A Golden family lawyer can help ensure your case moves efficiently and all legal requirements are handled correctly.
What if my spouse and I already agree on all divorce terms?
If both spouses agree on parenting schedules, asset division, and support, you can submit your settlement to the court for approval. This is called an uncontested divorce. Uncontested divorces in Golden are generally faster and more affordable than contested cases. A Golden family law attorney will review your financial disclosures, parenting plan, and agreements to ensure everything meets Colorado law, then file the necessary documents to finalize your divorce smoothly.
Can child custody or support orders be changed in later?
Yes. Custody and child support orders can be modified in Golden if circumstances change, such as a job loss, relocation, or changes in a child’s needs. To request a modification, you must show that the new situation significantly affects the original order. A Golden family law attorney can help prepare and file your request and advocate for adjustments that reflect your current reality.
