## Paternity in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/paternity/

Paternity in Colorado
The Drake Law Firm, P.C., helps parents establish paternity so they can create child custody and support agreements.
Questions about paternity rights and obligations arise when an unmarried father seeks parental recognition, when a mother needs financial support enforced, or when a child’s legal identity requires formal resolution. This page explains how Colorado law defines and establishes parentage, the procedures involved, and what each party can expect after a legal determination is made. The Drake Law Firm, PC represents clients throughout Colorado in paternity proceedings, applying the statutory framework below to the specific facts of each case.
Why Establishing Paternity Matters in Colorado
A clear legal distinction separates biological fatherhood from legal fatherhood. Biological ties simply confirm shared DNA. Legal fatherhood is a court-recognized status that creates binding, enforceable rights and obligations governed by the Colorado Children’s Code. If parents are unmarried at the time of birth, the state does not automatically grant the biological father legal standing. Without a formal determination of parentage, an unmarried biological father cannot pursue allocation of parental responsibilities to demand physical care or make legal decisions for his child.
The Benefits of Legal Paternity
Securing a legal finding of parentage activates essential statutory protections.
For the Father: A legal father gains standing to petition for an Allocation of Parental Responsibilities under C.R.S. § 14-10-124. This includes the right to seek physical parenting time and legal decision-making authority.
For the Mother: Establishing paternity triggers the court’s authority to order child support obligations and guidelines under C.R.S. § 14-10-115. It provides a mechanism to legally enforce financial contributions.
For the Child: Children gain a recognized legal relationship. This unlocks inheritance rights, access to complete medical histories, and eligibility for derivative benefits like Social Security.
Three Ways to Establish Paternity in Colorado
Colorado provides three legal pathways to establish paternity: a statutory presumption based on marriage, a signed Voluntary Acknowledgment of Parentage, or a judicial court order following a Petition to Determine Paternity. Each method carries distinct legal requirements and deadlines.
1. Marriage (The Presumption)
Under C.R.S. § 19-4-105, a man is presumed to be the natural father if he and the mother are married when the child is born. This statutory presumption also applies if the child is born within 300 days after a marriage is terminated by death or dissolution. Rebutting this presumption requires filing a specific legal action to declare the nonexistence of the parent-child relationship.
2. Voluntary Acknowledgment (At the Hospital)
Unwed parents can establish legal fatherhood without court intervention. Under C.R.S. § 19-4-105(2)(a.5), parties can sign a Voluntary Acknowledgment of Parentage. Parents typically complete this form at the hospital after birth or later through the state vital records office. A duly executed acknowledgment acts as a binding legal finding. Per C.R.S. § 19-4-105(2)(b)(I), either party has a strict 60-day window to rescind the acknowledgment. After 60 days pass, challenging the document requires proving fraud, duress, or a material mistake of fact.
3. Court Order (Judicial Paternity)
A judicial order becomes necessary when parents disagree on parentage or when an unmarried father needs a specific, enforceable parenting plan. The process begins by filing a Petition to Determine Paternity. A court order is the most secure method because it establishes paternity, an enforceable parenting plan, and a child support obligation simultaneously.
Statutory deadlines for paternity actions in Colorado are strict. Schedule a paternity case review with The Drake Law Firm, PC to evaluate your specific circumstances.
The Paternity Process: From Petition to Final Judgment
Step 1: Filing and Standing
Colorado law outlines exactly who has standing to file a paternity petition. Under C.R.S. § 19-4-107, the mother, the child, the alleged father, or the state department of human services can initiate the action. C.R.S. § 19-4-108 allows an action to be brought at any time prior to the child’s eighteenth birthday. If the child brings the action directly, they have until their twenty-first birthday to file. Our Colorado paternity and family law attorneys represent both mothers and fathers at every stage of this process.
Step 2: Genetic Testing (DNA)
When paternity is disputed, the court will order the parties to submit to genetic testing. A court-admissible test typically involves a buccal (cheek) swab from the child and the alleged father, collected at an accredited laboratory under a strict chain-of-custody protocol — over-the-counter kits are not sufficient for legal proceedings. The laboratory then compares DNA markers from both samples. Under C.R.S. § 13-25-126, if genetic test results show a 97 percent or higher probability of paternity, the court applies a legal presumption that the man is the biological father. Refusing to submit to a court-ordered test can lead the judge to enter a default judgment against the non-compliant party.
Step 3: The Final Judgment and Parenting Plan
Once the court confirms parentage, the judge issues a final decree. This official ruling establishes the legal relationship permanently. The court then transitions to establishing a formal parental responsibilities and parenting time order and a child support obligation. Fathers should note that establishing paternity without securing a court-ordered parenting plan leaves them with recognized status but no enforceable right to see the child.
Rights and Responsibilities After Paternity Is Established
Once paternity is legally established, both parents acquire enforceable rights and obligations. The court will allocate parental responsibilities, set a parenting time schedule, and issue a child support order. These orders govern the legal and financial relationship between the parents and child going forward — informal arrangements made before paternity was established are not enforceable.
Parenting Time and Decision-Making
The court crafts a parenting plan based on the best interests of the child under C.R.S. § 14-10-124. This plan dictates the specific schedule for physical care and allocates legal decision-making authority over matters such as education, healthcare, and religious upbringing. When a father has been absent for an extended period, Colorado courts often implement step-up plans that gradually increase parenting time to help the child adjust safely.
Financial Obligations
Courts calculate child support obligations based on the statutory guidelines found in C.R.S. § 14-10-115, factoring in both parents’ gross incomes and the parenting time schedule. Under C.R.S. § 19-4-116, the court may also direct the father to pay the reasonable expenses of the mother’s pregnancy and confinement. The final financial order will address the allocation of health insurance coverage and tax dependency exemptions. Our team can assist with support calculations and enforcement from any of our Colorado family law offices.
Frequently Asked Questions About Paternity in Colorado
How early can you get a paternity test?
Prenatal paternity testing is available as early as seven to nine weeks into the pregnancy through Non-Invasive Prenatal Paternity (NIPP) testing, which uses a blood draw from the mother and carries no procedural risk to the pregnancy. Amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling (CVS) can also determine paternity earlier in pregnancy but carry procedural risks. Colorado courts generally wait until after the child is born before issuing formal legal orders regarding parentage and support.
Can you get a paternity test while pregnant in Colorado?
Yes. Non-Invasive Prenatal Paternity testing can be performed during pregnancy and produces results that are accurate and legally admissible when both parties consent voluntarily. If the alleged father refuses to test, Colorado courts generally wait until the child is born before compelling a court-ordered genetic test in order to avoid risk to the pregnancy.
How much does a paternity test cost in Colorado?
The cost of a legally admissible, chain-of-custody DNA test generally ranges from $300 to $500. At-home kits are less expensive but are not admissible in court proceedings. Under C.R.S. § 19-4-117, the court may order one or both parties to pay the cost of genetic testing.
How long does a paternity test take to get results?
Results from an accredited laboratory typically take between three and five business days once all required genetic samples are collected. Expedited processing is available at some laboratories for an additional fee. The legal process to compel an unwilling party to submit to testing can take considerably longer depending on court scheduling.
Do I have to put the father on the birth certificate in Colorado?
If parents are unmarried, the father’s name cannot be added to the birth certificate unless both parties sign a Voluntary Acknowledgment of Parentage. This is a Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment rule — not simply the mother’s choice. Without a signed VAP or a court order, the biological father has no legal rights to the child.
Why Choose The Drake Law Firm, PC?
Paternity actions require a precise understanding of the Uniform Parentage Act and strict adherence to statutory deadlines. The Drake Law Firm, PC is committed to guiding clients through this highly technical process. We commonly see clients who risk losing their parental rights because they misunderstood the strict 60-day rescission window for voluntary acknowledgment forms — our team works to prevent those critical errors and secure enforceable rights from the outset. Schedule a paternity case review to discuss the specific facts of your case.

## Prenuptial & Postnuptial Agreements in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/prenup-postnup/

Colorado Prenuptial
& Postnuptial Agreements
The Drake Law Firm, P.C., protects individuals before and during marriage with prenup and postnuptial agreements.
When you enter into a marriage, you expect it to last forever. However, you also realize that life can change in an instant, and there might come a time when you decide to part ways. If that happens, you want it to be as easy as possible. That’s where a prenup or postnuptial agreement can help. These marriage agreements allow you to protect your property and interests in the case of divorce. Then, you can feel secure in your marriage.
Contact our Golden, CO, prenup and postnuptial agreements lawyer today to discuss your needs. We can help you create a prenuptial agreement if you’ve yet to walk down the aisle or a postnuptial agreement if you’re already married.
When to Get a Prenup or Postnuptial Agreement
While anyone can benefit from a prenup or postnuptial agreement, the documents are especially important in certain cases. Consult with a Golden, CO, prenup and postnuptial agreement lawyer if one or more parties:
Owns significant assets
Has assets that they want to own privately
Owns a business
Has children from a previous marriage and wants to preserve the children’s inheritance rights
Is going to receive a significant inheritance
Do You Need A Prenup Or A Postnuptial Agreement?
If you are yet to be married, you can benefit from a prenuptial agreement. This agreement will allow you to decide how to divide your property and debt if the marriage doesn’t work. You can also choose what to do with inheritances, retirement accounts, beneficiary designations, and alimony when creating this agreement.
If you are already married, a postnuptial agreement is an option. This is most often used when one party starts a business or discovers an upcoming inheritance. The agreement allows the party to protect his or her financial interests. As long as you are still married and both parties agree, you can enter into a postnuptial agreement.
Enforceable Prenup And Postnuptial Agreements
Creating an enforceable marital agreement is critical. If it isn’t enforceable, the judge can throw it out when the marriage ends. Thus, your agreement must be in writing, and both parties must voluntarily sign it. In addition, both sides must exchange financial disclosures and have the ability to discuss the document with a Golden, CO, prenup or postnuptial agreements lawyer.
If one party is coerced into signing it, the document won’t be valid. Discuss this with your attorney to ensure that your marital agreement will stand up in a court of law.
Are Marital Agreements Only For The Wealthy?
While some believe that marital agreements are only for the wealthy, that’s simply not true. It’s a good option for business owners, as well as people who want to protect their property and avoid high debts. If you are unsure if you should get a marital agreement, consult with a Golden, CO, prenup and postnuptial agreements lawyer. After going over your specific case, your attorney can provide legal guidance on the matter.
Can You Include Child Support In A Marital Agreement?
While a prenup or postnuptial agreement can help you decide many matters, you cannot use it to determine child support. Instead, you must come up with a support agreement that’s in the best interests of the child. Interests can change, so you’ll need to evaluate the situation at the time of the divorce. Then, you can negotiate an agreement or go to court and have a judge decide.
Prenuptial & Postnuptial Agreements FAQs
Can you get a "prenup" after you are already married?
Yes, but once you are married, the document is legally called a Postnuptial Agreement. Because spouses have a higher duty of care to one another, these agreements are scrutinized more strictly by the courts and generally require independent legal counsel for both parties to be enforceable.
How much does a prenuptial agreement cost?
Fees vary based on the complexity of your assets and the level of negotiation required between parties. Contact The Drake Law Firm, PC for a consultation to discuss your specific assets and receive a transparent pricing assessment.
What does a prenup cover in Colorado?
A prenup can protect pre-marital assets, define debt responsibility, and pre-determine alimony (maintenance), but it cannot dictate child custody or support. Colorado courts always retain the right to determine what is in the best interests of the child at the time of divorce.
When should we sign a prenuptial agreement?
You should aim to sign the agreement at least 30 days before the wedding. If a prenup is presented too close to the wedding date, a court may later invalidate it by arguing the other spouse signed it under “duress” or pressure. Start the process early to ensure the agreement is ironclad.
Are postnuptial agreements enforceable in Colorado?
Yes, but they are scrutinized more strictly than prenups because married spouses have a “fiduciary duty” to one another. For a postnup to hold up in court, both parties must provide full financial disclosure, and it is highly recommended that both sides have their own independent lawyer to prove the agreement wasn’t signed under coercion.

## Property Division in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/colorado/property-division/

Property Division in Colorado
The Drake Law Firm, P.C., helps clients receive an equitable share of marital property.
If you are going through a divorce and need to understand how your assets and debts will be handled, you are in the right place. Colorado has a specific legal framework that governs what gets divided, how it is valued, and what standards courts apply when spouses cannot agree. This page covers the statutes, processes, and key legal distinctions that determine how marital property is distributed.
Understanding Property Division in Colorado
Colorado property division is governed by C.R.S. § 14-10-113, which directs courts to divide marital property in a manner that is equitable — meaning fair — after considering all relevant factors.
The Legal Standard: Equitable Distribution
Colorado is an equitable distribution state. Equitable does not mean equal. The court reviews the totality of the marital estate and each spouse’s circumstances, then divides property in a way that is fair — which may or may not result in a 50/50 split. Factors the court considers under C.R.S. § 14-10-113(1) include:
Each spouse’s contribution to the acquisition of marital property, including contributions as a homemaker
The value of each spouse’s separate property
The economic circumstances of each spouse at the time of division, including whether the custodial parent should retain the family home
Any increase or decrease in the value of separate property during the marriage
The depletion of separate property for marital purposes
The Colorado property division attorneys at The Drake Law Firm, PC analyze these factors at the outset of every case, because the weight each one carries depends entirely on the composition of the marital estate and the specific circumstances of the marriage.
Marital vs. Separate Property
Colorado law distinguishes between marital property — subject to division — and separate property, which belongs solely to one spouse. Under C.R.S. § 14-10-113(2), separate property includes:
Property acquired before the marriage
Property received as a gift or inheritance during the marriage
Property acquired after a legal separation decree
Property excluded by a valid prenuptial or postnuptial agreement
Marital property, by contrast, is generally all property acquired by either spouse during the marriage, regardless of whose name is on the title. Common examples include:
The family home and other real estate purchased during the marriage
Bank accounts and investment accounts funded with marital earnings
Stocks, mutual funds, and brokerage accounts
Vehicles purchased during the marriage
Pension and retirement accounts accrued during the marriage
Business interests acquired or grown during the marriage
The increase in value of separate property attributable to marital contributions
Valuation Date in Colorado
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-113(5), Colorado courts value marital property as of the date of the dissolution decree, or — if a permanent orders hearing on property disposition precedes the decree — as of the date of that hearing. In litigated cases, the permanent orders hearing typically occurs days or weeks before the judge signs the final decree, making the hearing date the functional valuation date for those proceedings. This distinction matters for volatile assets like stock portfolios or business interests, where value can shift significantly in a short period.
The Danger of Commingling Separate and Marital Property
Separate property can lose its protected status if it becomes so intertwined with marital property that tracing it becomes impossible. This is called commingling. It is one of the most common ways that assets people expect to keep — including pre-marital savings, inherited funds, and property owned before the marriage — end up subject to division. Common examples include:
Depositing an inheritance into a joint checking account used for household expenses
Using pre-marital savings as a down payment on a home titled in both spouses’ names
Reinvesting the proceeds from selling separate-property stock into jointly held investments
The same principle applies to property owned before the marriage. A home, investment account, or business you brought into the marriage is separate property — but if marital funds were used to pay down the mortgage, fund improvements, or grow the business during the marriage, the appreciation attributable to those contributions may be treated as marital. The burden is on the spouse claiming separate property to trace and document it through financial records. Without clear documentation, Colorado courts will often treat the asset as marital.
The Three-Step Process of Asset Division
Colorado courts and practitioners follow a structured process to divide property, whether in litigation or through negotiated settlement.
Step 1: Identification and Financial Disclosure
Both spouses are required to complete a Sworn Financial Statement (JDF 1111) disclosing all assets, liabilities, income, and expenses. Colorado Rule 16.2 of the Colorado Rules of Civil Procedure mandates automatic financial disclosures early in the case. The JDF 1111 is filed with the court; the supporting documents (bank statements, tax returns, pay stubs) are exchanged directly with the other party. A Certificate of Compliance (JDF 1104) is filed with the court to confirm that disclosures have been made. Failure to disclose can result in sanctions and, in cases of intentional concealment, a court may award the concealed asset entirely to the other spouse.
Step 2: Valuation
Once assets are identified, they must be assigned a fair market value. Book value or account statements alone are often insufficient. Real property requires a formal appraisal. Business interests typically require a certified business valuator. Retirement accounts may need actuarial analysis to determine the present value of future benefits. The valuation process is especially critical for closely held businesses, professional practices, and defined benefit pensions, where parties often hire competing experts.
Step 3: Distribution
Once assets and debts are identified and valued, the parties negotiate — or the court decides — who receives which assets and who assumes which debts. Sophisticated settlements account for tax consequences, liquidity needs, and the long-term financial position of each spouse, not just the gross value of the assets exchanged. Final property awards are also frequently structured alongside spousal support and alimony, since maintenance obligations directly affect each spouse’s post-divorce financial position.
Navigating Major Assets and Complex Holdings
Certain categories of assets present particular complexity and require careful legal and financial analysis, regardless of how the overall divorce is resolved.
The Marital Home
The family home is often the most valuable asset in a marital estate. Colorado courts recognize three primary approaches to disposition:
Sale and division of net proceeds — the most straightforward approach, especially when neither spouse can afford to carry the mortgage alone
Buyout — one spouse refinances the mortgage in their name alone, compensating the other for their equity share. The buyout amount is based on net equity: fair market value minus the outstanding mortgage balance. Unlike a sale, no actual selling costs are incurred, so hypothetical realtor fees or closing costs are generally not deducted from the equity figure in a court-ordered buyout — though parties sometimes negotiate this in a settlement
Deferred sale — common when minor children are involved; one spouse retains exclusive possession until a triggering event (e.g., the youngest child reaches 18), at which point the home is sold
A spouse who cannot qualify for refinancing independently should address this before agreeing to a buyout. If the buyout falls through, both parties remain jointly liable on the original mortgage.
Retirement Accounts and Pensions
Retirement benefits earned during the marriage are marital property under Colorado law, regardless of which spouse’s employer provided them. How the marital portion is calculated depends on the type of plan.
For defined contribution plans — 401(k)s, 403(b)s, and IRAs — the marital share is determined by tracing actual dollars: the account value at the date of marriage is compared to the value at dissolution, with adjustments for any loans or withdrawals taken during the marriage. Growth on pre-marital contributions remains separate; only contributions and corresponding growth from during the marriage are marital.
For defined benefit pensions, Colorado courts apply the time-rule formula (sometimes called the coverture or Hunt formula). The marital share is calculated as the number of months of plan participation during the marriage divided by the total months of participation through the date of the decree, multiplied by the benefit amount. This produces the marital fraction — typically split equally — that the non-employee spouse is entitled to receive.
To divide a 401(k), 403(b), or pension without triggering early withdrawal penalties or income taxes, a Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) is required. A QDRO is a separate court order, distinct from the divorce decree, that instructs the plan administrator to transfer a specified portion of the account to the alternate payee (the non-employee spouse). Each retirement plan has its own QDRO requirements, and errors in drafting can result in delays or forfeiture of benefits. Our Colorado family law offices work with qualified financial professionals on QDRO drafting to ensure each order is calculated correctly and accepted by the plan administrator on the first submission.
IRAs are divided through a transfer incident to divorce — a different mechanism than a QDRO but equally important to execute correctly to avoid taxable distributions.
Business Interests and Professional Practices
Valuing a business in a Colorado divorce requires a certified business valuator and often involves competing expert opinions. One of the most contested issues is the treatment of goodwill.
Colorado courts distinguish between enterprise goodwill and personal goodwill. Enterprise goodwill — the value attributable to the business’s established client base, systems, brand, and reputation independent of any specific individual — is considered marital property and subject to division. Personal goodwill — the value that exists solely because of an individual owner’s skills, reputation, and relationships — may be treated as separate property in some circumstances, but this is a highly contested, fact-specific analysis. Colorado courts have, in certain cases, found that goodwill tied to an owner’s reputation developed during the marriage constitutes a marital asset. Expert testimony is typically required to allocate between the two categories.
This distinction is particularly significant for professional practices in medicine, law, dentistry, and accounting, where much of the business value may be tied to the individual practitioner rather than the practice entity.
Stock Options and Restricted Stock Units (RSUs)
Equity compensation requires careful analysis of vesting schedules to determine what portion is marital. Options or RSUs that vested during the marriage are marital property. Those that vest after the marriage may be partially marital (to the extent they compensate for past marital-period service) and partially separate (to the extent they compensate for future service). Colorado courts commonly apply a time-rule formula to allocate the marital versus separate portions.
Handling Debts and Liabilities
Marital debts — those incurred during the marriage for marital purposes — are subject to division just as assets are. Colorado courts have discretion to allocate debts equitably, considering factors such as who incurred the debt, who benefited from it, and each spouse’s ability to pay.
The Critical Warning: Divorce Decrees Do Not Bind Creditors
One of the most important and frequently misunderstood points in Colorado property division: a divorce decree assigning a debt to one spouse does not eliminate the other spouse’s liability to the creditor. If a joint credit card is awarded to your spouse but they fail to pay it, the card issuer can still pursue you for the full balance — because your name remains on the account. The decree only gives you a legal claim against your ex-spouse for reimbursement, which may be difficult to enforce. The practical solution is to pay off and close all joint accounts before or at the time of divorce, or to refinance joint debt into the responsible spouse’s name alone.
Student Loans
In Colorado, student loans are generally assigned to the spouse who received the degree and corresponding earning benefit. However, if the marriage significantly benefited from the educated spouse’s increased income — or if marital funds were used to repay the loans — a court may allocate a portion to the marital estate. The analysis turns on who received the primary benefit of the educational debt.
Frequently Asked Questions About Property Division​
How is a living trust treated in a Colorado divorce?
Property held in a revocable living trust is generally treated the same as property held outright by the spouse who created or funded it. Because a revocable trust can be amended or revoked by the grantor, Colorado courts look through the trust structure to the underlying assets. If those assets were acquired during the marriage, they are marital property subject to division regardless of whether they were transferred into a trust. Irrevocable trusts present a more complex analysis and depend on whether the beneficiary spouse has actual control or beneficial interest in the trust assets.
Does adultery affect property division in Colorado?
Colorado is a no-fault divorce state, and courts do not penalize a spouse for marital misconduct when dividing property. However, if one spouse dissipated marital assets — spending significant marital funds on an extramarital affair, gambling, or other wasteful conduct — the court may take that dissipation into account. The affected spouse can seek to have the dissipated value credited back to their share of the estate.
Can we agree to our own property division?
Yes. Colorado courts strongly favor negotiated settlements. Spouses may enter into a Separation Agreement (also called a Marital Settlement Agreement) that divides property in whatever manner they agree upon — even if that division is not what a court would impose. The agreement must be in writing, signed by both parties, and approved by the court. Courts will reject agreements that are unconscionable or the product of fraud or duress.
What if my spouse is hiding assets?
Colorado Rule 16.2 mandates automatic financial disclosures. If you suspect your spouse is concealing assets, your attorney can use formal discovery tools — interrogatories, depositions, subpoenas to financial institutions — to uncover hidden accounts, undervalued business interests, or undisclosed income. In complex cases, a forensic accountant may be engaged. Courts take asset concealment seriously; a spouse found to have fraudulently concealed assets may be ordered to pay the other spouse’s attorney fees, or the court may award the concealed asset entirely to the other side.
How does Colorado treat pets in a divorce?
Under current Colorado law, pets are legally classified as personal property and are subject to the same equitable distribution analysis as other marital assets. Courts do not apply a “best interest of the pet” standard under existing statutes. However, Colorado House Bill 26-1131 — introduced in February 2026 — would, if enacted, grant courts explicit authority to consider a pet’s health, safety, and well-being when awarding sole or shared custody in dissolution proceedings. The bill passed the House Judiciary Committee on February 24, 2026 by a narrow 6-5 vote and was advanced to the House Appropriations Committee, where it faces an uncertain path. If passed by the General Assembly and signed into law, it would take effect August 12, 2026. Until that occurs, pets remain property under Colorado divorce law.
Are assets always split 50/50 in a divorce?
No. Colorado courts begin with equitable distribution under C.R.S. § 14-10-113, which means fair — not automatically equal. Judges have discretion to deviate from a 50/50 split based on statutory factors including each spouse’s economic circumstances at the time of division, their respective contributions to the marriage (including homemaking), the value of each spouse’s separate property, any dissipation of marital assets, and whether the custodial parent should retain the family home. In practice many cases do result in a roughly equal division, but high-asset estates and cases with significant separate property or dissipation are more likely to produce an unequal outcome.
What assets are protected from division in a Colorado divorce?
Separate property is not subject to equitable distribution. Under C.R.S. § 14-10-113(2), separate property includes assets owned before the marriage, inheritances and gifts received during the marriage, property acquired after a legal separation decree, and property excluded by a valid prenuptial or postnuptial agreement. The key condition is that separate property must have remained separate — once it is commingled with marital funds, it may lose its protected status entirely and become subject to division. Maintaining clear financial records and separate accounts is the most reliable way to preserve the separate character of these assets.
How Our Property Division Lawyers Can Help
Property division is rarely just about splitting a list of assets — the decisions made during this process carry long-term financial consequences that extend well beyond the date of the divorce decree. At The Drake Law Firm, PC, our attorneys approach each case with a focus on the real, after-tax value of what our clients are keeping or giving up, not just the numbers on paper.
Strategic Negotiation
Not all assets of equal dollar value are equally desirable. A retirement account worth $200,000 is not the same as $200,000 in a brokerage account — one has deferred tax obligations, the other may be taxed at capital gains rates. Our attorneys analyze the tax basis, liquidity, and long-term implications of every asset before recommending a division strategy, so clients understand what they are actually receiving.
Complex Valuation and Expert Coordination
For high-asset cases involving business interests, real estate portfolios, stock compensation, or defined benefit pensions, we work with a network of qualified appraisers, forensic accountants, and business valuation experts. Our goal is to ensure that your marital estate is fully and accurately valued — and that you receive your fair share of it.
Protecting Your Separate Property
If you brought significant assets into the marriage or received an inheritance during it, we help you document and trace those assets through every transaction to preserve their separate character. Early analysis of financial records can make the difference between keeping your pre-marital assets and losing them to commingling arguments.
Discuss Your Property Division Case
Property division is one of the most financially significant decisions of your life. The outcome depends heavily on the quality of legal representation you have during the process. From ensuring complete financial disclosure to litigating the value of a complex business, our attorneys are prepared to advocate for your interests at every step. Contact The Drake Law Firm, PC to discuss your case.

Lakewood Common Law Marriage FAQs:
How do I know if I’m in a common law marriage in Colorado?
In Colorado, a common law marriage exists when both partners agree they are married and present themselves publicly as a married couple. This can include using the same last name, sharing bank accounts, filing joint taxes, or introducing each other as spouses. A common law marriage attorney in Lakewood, CO can help you evaluate your situation and determine whether the law recognizes your relationship.
Can a common law marriage be ended without a divorce?
No. Once a common law marriage is established in Colorado, it must be dissolved through the same court process as a ceremonial marriage. This includes dividing property, determining parental responsibilities, and resolving spousal maintenance. Working with a common law marriage attorney in Lakewood can make this process smoother and more predictable.
Do I need to register my common law marriage?
There is no formal registration requirement in Colorado. However, couples sometimes sign an affidavit of common law marriage to use for benefits or official purposes. This can serve as evidence if the marriage is later questioned. A Lakewood common law marriage attorney can prepare or review this document with you.
What happens to property in a common law marriage separation?
Property acquired during the relationship is generally considered marital property, subject to equitable division by the court. This includes real estate, retirement accounts, vehicles, and debts. A common law marriage attorney in Lakewood can help protect your financial interests.
Can I get spousal support after ending a common law marriage?
Yes, spousal maintenance (alimony) is available under the same conditions as a formal marriage. The court looks at factors like income differences, length of the marriage, and each party’s ability to be self-supporting. Speaking with a common law marriage attorney in Lakewood, CO will help you understand what applies in your case.

## Contested Divorce – Lakewood, Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/contested-divorce-attorney-lakewood-colorado/

Divorce in Colorado
Ending a marriage is rarely a sudden decision. It is often the result of months or even years of trying to make things work, followed by the difficult realization that moving forward requires letting go. Colorado courts address four primary issues in a dissolution proceeding: allocation of parental responsibilities, parenting time, division of marital property and debt, and spousal maintenance. Each is governed by its own statutory framework and evaluated independently.
At The Drake Law Firm, PC, we understand that divorce is not just a legal transaction; it is a profound life transition. Our family law and divorce lawyers operate with a philosophy of compassionate strength. We are here to help you close this chapter with dignity and clarity, dedicated to securing the protection you need to build a stable, successful future.
Get A Divorce Lawyer Now
Types of Divorce in Colorado
Colorado is a no-fault state under C.R.S. § 14-10-106 — the only legal ground for dissolution is that the marriage is irretrievably broken. Neither party is required to prove fault, misconduct, or wrongdoing. The path a case takes depends on the degree of agreement between the parties and the complexity of the issues involved.
An uncontested divorce occurs when both spouses reach full agreement on every issue before or shortly after filing — including the division of all marital property and debt, spousal maintenance, and all parenting matters. Because no disputes require court resolution, uncontested cases move through the system significantly faster and at lower cost than contested proceedings.
When a complete agreement is in place, parties may file a Decree upon Affidavit under C.R.S. § 14-10-120.3, which allows the judge to review and sign the decree without requiring either party to appear in court. The agreement must still satisfy the court’s review — a judge will not approve a Separation Agreement that is unconscionable or that fails to adequately address the interests of any minor children.
The mandatory 91-day waiting period under C.R.S. § 14-10-106 applies regardless of how quickly the parties agree. No decree can be entered before that period expires from the date of service or joint filing. For couples with straightforward finances and no children, an uncontested case finalized shortly after the waiting period represents the most efficient resolution available under the law.
A contested divorce does not require hostility — it simply means that at least one issue remains unresolved between the parties. Common disputed issues include the characterization or valuation of marital assets, the division of a business or retirement accounts, the amount or duration of spousal maintenance, and the allocation of parental responsibilities or parenting time.
When disputes cannot be resolved through negotiation, Colorado courts use a structured litigation process to reach resolution. Every divorce, contested or not, includes mandatory financial disclosure under C.R.C.P. 16.2, an Initial Status Conference to establish deadlines, discovery if needed, and in most jurisdictions, mandatory mediation before any trial will be scheduled. More often than not, the parties begin negotiating with one another or through their attorneys once they have exchanged mandatory financial disclosures. If mediation does not resolve all issues, the case proceeds to a Permanent Orders Hearing where a District Court judge makes final binding determinations on every unresolved matter.
Colorado courts applying equitable distribution under C.R.S. § 14-10-113 have broad discretion in how they divide marital property. Similarly, Best Interests of the Child determinations under C.R.S. § 14-10-124 give judges significant latitude in parenting matters. The outcome of a contested hearing is therefore much less predictable than a negotiated settlement, which is why resolution short of trial — through negotiation or mediation — is generally preferable when achievable.
Legal Separation
Legal separation in Colorado is a distinct legal proceeding governed by C.R.S. § 14-10-107. It produces a court order that resolves all the same issues as a divorce — property division, debt allocation, spousal maintenance, and parental responsibilities — but does not legally terminate the marriage. The parties remain legally married after a decree of legal separation.
Legal separation is used in circumstances where the parties choose not to divorce for religious, financial, or personal reasons, but require the legal structure of a court order to govern their separated lives. Common reasons include preserving eligibility for a spouse’s health insurance coverage, maintaining certain federal benefits tied to length of marriage, or satisfying religious constraints on divorce.
Either party may file a motion under C.R.S. § 14-10-107(5) requesting the court convert a decree of legal separation into a decree of dissolution of marriage after six months have elapsed. The court applies the same statutory standards to legal separation proceedings as it does to dissolution — including the Best Interests standard for parenting matters and the equitable distribution framework for marital property division.
Collaborative divorce is a structured, non-adversarial resolution process in which both parties and their attorneys sign a Participation Agreement committing to resolve all issues outside of court. The collaborative process typically involves a team of professionals beyond the two attorneys — including a neutral financial specialist who analyzes the marital estate, and a divorce coach or mental health professional who helps manage communication between the parties.
The defining feature of the collaborative process is the withdrawal obligation: if either party terminates the collaborative process and elects to proceed to litigation, both collaborative attorneys must withdraw entirely. The parties must then retain new litigation counsel. This provision creates a strong structural incentive for all participants to work toward resolution, since abandoning the process is costly for both sides.
Collaborative divorce is best suited to cases where both parties are committed to a cooperative resolution and where the financial or parenting issues are sufficiently complex to benefit from neutral professional input. It is generally not appropriate where there is a significant power imbalance, a history of domestic violence, or reason to believe one party is withholding financial information.
Mediation is a structured negotiation process in which a neutral third-party mediator facilitates discussion between the parties to help them reach agreement on contested issues. The mediator does not represent either party, does not provide legal advice, and cannot impose a resolution — their role is to create conditions under which the parties can negotiate effectively.  Mediation in Colorado is almost always conducted remotely, often on Zoom.
In Colorado, mediation is not optional in most contested cases. Courts in Denver and across the state’s judicial districts require parties to attempt mediation before a Permanent Orders Hearing can be scheduled. In Jefferson County though, a Permanent Orders Hearing will be set but it will not occur if the parties have not mediated or attempted to mediate prior to the trial date. This mediation requirement is built into the case management process as detailed in the Case Management Order issued shortly after the Petition for Dissolution is filed and then further established, if necessary, at the Initial Status Conference. Failure to participate in good faith can result in sanctions.
If mediation produces a full agreement, the terms are memorialized in a mediator-drafted agreement called a Memorandum of Understanding or, in a written Separation Agreement and Parenting Plan, which are submitted to the court for approval as part of the final decree. If mediation resolves only some issues, the remaining disputes proceed to a hearing. Mediation can occur at any point in the process — many cases settle in mediation after discovery is complete and both parties have a clear picture of the financial landscape.
Which Process Applies to Your Situation
The appropriate process depends on the level of agreement between the parties, the complexity of the marital estate, and whether children are involved. Uncontested proceedings are available only when full agreement is reached on every issue. Contested proceedings apply when any dispute remains unresolved. Collaborative divorce and mediation are tools for reaching resolution — they are not separate types of divorce but alternative paths to the same court-approved outcome.
Legal separation is a distinct proceeding with specific eligibility requirements that differ substantially from dissolution. Colorado courts handle all of these proceedings in the District Court of the county where either spouse is domiciled.
The Colorado Divorce Process
The state’s legal system follows a specific statutory roadmap governed by the Colorado Revised Statutes and the Colorado Rules of Civil Procedure.
Step 1 — File the Petition. The process begins with the filing of a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage (JDF 1101). Once filed and served, a mandatory 91-day statutory waiting period begins under C.R.S. § 14-10-106. The divorce cannot be finalized until at least 91 days have passed from the date of service or joint filing.
Step 2 — Mandatory Financial Disclosures. Colorado law (C.R.C.P. 16.2) requires full financial transparency from both parties. Within 42 days of service, both parties must exchange mandatory financial disclosures (Form 35.1), including pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements, and credit card bills. Failure to disclose assets fully can result in severe penalties and reopening of the case.
Step 3 — Initial Status Conference (ISC). Shortly after filing, the court schedules an Initial Status Conference with a Court Facilitator or Magistrate. This sets the case timeline, including deadlines for expert disclosure, mediation, and hearings.
Step 4 —Mandatory Mediation. Colorado courts require mediation in all divorce cases, often before the court will even set a final hearing. Mediation is a necessary process, and a mediator can help parties, including parties with counsel, reach a facilitated agreement or partial agreement, which saves time, money and appearances before a judge.
Step 5 — Resolution or Trial. If the parties reach a full agreement, a Separation Agreement and Parenting Plan are drafted and submitted for court approval. If disputes remain unresolved, the case proceeds to a Permanent Orders Hearing where the judge issues a final Decree of Dissolution of Marriage.
Colorado law no longer uses the term “custody.” Under C.R.S. § 14-10-124, courts determine the Allocation of Parental Responsibilities (APR) under Colorado child custody and parenting time law. APR is divided into two components:
Parenting Time — The actual schedule of overnights the child spends with each parent.
Decision-Making Responsibility — Who decides major issues regarding education, religion, and non-emergency medical care (Sole vs. Joint).
The court’s only standard is the best interests of the child. Colorado does not presume that equal parenting time is automatically in the child’s best interests — the court evaluates the specific circumstances of each family. When parenting matters are contested, child support obligations are calculated in conjunction with the parenting time schedule under C.R.S. § 14-10-115.
Equitable Division of Assets
Colorado is an equitable distribution state, not a community property state. Under Colorado’s equitable property division statute, C.R.S. § 14-10-113, the court divides marital property equitably — meaning fairly, not necessarily equally. Factors include:
Each spouse’s contribution to the acquisition of marital property, including homemaking contributions.
The economic circumstances of each spouse at the time of division.
Whether property is marital (acquired during the marriage) or separate (owned prior to marriage or received by inheritance or gift).
Marital property subject to division includes real estate, bank and investment accounts, retirement accounts, business interests, and debt accumulated during the marriage. Separate property — assets owned before the marriage or received as individual gifts or inheritance — is generally excluded from division, though commingling with marital assets often affects that characterization because placing separate property into joint ownership means that property is a presumed gift to the marriage.
Spousal Maintenance
Under Colorado spousal maintenance law, C.R.S. § 14-10-114, maintenance is not automatic. Courts apply advisory guidelines for couples with combined gross incomes under $240,000 per year. The formula calculates maintenance as approximately 40% of the higher earner’s monthly adjusted gross income minus 50% of the lower earner’s monthly adjusted gross income. The duration of maintenance is also guideline-based, scaled to the length of the marriage. Courts retain discretion to deviate from the guidelines based on the specific circumstances of each case.
Colorado Divorce FAQs
How to get a divorce in Colorado?
To obtain a divorce, at least one spouse must be a resident for 91 days before filing a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage. The process involves serving your spouse and waiting a mandatory 91-day “cooling-off” period, during which financial disclosures are exchanged. Hiring a Colorado divorce lawyer at The Drake Law Firm, PC can streamline this process and ensure all legal requirements are met.
How much does a divorce cost in Colorado?
The court charges a standard filing fee to initiate the case, which is $230 as of January 1, 2026 within Colorado. However, the total cost depends heavily on whether the divorce is contested or uncontested. An uncontested divorce is significantly less expensive, whereas a contested case involving a divorce attorney can range from $10,000 to $50,000 or more depending on litigation needs.
How long does divorce take?
Colorado law mandates a minimum 91-day waiting period after the petition is filed and served before a court can issue a final decree. While uncontested divorces can be wrapped up in approximately 4 months, complex cases often take at least a year to resolve.
Are divorce records public?
Yes, certain divorce records are generally public and accessible to anyone after the decree is finalized; however sworn financial statements, supporting financial schedules, child support worksheets and parenting plans are commonly suppressed.  In addition, parties can request that the court seal or redact sensitive documents to protect their privacy, but those requests are not automatically granted.
Is Colorado a no-fault state for divorce?
Yes, Colorado is strictly a “no-fault” divorce state. You do not need to prove marital misconduct such as adultery; you only need to demonstrate to the court that the marriage is “irretrievably broken.
Is Colorado a 50/50 split in divorce?
Colorado is an “equitable distribution” state rather than a community property state, so assets are not automatically split 50/50. Instead, the court divides property in a manner it deems fair and equitable based on the contributions and economic circumstances of each spouse.
What is a spouse entitled to in a divorce in Colorado?
A spouse is entitled to an equitable portion of the marital property and, in certain cases, spousal maintenance (alimony) if he or she earns significantly less than his or her spouse. Navigating these entitlements can be complex, so consulting a Colorado divorce lawyer is highly encouraged to protect your family’s financial future.

You do not have to face this uncertainty alone. Whether you are ready to file or just need to understand your rights, we are here to help. Contact The Drake Law Firm, P.C and talk about your situation so we can map out a clear path forward.

Lakewood Family Law Attorney FAQs
What does a Lakewood family law attorney do?
A Lakewood family law attorney helps clients resolve legal matters that affect their families, such as divorce, custody, parenting plans, child support, and property division. At The Drake Law Firm, we work closely with Lakewood clients to understand their goals and take practical steps that protect their future. Whether you’re filing for divorce or modifying custody, a family lawyer helps you understand your rights, complete paperwork, and reach workable agreements.
Do I have to go to court for a family law case in Lakewood?
No, not every family law case in Lakewood has to go to court in person, although most new cases require a virtual court appearance called an Initial Status Conference. Many issues, like child custody,  support, or separation terms—can be settled through negotiation or mediation. If both parties are willing to cooperate, your Lakewood family lawyer can help draft legally binding agreements without having to visit a courtroom. But if cooperation breaks down, your attorney is prepared to represent you at hearings to resolve the remaining disputes.
How long does it take to get divorced in Colorado?
Colorado has a mandatory 91-day waiting period before a divorce can be finalized. This clock starts once your spouse has been served, or immediately if you filed together. After that, the timeline depends on how quickly you and your spouse agree on key issues like custody, support, and property division. A Lakewood family lawyer can help move things forward efficiently and make sure everything is handled correctly from the start.
What happens if we already agree on everything?
If both spouses agree on all terms, like parenting time, asset division, and support—you can submit your documents and your settlement for the court to approve.  This is called an uncontested divorce. Uncontested divorces are usually faster and more affordable than a fight. Your Lakewood CO family law attorney will still review your mandatory financial disclosures, your parenting plan, and the agreement on assets and debts to protect your interests, make sure everything complies with Colorado law, and file the necessary documents so the court can finalize the divorce without delay.
Can I change my custody or support order later?
Yes, custody and child support orders can be modified if your circumstances change. This might include a job loss, relocation, changes in parenting time, or shifts in a child’s needs. To request a change, you must show that the new situation is significant and affects the original order. A Lakewood family lawyer can help you prepare the request, file it with the court, and advocate for terms that reflect your current reality.

Understanding Divorce in Colorado
Colorado is a no-fault divorce state, meaning you don’t have to prove that the other party did anything wrong to end your marriage. Instead, you can get a divorce if your marriage is irretrievably broken. First, your divorce lawyer will file a petition to dissolve the marriage. Then, you can obtain the divorce decree 91 days after the other party was notified of the petition. If you filed a co-petition, you could receive the divorce decree 91 days after filing the paperwork.
While some divorces move through quickly, other times, there are numerous issues that must be settled beforehand. These issues might include alimony, the division of property, and child custody and support. Your divorce attorney can help you settle all issues related to the divorce so you don’t have to go to court. However, if the other party refuses to negotiate in good faith, your attorney can try the case in front of a judge. Then, the judge can dissolve the marriage and rule on the other factors involved in the divorce.

Child custody is one of the most important family law matters. You have to determine both legal and physical custody. Legal custody describes who makes decisions regarding how the child is raised. Physical custody determines how the child divides time between the parents. While sole legal and physical custody is an option, most parents enter into joint custody agreements. Then, the child alternates between homes, and both parents are involved in the decision-making process.
There is a belief that mothers are more likely to be granted custody of their children. However, men have equal parenting rights. Your Colorado family law attorney can help you fight for legal custody and parenting time, regardless of gender.
Parents are legally required to support their children, even if they do not have legal or physical custody. The state uses the income shares model when determining child support payments. Because the formula is relatively complex, it’s wise to consult with a Colorado family law attorney to find out how much you should receive or pay. Also, your attorney can help you modify your existing child support agreement if there has been a change in circumstances substantial enough to warrant it.
Spousal Support
Are you having trouble making ends meet since your divorce? If you rely on the supporting spouse’s income, you might be eligible for alimony. The court considers the ability to pay, income, the length of the marriage, and other factors when determining alimony. In addition, your attorney can negotiate with the other side to come to a fair agreement. Consult with an attorney to decide if you should negotiate or go to court with your case.

## Parental Alienation Lawyer in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/family-law/parental-alienation-lawyer/

Addressing Parental Alienation in Colorado
The Drake Law Firm, P.C., protects parents’ rights when dealing with parental alienation.
Parental Alienation in Golden, CO
Splitting from a spouse or partner is exceptionally difficult when children are involved. Parents have to balance ironing out parenting agreements and child support payments while maintaining a close relationship with their kids. This is more difficult when one parent engages in alienation tactics. Parental alienation is a form of psychological abuse and can push your kids away from you. While alienation can range from mild to severe, the consequences are always serious.
Our Golden, CO parental alienation lawyer can stand up for your rights. We will take steps to put a stop to the psychological abuse so you can strengthen your bond with your child. Contact us to discuss your case, including any evidence you’ve collected.
Examples of Parental Alienation
Parental alienation comes in numerous forms. However, common examples include one parent:
Making disparaging comments about the other parent
Forcing the child to choose between the parents
Controlling communication between the child and the other parent
Providing detailed information about the dissolution of the marriage
Forcing the child to parent them
Purposefully limiting the other parent’s involvement
Telling lies about the other parent
Gathering Evidence In Child Alienation Cases
Child alienation can occur slowly and build over time. At first, you might notice subtle changes that get more pronounced as your child becomes increasingly alienated. When you start to notice changes, it’s important to begin gathering evidence. First, keep a journal of your observations. For instance, if your child repeats disparaging comments made by the other parent, write them down, including the date and time. Your journal can be used to show a pattern of alienation that has developed over time.
You can also use voicemails, text messages, and social media posts for evidence. For example, if your spouse records a voicemail full of hateful rhetoric, and you can hear your child in the background, save it.
While some parents record videos of their children to prove alienation, this is a legally murky subject. Consult with your Golden, CO, parental alienation lawyer before recording your child for evidence.
How Is Parental Alienation Addressed?
Colorado’s family court system is designed to ensure that the best interests of the child are always met. The court understands that parental alienation negatively impacts children. Thus, if they are involved in this emotionally abusive situation, they can experience psychological harm.
Once your Golden, CO, parental alienation order files a claim, the judge can appoint a parental responsibilities evaluator or a child and family investigator to review the case. Then, the judge can choose to modify the parenting agreement based on the report. Thus, you can end up getting more time with your child. The court can also take additional actions to put an end to parental alienation, such as ordering therapy or changing the parenting plan to forbid disparaging language.
Therapy For Child Alienation
If the other parent has emotionally abused your child, therapy might be a wise choice for your child. The therapist probably won’t testify in the parental alienation case. However, the therapist can play a vital role if the court assigns a child custody expert to your case. In addition, therapy can make it easier for your child to navigate the emotional turmoil of parental alienation. It can also help your child open up and strengthen their bond with you.
Are You Unsure If Parental Alienation Is Occurring?
Do you feel that the dynamic between you and your child has shifted, and you aren’t sure why? You think it might be parental alienation, but you don’t have the evidence to prove it. Consult with a Golden, CO, parental alienation lawyer to go over your case. You could have evidence that you aren’t aware of having. If you do have a claim, your lawyer can then take the next steps.

## Post-Decree Modification in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/family-law/post-decree-modification/

Post-Decree Modification in Colorado
Post-decree Modification in Golden, CO
Life is constantly changing. It’s normal to switch jobs, homes, and more throughout your life. As you go through life’s numerous changes, you might discover that your divorce settlement no longer meets your needs. For instance, your spousal maintenance or support might not make sense for your current situation. Fortunately, you can hire a Golden, CO, post-decree modification lawyer to review your case and petition for a modification.
Whether you are a non-custodial or custodial parent, we can help you obtain a modification. Contact us today to discuss your legal needs.
Post-decree Modification Options
Our Golden, CO, post-decree modification lawyer can help you make changes to:
Division of property
Assignment of debts
Physical and legal custody
Child support
Spousal support
Modifying a Child Custody Agreement
Your Golden, CO, post-decree modification lawyer can assist you with your custody agreement. First, you must show that your circumstances have changed, requiring modification. For example, if the other parent moved far away or has become abusive, you can petition to alter the custody agreement.
The court will review the evidence and determine what’s in the child’s best interests. That means the judge will consider the child’s physical, nutritional, and educational needs. In addition, the child’s emotional well-being will be considered. Then, the judge will decide to keep the agreement as is or modify it.
Modifying Child Support Agreement
Your post-decree modification lawyer can provide evidence to support a petition to modify your child support agreement. One party must have experienced a significant change in circumstances to modify the order. This could be the sudden loss of a job, a significant reduction in income, or the changing needs of the child.
As with child custody, the court will determine what’s in the best interests of the child. The judge will make sure that the child has ample support in both homes, if applicable. Then, the judge might order that the obligator pay less or more in support, depending on the circumstances.
Modifying Spousal Support
While rare, the court occasionally modifies spousal support agreements. Your lawyer must first prove that you meet the qualifications for a modification. You must show a sudden increase or decrease in income, change in child-related expenses, or sudden loss of assets to qualify. Then, you can petition to either increase or decrease the support payments. Because these cases are rarely approved, hiring a Golden, CO, post-decree modification lawyer is critical.
Financial Settlements
Did the other party commit fraud when disclosing his or her assets? If so, you might qualify for a modification of your financial settlements. First, your attorney must provide evidence to prove the fraud. Then, the judge can change the agreement based on the new evidence. Contact a Golden, CO, post-decree modification lawyer to discuss changing your financial settlements.
