The First Steps to an uncontested Divorce in Colorado
To seek an uncontested divorce in Colorado, certain requirements must be met. Firstly, both you and your spouse should agree to dissolve the marriage. Secondly, you must have resided in Colorado for 90 days or more before filing. Additionally, a signed separation agreement that outlines key points such as the division of assets, child custody, and child support is necessary.
When both parties have legal representation, a court appearance typically isn’t necessary, and the decree of dissolution is issued without a hearing. However, if one or both parties don’t have an attorney, a short court appearance may be necessary, allowing the judge to officially grant the divorce.
How to get an uncontested divorce
When seeking an uncontested divorce, you have several options to negotiate a separation agreement.  We can help you come to an agreement before filing for divorce. This allows you to include the separation agreement with your divorce paperwork, potentially expediting the proceedings. You can expect to receive your divorce decree approximately 91 days after submission. You also have the option of filing for divorce and then negotiate a separation agreement. This option can still avoid court but it could take a bit longer overall.
Mediation is another option. A third-party mediator can collaborate with you and your spouse to establish the details of the separation agreement, either before or after filing for divorce.

## Uncontested Divorce Lawyer in Colorado
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/family-law/uncontested-divorce-lawyer/

Divorce in Colorado
Ending a marriage is rarely a sudden decision. It is often the result of months or even years of trying to make things work, followed by the difficult realization that moving forward requires letting go. Colorado courts address four primary issues in a dissolution proceeding: allocation of parental responsibilities, parenting time, division of marital property and debt, and spousal maintenance. Each is governed by its own statutory framework and evaluated independently.
At The Drake Law Firm, PC, we understand that divorce is not just a legal transaction; it is a profound life transition. Our family law and divorce lawyers operate with a philosophy of compassionate strength. We are here to help you close this chapter with dignity and clarity, dedicated to securing the protection you need to build a stable, successful future.
Get A Divorce Lawyer Now
Types of Divorce in Colorado
Colorado is a no-fault state under C.R.S. § 14-10-106 — the only legal ground for dissolution is that the marriage is irretrievably broken. Neither party is required to prove fault, misconduct, or wrongdoing. The path a case takes depends on the degree of agreement between the parties and the complexity of the issues involved.
An uncontested divorce occurs when both spouses reach full agreement on every issue before or shortly after filing — including the division of all marital property and debt, spousal maintenance, and all parenting matters. Because no disputes require court resolution, uncontested cases move through the system significantly faster and at lower cost than contested proceedings.
When a complete agreement is in place, parties may file a Decree upon Affidavit under C.R.S. § 14-10-120.3, which allows the judge to review and sign the decree without requiring either party to appear in court. The agreement must still satisfy the court’s review — a judge will not approve a Separation Agreement that is unconscionable or that fails to adequately address the interests of any minor children.
The mandatory 91-day waiting period under C.R.S. § 14-10-106 applies regardless of how quickly the parties agree. No decree can be entered before that period expires from the date of service or joint filing. For couples with straightforward finances and no children, an uncontested case finalized shortly after the waiting period represents the most efficient resolution available under the law.
A contested divorce does not require hostility — it simply means that at least one issue remains unresolved between the parties. Common disputed issues include the characterization or valuation of marital assets, the division of a business or retirement accounts, the amount or duration of spousal maintenance, and the allocation of parental responsibilities or parenting time.
When disputes cannot be resolved through negotiation, Colorado courts use a structured litigation process to reach resolution. Every divorce, contested or not, includes mandatory financial disclosure under C.R.C.P. 16.2, an Initial Status Conference to establish deadlines, discovery if needed, and in most jurisdictions, mandatory mediation before any trial will be scheduled. More often than not, the parties begin negotiating with one another or through their attorneys once they have exchanged mandatory financial disclosures. If mediation does not resolve all issues, the case proceeds to a Permanent Orders Hearing where a District Court judge makes final binding determinations on every unresolved matter.
Colorado courts applying equitable distribution under C.R.S. § 14-10-113 have broad discretion in how they divide marital property. Similarly, Best Interests of the Child determinations under C.R.S. § 14-10-124 give judges significant latitude in parenting matters. The outcome of a contested hearing is therefore much less predictable than a negotiated settlement, which is why resolution short of trial — through negotiation or mediation — is generally preferable when achievable.
Legal Separation
Legal separation in Colorado is a distinct legal proceeding governed by C.R.S. § 14-10-107. It produces a court order that resolves all the same issues as a divorce — property division, debt allocation, spousal maintenance, and parental responsibilities — but does not legally terminate the marriage. The parties remain legally married after a decree of legal separation.
Legal separation is used in circumstances where the parties choose not to divorce for religious, financial, or personal reasons, but require the legal structure of a court order to govern their separated lives. Common reasons include preserving eligibility for a spouse’s health insurance coverage, maintaining certain federal benefits tied to length of marriage, or satisfying religious constraints on divorce.
Either party may file a motion under C.R.S. § 14-10-107(5) requesting the court convert a decree of legal separation into a decree of dissolution of marriage after six months have elapsed. The court applies the same statutory standards to legal separation proceedings as it does to dissolution — including the Best Interests standard for parenting matters and the equitable distribution framework for marital property division.
Collaborative divorce is a structured, non-adversarial resolution process in which both parties and their attorneys sign a Participation Agreement committing to resolve all issues outside of court. The collaborative process typically involves a team of professionals beyond the two attorneys — including a neutral financial specialist who analyzes the marital estate, and a divorce coach or mental health professional who helps manage communication between the parties.
The defining feature of the collaborative process is the withdrawal obligation: if either party terminates the collaborative process and elects to proceed to litigation, both collaborative attorneys must withdraw entirely. The parties must then retain new litigation counsel. This provision creates a strong structural incentive for all participants to work toward resolution, since abandoning the process is costly for both sides.
Collaborative divorce is best suited to cases where both parties are committed to a cooperative resolution and where the financial or parenting issues are sufficiently complex to benefit from neutral professional input. It is generally not appropriate where there is a significant power imbalance, a history of domestic violence, or reason to believe one party is withholding financial information.
Mediation is a structured negotiation process in which a neutral third-party mediator facilitates discussion between the parties to help them reach agreement on contested issues. The mediator does not represent either party, does not provide legal advice, and cannot impose a resolution — their role is to create conditions under which the parties can negotiate effectively.  Mediation in Colorado is almost always conducted remotely, often on Zoom.
In Colorado, mediation is not optional in most contested cases. Courts in Denver and across the state’s judicial districts require parties to attempt mediation before a Permanent Orders Hearing can be scheduled. In Jefferson County though, a Permanent Orders Hearing will be set but it will not occur if the parties have not mediated or attempted to mediate prior to the trial date. This mediation requirement is built into the case management process as detailed in the Case Management Order issued shortly after the Petition for Dissolution is filed and then further established, if necessary, at the Initial Status Conference. Failure to participate in good faith can result in sanctions.
If mediation produces a full agreement, the terms are memorialized in a mediator-drafted agreement called a Memorandum of Understanding or, in a written Separation Agreement and Parenting Plan, which are submitted to the court for approval as part of the final decree. If mediation resolves only some issues, the remaining disputes proceed to a hearing. Mediation can occur at any point in the process — many cases settle in mediation after discovery is complete and both parties have a clear picture of the financial landscape.
Which Process Applies to Your Situation
The appropriate process depends on the level of agreement between the parties, the complexity of the marital estate, and whether children are involved. Uncontested proceedings are available only when full agreement is reached on every issue. Contested proceedings apply when any dispute remains unresolved. Collaborative divorce and mediation are tools for reaching resolution — they are not separate types of divorce but alternative paths to the same court-approved outcome.
Legal separation is a distinct proceeding with specific eligibility requirements that differ substantially from dissolution. Colorado courts handle all of these proceedings in the District Court of the county where either spouse is domiciled.
The Colorado Divorce Process
The state’s legal system follows a specific statutory roadmap governed by the Colorado Revised Statutes and the Colorado Rules of Civil Procedure.
Step 1 — File the Petition. The process begins with the filing of a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage (JDF 1101). Once filed and served, a mandatory 91-day statutory waiting period begins under C.R.S. § 14-10-106. The divorce cannot be finalized until at least 91 days have passed from the date of service or joint filing.
Step 2 — Mandatory Financial Disclosures. Colorado law (C.R.C.P. 16.2) requires full financial transparency from both parties. Within 42 days of service, both parties must exchange mandatory financial disclosures (Form 35.1), including pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements, and credit card bills. Failure to disclose assets fully can result in severe penalties and reopening of the case.
Step 3 — Initial Status Conference (ISC). Shortly after filing, the court schedules an Initial Status Conference with a Court Facilitator or Magistrate. This sets the case timeline, including deadlines for expert disclosure, mediation, and hearings.
Step 4 —Mandatory Mediation. Colorado courts require mediation in all divorce cases, often before the court will even set a final hearing. Mediation is a necessary process, and a mediator can help parties, including parties with counsel, reach a facilitated agreement or partial agreement, which saves time, money and appearances before a judge.
Step 5 — Resolution or Trial. If the parties reach a full agreement, a Separation Agreement and Parenting Plan are drafted and submitted for court approval. If disputes remain unresolved, the case proceeds to a Permanent Orders Hearing where the judge issues a final Decree of Dissolution of Marriage.
Colorado law no longer uses the term “custody.” Under C.R.S. § 14-10-124, courts determine the Allocation of Parental Responsibilities (APR) under Colorado child custody and parenting time law. APR is divided into two components:
Parenting Time — The actual schedule of overnights the child spends with each parent.
Decision-Making Responsibility — Who decides major issues regarding education, religion, and non-emergency medical care (Sole vs. Joint).
The court’s only standard is the best interests of the child. Colorado does not presume that equal parenting time is automatically in the child’s best interests — the court evaluates the specific circumstances of each family. When parenting matters are contested, child support obligations are calculated in conjunction with the parenting time schedule under C.R.S. § 14-10-115.
Equitable Division of Assets
Colorado is an equitable distribution state, not a community property state. Under Colorado’s equitable property division statute, C.R.S. § 14-10-113, the court divides marital property equitably — meaning fairly, not necessarily equally. Factors include:
Each spouse’s contribution to the acquisition of marital property, including homemaking contributions.
The economic circumstances of each spouse at the time of division.
Whether property is marital (acquired during the marriage) or separate (owned prior to marriage or received by inheritance or gift).
Marital property subject to division includes real estate, bank and investment accounts, retirement accounts, business interests, and debt accumulated during the marriage. Separate property — assets owned before the marriage or received as individual gifts or inheritance — is generally excluded from division, though commingling with marital assets often affects that characterization because placing separate property into joint ownership means that property is a presumed gift to the marriage.
Spousal Maintenance
Under Colorado spousal maintenance law, C.R.S. § 14-10-114, maintenance is not automatic. Courts apply advisory guidelines for couples with combined gross incomes under $240,000 per year. The formula calculates maintenance as approximately 40% of the higher earner’s monthly adjusted gross income minus 50% of the lower earner’s monthly adjusted gross income. The duration of maintenance is also guideline-based, scaled to the length of the marriage. Courts retain discretion to deviate from the guidelines based on the specific circumstances of each case.
Colorado Divorce FAQs
How to get a divorce in Colorado?
To obtain a divorce, at least one spouse must be a resident for 91 days before filing a Petition for Dissolution of Marriage. The process involves serving your spouse and waiting a mandatory 91-day “cooling-off” period, during which financial disclosures are exchanged. Hiring a Colorado divorce lawyer at The Drake Law Firm, PC can streamline this process and ensure all legal requirements are met.
How much does a divorce cost in Colorado?
The court charges a standard filing fee to initiate the case, which is $230 as of January 1, 2026 within Colorado. However, the total cost depends heavily on whether the divorce is contested or uncontested. An uncontested divorce is significantly less expensive, whereas a contested case involving a divorce attorney can range from $10,000 to $50,000 or more depending on litigation needs.
How long does divorce take?
Colorado law mandates a minimum 91-day waiting period after the petition is filed and served before a court can issue a final decree. While uncontested divorces can be wrapped up in approximately 4 months, complex cases often take at least a year to resolve.
Are divorce records public?
Yes, certain divorce records are generally public and accessible to anyone after the decree is finalized; however sworn financial statements, supporting financial schedules, child support worksheets and parenting plans are commonly suppressed.  In addition, parties can request that the court seal or redact sensitive documents to protect their privacy, but those requests are not automatically granted.
Is Colorado a no-fault state for divorce?
Yes, Colorado is strictly a “no-fault” divorce state. You do not need to prove marital misconduct such as adultery; you only need to demonstrate to the court that the marriage is “irretrievably broken.
Is Colorado a 50/50 split in divorce?
Colorado is an “equitable distribution” state rather than a community property state, so assets are not automatically split 50/50. Instead, the court divides property in a manner it deems fair and equitable based on the contributions and economic circumstances of each spouse.
What is a spouse entitled to in a divorce in Colorado?
A spouse is entitled to an equitable portion of the marital property and, in certain cases, spousal maintenance (alimony) if he or she earns significantly less than his or her spouse. Navigating these entitlements can be complex, so consulting a Colorado divorce lawyer is highly encouraged to protect your family’s financial future.

You do not have to face this uncertainty alone. Whether you are ready to file or just need to understand your rights, we are here to help. Contact The Drake Law Firm, P.C and talk about your situation so we can map out a clear path forward.

Frequently Asked Questions About Family Law

## Golden Child Custody
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/golden-child-custody/

Child Custody in Colorado
Most parents searching for custody information in Colorado quickly discover that the state does not use the word ‘custody’ in its family law statutes at all. If you are trying to understand how parenting time or decision-making authority works in Colorado, this is where to start.
Colorado governs these decisions through a framework called the Allocation of Parental Responsibilities (APR), which replaces the traditional terms “custody” and “visitation” with two distinct legal concepts: decision-making responsibility and parenting time. These two components are evaluated and allocated independently under Colorado Revised Statutes Title 14, Article 10.
APR proceedings arise in two primary contexts: as part of a divorce and dissolution of marriage under C.R.S. § 14-10-106, or as a standalone action when parents were never married. In the latter case, establishing paternity in Colorado is typically a prerequisite before APR can be formally addressed by the court.
Decision-Making Responsibility
Decision-making responsibility governs which parent—or both parents jointly—holds the legal authority to make major decisions affecting the child’s life during and after a divorce. While Colorado statute covers various areas, these typically center around the “Big Three”: medical care, education, and religious upbringing. It also frequently addresses the child’s involvement in extracurricular activities.
Joint Decision-Making
Under joint decision-making, both parents share equal authority over major decisions and must confer before implementing significant changes in the child’s life. Joint decision-making is the statutory presumption in Colorado. It does not dictate the parenting time schedule and is evaluated independently of where the child physically resides.
C.R.S. § 14-10-124(1.5) permits the court to allocate decision-making independently across categories. For example, one parent may be granted sole authority over educational decisions while the parties retain joint authority over healthcare.
Sole Decision-Making
Sole decision-making grants one parent exclusive authority without requiring consultation with the other. Courts award it when joint decision-making would endanger the child’s physical health or significantly impair emotional development. Statutory grounds include:
A history of domestic violence or child abuse (C.R.S. § 14-10-124(4)(a))
Substance abuse that impairs parenting capacity
A documented inability of the parties to cooperate without conflict
Even where sole decision-making is ordered, the non-custodial parent generally retains parenting time unless that contact would also endanger the child.
Parenting Time
Parenting time defines the physical schedule under which the child resides with and is cared for by each parent. It is determined independently of decision-making responsibility.
Equal Parenting Time (50/50)
Colorado courts have moved toward equal parenting time as a general preference when both parents are fit and geographically proximate. Common schedules include the 2-2-3 rotation and alternating week arrangements. Equal parenting time does not eliminate child support obligations—support is calculated based on income differential and number of overnights regardless of schedule symmetry (see managing child support in Colorado for how the Income Shares model applies to equal-time arrangements).
Majority Parenting Time
In majority parenting time arrangements, the child resides primarily with one parent and spends designated time with the other. This structure is common when parents reside in different school districts or when a parent’s employment schedule makes equal time impractical.
Supervised Parenting Time
When the court finds that unsupervised parenting time would endanger the child’s physical or emotional health, it may order supervised parenting time under C.R.S. § 14-10-129. Supervision may be conducted by a designated family member or a professional agency and is typically a transitional arrangement subject to review upon demonstrated behavioral change.
The Best Interests Standard: C.R.S. § 14-10-124
All APR determinations in Colorado are governed by the best interests of the child standard codified at C.R.S. § 14-10-124. Colorado courts do not apply a maternal or paternal preference. The statute enumerates specific factors the court must consider.
Parenting history and caretaking function: The court examines which parent has historically performed caretaking functions—medical appointments, school involvement, daily care routines—and the quality of the parent-child relationship with each parent.
Physical and emotional safety: Any history of child abuse, domestic violence (C.R.S. § 14-10-124(1.5)(b)), neglect, or substance abuse is weighted heavily. A documented history of domestic violence triggers mandatory statutory consideration and may result in restricted or supervised parenting time.
Ability to encourage the other parent’s relationship: Courts explicitly consider which parent is more likely to facilitate frequent and continuing contact between the child and the other parent. A parent who attempts to limit or obstruct the child’s relationship with the other parent—absent legitimate safety concerns—may receive an unfavorable allocation.
Geographic proximity: The physical distance between parents’ residences affects the practical viability of equal time schedules and informs the court’s analysis of what arrangement best supports the child’s routine and schooling. The Drake Law Firm handles APR cases across Colorado’s judicial districts, including cases where parents reside in different counties or regions.
The child’s adjustment: The court considers the child’s adjustment to home, school, and community, and the degree of disruption a particular allocation would cause.
The child’s wishes: A child’s preference is a statutory factor under C.R.S. § 14-10-124(1)(b)(III). There is no fixed age at which preference becomes controlling. Courts weigh preference against the child’s age and maturity, but the judge retains final decision-making authority.
The APR Legal Process in Colorado
Initiating the Case
APR proceedings are initiated by filing a Petition for Allocation of Parental Responsibilities in the district court of the county where the child has resided for at least six months, establishing jurisdiction under the UCCJEA (C.R.S. § 14-13-201). If filed as part of a dissolution proceeding, APR is addressed within that case. The petitioner must submit a proposed parenting plan outlining both decision-making allocation and a parenting time schedule, along with required financial disclosures. The Colorado child custody attorneys at The Drake Law Firm can help ensure your petition and proposed parenting plan are properly prepared from the outset.
Initial Status Conference
Following service, the court schedules an Initial Status Conference to establish the case timeline and procedural deadlines. Where a party demonstrates urgency—such as one parent denying the other access to the child—a temporary orders hearing may be requested at or prior to the ISC.
Temporary orders establish the interim parenting schedule while the case is pending. Courts are reluctant to disrupt arrangements that appear to be working, so temporary orders often carry weight through the final hearing. They address both parenting time and, where applicable, interim decision-making authority.
Mandatory Mediation
Colorado courts require parties to attempt mediation before proceeding to a final orders hearing. C.R.S. § 13-22-311 governs court-ordered mediation. The mediator is a neutral third party; attorneys may attend. Agreements reached in mediation are typically incorporated into stipulated orders and entered as a final judgment.
Parenting Education
Most Colorado judicial districts require both parents to complete a court-approved parenting education course before final orders are entered. Completion is a prerequisite to finalizing the case in most districts
Child and Family Investigators (CFIs)
When contested issues require independent fact-finding, the court may appoint a Child and Family Investigator (CFI) under C.R.S. § 14-10-116.5. The CFI conducts interviews with both parents, the child, and relevant third parties; reviews records; and submits a written report with recommendations to the court. CFI recommendations are not binding, but they are given substantial weight by the judge.
Final Orders Hearing
If mediation does not resolve all issues, the case proceeds to a final orders hearing. The court hears testimony, reviews evidence, and may receive the CFI’s report. The judge issues permanent orders governing decision-making and parenting time, which remain in effect until modified by subsequent court order or until the child reaches the age of majority.
Parenting Plans
A parenting plan is a written document required by Colorado courts that specifies the parenting time schedule, holiday allocations, and decision-making protocols. Required elements include:
The regular parenting time schedule (school year and summer)
Holiday, school break, and vacation schedules
Transportation responsibilities and exchange locations
Communication protocols between parents
Process for resolving future disputes
Colorado courts encourage parents to submit an agreed parenting plan. If no agreement is reached, the court issues its own plan based on the evidence presented.
Modifying an APR Order
An existing APR order may be modified under C.R.S. § 14-10-129. The threshold showing depends on what is being modified.
Decision-making modification requires a showing of a substantial and continuing change in circumstances and that modification is in the child’s best interests. The statute imposes a two-year waiting period after entry of final orders before a decision-making modification may be sought, absent specified emergency circumstances.
Parenting time modification (non-majority) may be sought upon showing the modification serves the child’s best interests, without the two-year waiting period.
Majority parenting time modification requires both the substantial change in circumstances showing and a best-interests analysis. Courts apply greater scrutiny to these modifications due to the disruption they cause to the child’s stability.
Emergency Restrictions on Parenting Time
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-129(4), a party may file a Motion to Restrict Parenting Time when the child is in imminent physical or emotional danger. Upon filing, the court must schedule a hearing within 14 days. This is a high-threshold remedy; filing without adequate factual support can damage credibility with the court and lead to sanctions.
Colorado Child Custody FAQs
How to get custody of a child in Colorado?
To obtain legal custody, formally known as the “Allocation of Parental Responsibilities,” you must file a petition with the district court in the county where the child has resided for at least the last 182 days. The court determines custody based on the “best interests of the child,” so submitting a comprehensive parenting plan is essential for a favorable outcome.
Who claims a child on taxes with 50/50 custody?
Technically, the IRS allows the parent with the higher number of overnight stays to claim the child, but in 50/50 scenarios, parents often rotate the tax deduction every other year. A Colorado child custody lawyer can help draft a specific provision in your parenting plan to ensure this agreement is legally binding and clearly understood by both parties.
What not to say in child custody mediation?
You should avoid badmouthing the other parent, making threats, or focusing solely on money rather than the child’s well-being. Comments that suggest you are using the child to punish your ex can backfire, as mediators look for parents willing to facilitate a positive relationship between the child and the other parent.
How to get full custody of a child?
Because Colorado courts presume that shared parenting is in a child’s best interest, obtaining “full custody”—which usually implies both primary parenting time and sole decision-making authority—is a high legal bar. You typically must prove that shared responsibility would endanger the child physically or emotionally. Since this requires presenting substantial evidence to the court, it is vital to work with an experienced child custody attorney to build your case.
How much does it cost to file for full custody in Colorado?
The court requires a filing fee to open the case, usually over $200, excluding additional costs for serving papers or mandatory mediation. However, if you are seeking full custody in a contested battle, total legal costs can vary widely depending on the complexity of litigation and the evidence required.
Contact The Drake Law Firm, PC
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents parents in Allocation of Parental Responsibilities proceedings throughout Colorado. Whether you are establishing a parenting plan for the first time, seeking to modify an existing order, or navigating a high-conflict custody dispute, our attorneys work to protect your parental rights and your child’s best interests under Colorado law.
Unfit Parents
Sadly, some parents are unfit to raise children. If a parent is an alcoholic, abusive, neglectful, or mentally ill, he or she might be deemed unfit. Then, the other parent can receive sole physical and legal custody. If you think the other parent is unfit, speak to your  child custody lawyer. Your child’s safety and well-being are at risk, so you need to move forward and take action quickly.
Unmarried Fathers
In Colorado, if a child is born to parents who are not married, the mother is automatically granted both full legal and physical custody of the child. The father does not have any custody or visitation rights unless a court order is obtained or if the parents reach an agreement. It’s important to note that the birth of a child does not immediately establish a legal parent-child relationship in this situation.
Can The Child Decide Where To Live?
While the child cannot choose the custody arrangement, the court will consider his or her opinion. First, the judge will assess the child’s maturity. If the judge believes he or she is mature enough to understand the situation, the child can then provide an opinion. The child’s opinion is just one of many factors that go into developing custody agreements.

## Golden Child Support
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/golden-child-support/

Child Support in Colorado
Most parents dealing with a separation or dissolution of marriage proceedings quickly encounter a system built around one central question: what financial support does the child need, and who pays it? Under Colorado law, child support is not discretionary. Both parents are legally obligated to support their child in proportion to their respective incomes, regardless of marital status. Understanding how that obligation is calculated — and what happens when circumstances change — is where to start.
Talk to a Child Support Lawyer Now
Colorado governs child support through C.R.S. § 14-10-115, which establishes the Income Shares Model as the mandatory calculation framework. This statute, along with the Colorado Child Support Guidelines periodically updated by the Colorado Child Support Commission, defines which income sources count, what adjustments are allowed, and when a court may depart from the standard formula. Significant updates to the guidelines took effect March 1, 2026, under House Bill 25-1159, and apply to all orders entered or modified on or after that date.
Colorado's Legal Framework for Child Support
The primary statute governing child support in Colorado is C.R.S. § 14-10-115. It establishes mandatory calculation worksheets, defines which income sources are included, identifies allowable adjustments, and sets out when courts may deviate from the guideline amount. Child support cases are handled in the district courts of each county and may arise in several contexts:
As part of a dissolution of marriage proceeding
As part of a legal separation
Within an Allocation of Parental Responsibilities (APR) case
As a standalone action through Colorado Child Support Services (CSS), an agency within the Colorado Department of Human Services
Before a support order can be entered against a legal father, legal paternity establishment is a prerequisite before child support can be ordered. The Drake Law Firm, PC handles paternity matters as part of its family law practice.
Statutory Definitions of Income
Colorado defines gross income broadly under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(5)(a). Includable income sources encompass wages, salaries, commissions, bonuses, dividends, severance pay, pensions, interest, trust income, Social Security benefits (including disability), workers’ compensation, unemployment insurance, and income from self-employment or operation of a business. Non-recurring or extraordinary income — such as a one-time capital gain — may be treated differently by the court depending on whether it reflects the parent’s ongoing financial capacity.
Income imputation rules apply when a parent is voluntarily unemployed or underemployed. In these situations, the court may attribute income based on the parent’s historical earnings, occupational qualifications, and the prevailing job market.
Certain items are excluded from the gross income calculation, including means-tested public assistance (such as TANF and SSI), child support received for children from other relationships, and income of the parent’s new spouse or partner.
How Child Support Is Calculated: The Income Shares Model
Colorado uses the Income Shares Model, which is based on the principle that a child should receive the same proportion of parental income as if the parents lived together. The calculation follows a structured worksheet process using the state’s official Child Support Schedule — a table of presumed combined support obligations based on combined adjusted gross income and number of children.
Step 1 — Determine Each Parent’s Gross Monthly Income
The court starts with each parent’s gross monthly income from all sources. For W-2 employees this is straightforward. For self-employed parents, net business income after ordinary and necessary business expenses (but before personal tax deductions) is used. For parents with variable income, courts often average the prior 12 to 36 months of earnings.
Step 2 — Calculate Combined Adjusted Gross Income
The two parents’ gross incomes are added together to arrive at the Combined Adjusted Gross Income (CAGI). Adjustments may include amounts paid for health insurance premiums for the child and child support obligations for children from prior relationships.
Step 3 — Look Up the Basic Child Support Obligation
The CAGI and the number of children are entered into the Colorado Child Support Schedule to determine the Basic Child Support Obligation (BCSO). This schedule is codified in C.R.S. § 14-10-115(7)(b) and reflects estimated expenditures on children at various income levels based on economic research. The 2026 updated schedule covers combined monthly adjusted gross incomes of up to $40,000 — increased from the prior $30,000 cap — and reflects current costs of raising a child based on the Betson-Rothbarth Study and 2023 Bureau of Labor Statistics data. For combined incomes above $40,000, courts retain discretion in determining the appropriate amount.
Step 4 — Add Work-Related Child Care and Health Insurance
Work-related child care costs and the cost of the child’s health insurance premium are added to the BCSO to produce the Total Child Support Obligation. The health insurance figure used is the cost of the child’s portion of the premium only — not the total family premium. Coverage through public programs such as Medicaid or CHP+ is also accounted for under this step. These are actual, documented costs — not estimates.
Step 5 — Apportion Between Parents
Each parent’s share of the Total Child Support Obligation is proportional to their contribution to the CAGI. For example, if Parent A earns 60% of the combined income, Parent A is responsible for 60% of the obligation. The residential parent is presumed to spend their share directly; the non-residential parent’s share is the payment amount.
Parenting Time and Child Support
For orders entered or modified on or after March 1, 2026, Colorado has eliminated the previous “93-overnight cliff” under the updated C.R.S. § 14-10-115(8). Prior law only recognized shared parenting time for child support purposes once a parent reached 93 or more overnights per year — meaning a parent with 90 overnights received the same credit as a parent with zero. That threshold no longer applies.
Under the 2026 framework, every overnight is formally recognized through a graduated Parenting Time Table. A parent receives incremental credit for parenting time expenses starting from the first overnight, scaled proportionally across the full range of parenting time. The prior dual-worksheet structure (Worksheet A for sole custody, Worksheet B for shared custody) has been replaced by a unified calculation: the basic support obligation is drawn from the standard schedule, allocated between parents in proportion to their adjusted gross incomes, and then each parent receives a parenting time credit based on their share of overnights as listed in the Parenting Time Table. The annual overnight count comes directly from the parenting schedule established in a parenting plan or custody order, making accurate documentation of that schedule essential.
At equal parenting time (182 or more overnights each), the parenting time credit is maximized, though a support obligation may still exist if there is a meaningful income disparity between the parents.
For very low-income parents, the Self-Support Reserve (SSR) and Low-Income Adjustment provisions may affect the final obligation. The SSR is calculated at 29 hours per week at the state minimum wage multiplied by 50 weeks and divided by 12 — a figure that adjusts as Colorado’s minimum wage changes. Parents whose income falls between $650 per month and the SSR are subject to a revised low-income schedule, and those whose income exceeds the SSR but remains near minimum wage have their total support obligation capped as a percentage of income.
Deviation from the Guidelines
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(3)(b), a court may deviate from the guideline amount if application of the formula would be inequitable, unjust, or inappropriate in a specific case. Grounds for deviation include:
Extraordinary medical needs of the child
Educational costs of the child
Special needs of the child
Financial resources of the child
Travel expenses for parenting time
Any deviation must be supported by written findings stating the amount that would have been ordered under the guidelines and why deviation serves the child’s best interests.
Establishing a Child Support Order in Colorado
Through Divorce or Allocation of Parental Responsibilities
When parents divorce or legal separation involves minor children, the court will enter a child support order as part of the final decree. The parties must file a completed Child Support Worksheet along with sworn financial disclosures. Colorado Rule of Civil Procedure 16.2 requires both parties to exchange mandatory financial disclosures, including three years of tax returns, two months of pay stubs, and documentation of all assets and debts. Working with Colorado child support attorneys during this stage helps ensure disclosures are complete and the worksheet accurately reflects each parent’s financial circumstances.
Through Colorado Child Support Services
Colorado Child Support Services (CSS), administered at the county level through local Child Support Units, provides services to establish, collect, and enforce child support orders. Services are available to any parent regardless of income and are required for families receiving TANF benefits. CSS can establish paternity, locate the other parent, establish a support order through the courts or through an administrative process, and collect payments through the Colorado Family Support Registry (CFSR).
During a pending divorce or APR case, either party may request temporary child support via a motion and financial affidavit. Temporary orders remain in effect until the court enters a final order at the permanent hearing. The temporary amount is calculated using the same guideline formula.
Payment, Collection, and the Colorado Family Support Registry
All child support payments ordered by Colorado courts are made through the Colorado Family Support Registry (CFSR), administered by the Colorado Department of Human Services. Direct payments between parents are not recognized as satisfying a court-ordered support obligation unless the order specifically authorizes them — paying directly to the other parent risks having those payments treated as gifts in any subsequent enforcement action.
Income Withholding Orders (IWO) are issued automatically in most cases under C.R.S. § 14-14-111.5. The IWO directs the paying parent’s employer to deduct support from wages and remit directly to the CFSR. IWOs can also be served on unemployment benefits and some other income sources. Parents who are self-employed or have variable income may be required to make direct payments to the CFSR on a scheduled basis.
Enforcement of Child Support in Colorado
When a parent fails to pay court-ordered child support, Colorado law provides a broad array of enforcement tools. Enforcement actions can be initiated by the receiving parent, by their attorney, or by Colorado Child Support Services.
Administrative Enforcement Remedies
C.R.S. § 26-13-122 and related statutes authorize CSS to take the following administrative actions without a court hearing:
License suspension: driver’s licenses, professional licenses, recreational licenses (hunting, fishing), and business licenses
Tax intercept: federal and Colorado state income tax refunds
Credit bureau reporting: delinquent support reported to consumer credit agencies once arrears exceed a threshold
Bank account seizure (FIDM): CSS can freeze and seize funds in bank accounts through the Financial Institution Data Match program
Lottery and gambling intercept: winnings above the statutory threshold are intercepted
Passport denial: the federal Office of Child Support Enforcement (OCSE) denies or revokes passports when arrears exceed $2,500
Judicial Enforcement Remedies
A party or CSS may also seek judicial enforcement through a motion for contempt of court (C.R.C.P. 107). If the court finds a parent in contempt for willful non-payment, remedies include fines, a remedial or punitive jail sentence, and entry of a judgment for arrears. Judgments for unpaid child support bear interest at the statutory rate. In egregious cases, criminal prosecution under C.R.S. § 14-14-104 (criminal nonsupport) may apply.
Interstate Enforcement — UIFSA
Colorado has adopted the Uniform Interstate Family Support Act (UIFSA), codified at C.R.S. § 14-5-101 et seq. Under UIFSA, a Colorado order can be registered and enforced in any other state, and orders from other states can be registered in Colorado. The issuing state retains continuing exclusive jurisdiction over the support order as long as a party or the child remains in that state.
Modifying Child Support in Colorado
A child support order may be modified when there has been a substantial and continuing change of circumstances that results in at least a 10% change in the monthly support amount under C.R.S. § 14-10-122(1)(a). This 10% threshold is the operative standard — a court will not grant a modification unless the recalculated amount reflects that change. The passage of time alone is generally not sufficient grounds for a judicial modification without a corresponding shift in financial circumstances or parenting time.
For cases managed by Colorado Child Support Services, CSS conducts an administrative review every three years. However, even in those reviews, a modification will only be entered if the recalculation produces at least a 10% change in the obligation amount.
What Constitutes a Substantial Change
Examples of changes that may support a modification petition include:
Significant increase or decrease in either parent’s income (including job loss, promotion, or career change)
A change in the number of overnights the child spends with each parent
The child gaining or losing health insurance coverage through a parent’s employer
Substantial changes in work-related child care costs
The child developing significant medical or educational needs not previously ordered • Emancipation of one child in a multi-child order, requiring recalculation for remaining children
The Modification Process
The requesting parent files a Motion to Modify Child Support along with an updated Child Support Worksheet and updated financial disclosures. If the parties agree on the new amount, a Stipulation and Proposed Order can be submitted for the court’s approval. If not, the matter proceeds to a hearing where both parties present current financial information.
The modification is effective from the date of filing of the motion — not the date of the hearing — so prompt filing is important. Until a court enters a modified order, the original obligation remains in full force. A parent experiencing sudden financial hardship, such as a layoff, should file the modification motion immediately rather than waiting to see if circumstances improve.
Duration and Termination of Child Support in Colorado
Under C.R.S. § 14-10-115(13), child support in Colorado terminates by operation of law when the last or only child covered by the order turns 19. No court motion is required for termination in that circumstance. However, if the order covers multiple children and only one reaches age 19, the obligation does not automatically reduce — the paying parent must file a motion to modify so the court can recalculate the amount for the remaining children.
Additional exceptions that may extend support beyond age 19 include:
The child has not yet graduated from high school at age 19 — support continues until graduation or age 21, whichever occurs first
The child is mentally or physically disabled — the court may order support beyond age 19 upon a showing of need
The parties have agreed in writing to extend support for post-secondary education or other purposes — Colorado courts cannot order a parent to pay college expenses over their objection, but such provisions are enforceable as contract terms if voluntarily agreed upon and incorporated into the court order
Support also terminates upon the child’s emancipation before age 19, which may occur through marriage, military enlistment, or a court order.
Tax Considerations
Child support payments are tax-neutral under both federal and Colorado state law. The paying parent may not deduct child support payments, and the receiving parent does not report them as taxable income. For divorce decrees entered after December 31, 2018, Colorado spousal maintenance is also tax-neutral at both the federal and state level under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act — the payer may not deduct it and the recipient does not report it as income. Both obligations are treated the same way for tax purposes under current law.
By default, the parent with the majority of overnights has the right to claim the child as a dependent for purposes of the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit. However, parents may agree — or the court may order — that the non-residential parent claim the child in alternating years or under other arrangements, formalized through IRS Form 8332.
Child Support and Paternity in Colorado
Before a child support order can be entered against a legal father, Colorado paternity law governs how legal fatherhood is determined. In Colorado, paternity is established in one of three ways:
The parents are married at the time of birth (the marital presumption under C.R.S. § 19-4-105)
Both parents sign a Voluntary Acknowledgment of Paternity (VAP) at the hospital or through the Colorado Vital Records office
A court or administrative order following genetic testing adjudicates paternity
Once legal paternity determination is complete, either parent may seek a child support order. The Colorado Child Support Services program provides administrative paternity establishment services at no cost to the applicant.
Frequently Asked Questions About Child Support
Is child support taxable in Colorado?
No, child support is tax-neutral. The parent receiving the payments does not report them as taxable income, and the parent paying support cannot claim them as a tax deduction on their state or federal return.
Does child support count as income?
For tax purposes, child support does not count as income. However, lenders may consider it as income when you apply for a mortgage or car loan, and state agencies may count it when determining eligibility for certain public assistance programs.
How is child support calculated in Colorado?
Colorado uses the Income Shares Model, which estimates the amount parents would have spent on the child if they were still together. The court inputs both parents’ gross monthly incomes, the number of overnight visits, and expenses like health insurance and childcare into a statutory formula to determine the final amount.
How to apply for child support?
You can apply directly through the Colorado Child Support Services (CSS) website or your county’s Department of Human Services. Alternatively, if you are going through a divorce or custody case, a Colorado child support lawyer at The Drake Law Firm, PC can file the necessary motions with the court to establish an order as part of your case.
What happens if a parent doesn't pay child support in Colorado?
Colorado takes non-payment seriously, and enforcement measures can include wage garnishment, interception of tax refunds, and suspension of driver’s or professional licenses. In severe cases, a motion for contempt of court may result in fines or jail time for the non-paying parent.
How The Drake Law Firm, PC Can Help with Child Support in Colorado
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents clients in child support matters at all stages — from initial establishment through modification and enforcement.
The firm’s attorneys bring direct experience with Colorado’s Income Shares Model, the financial disclosure requirements of C.R.C.P. 16.2, and the practical realities of income withholding, CSS enforcement actions, and post-decree modifications in Jefferson County and the surrounding district courts served by our family law offices in Colorado. The firm offers both non-adversarial resolution strategies and courtroom advocacy when litigation is required.
Taking the Next Steps for Your Children
The Drake Law Firm, PC represents parents in child support matters throughout Colorado. Whether you are establishing a support order for the first time, seeking support modification after a change in income or parenting time, or enforcing an order that isn’t being followed, our attorneys work to protect your child’s financial security and your rights under Colorado law.

## Spousal Support Lawyer in Jefferson County Colorado

Jefferson County Spousal Support Lawyer
Going Through a Divorce and Have Questions about Maintenance or Spousal Support and Looking for a Golden Area Spousal Support Attorney That Covers All the Bases, Does Not Complicate Cases for Extra Billing, Really Cares and Keeps Focused on the Best Interests of You & Your Family?
Alimony and Spousal Support in Golden
You were prepared for the emotional impact of your divorce, but the financial impact might have taken you by surprise. You’ve become accustomed to a certain standard of living while married, and now, you’re having a hard time making ends meet. Fortunately, you can file a petition for alimony or request a modification for spousal maintenance.
Spousal support was created to help men and women who didn’t work outside of the home during the marriage or who make significantly less money than their former partners. Numerous factors go into the size of the support payment, including the length of the marriage and the income disparity. Contact our Golden alimony and spousal support lawyers to find out if you’re eligible. We can also calculate the amount of money that the other party owes you in spousal support.
Types of Alimony in Colorado
Our Golden, CO, alimony and spousal support lawyers can help you apply for:
Temporary maintenance
Rehabilitative maintenance
Reimbursement maintenance
Permanent maintenance
Consult with us today to learn more about your options for alimony.
Straight Shooters – You’ve made an important decision in your life. We respect you for that. You can count on us to give you the honest (sometimes hard) truth about what to expect on the road ahead so that you can be prepared in every way possible.
Because Your Family and Happiness Are at Stake – The smoother and fairer this process goes, the better the post-divorce interactions tend to be. This is better for everyone involved.
Aspects of Maintenance We Assist You With
If you are currently going through a divorce, your Golden alimony and spousal support lawyer can help you get temporary support. These payments can continue through the divorce. When the divorce is finalized, you can transition to another alimony type. Often, the transition is made to rehabilitative support payments. If you receive rehabilitative support, you’ll continue to get payments until you become financially independent. Thus, once you get a stable job, the payments will end.
Reimbursement support is also an option. The judge might grant this if you paid for professional certificates or education expenses. This alimony allows the other party to pay you back and will end once you’re paid in full.
Finally, there is permanent alimony. As the name suggests, this goes on forever. However, it’s only granted in exceptional circumstances. For instance, if you have a chronic illness or disability, you might qualify for permanent support.
Consult with a Golden alimony and spousal support lawyer if you want to modify the agreement. The attorney can review your case to see if you’re eligible for a modification. If you are, your attorney can file the necessary paperwork.
Calculating Spousal Support In Colorado
Your Golden alimony and spousal support lawyer can negotiate maintenance payments for you or represent you in court. If the case goes to court, the judge will consider various factors to determine your eligibility and the amount of the support order. First, you must have been married for a minimum of three years unless you meet specific requirements.
Then, the judge will consider the income of both parties, including the potential income. Other factors include employability, property distribution, child support payments, and lifestyle during the marriage. In addition, both parties’ age and health factor into the decision. Finally, the judge will determine if one spouse should provide support so the other could get an education and work.

When to Get a Prenuptial or Postnuptial Agreement
A prenuptial agreement is a contract between two people who plan to marry. Many people hesitate to discuss this planning tool with their future spouses for fear of offending them before marriage. However, an open discussion about assets and what each person expects in the event of a breakup and divorce can lead to a trust-filled relationship.
So you got married without a prenuptial agreement? You can still enter into a postnuptial agreement to document how you have agreed to divide property in the event of a divorce.
The main benefit of a postnuptial agreement is to keep any property you owned before the marriage as non-marital and separate from property acquired during the marriage. Over time, assets tend to shift around and get commingled, and the postnuptial agreement will help document the non-marital assets.

Alimony award limitations or exclusions to prevent expensive litigation in the event of a divorce

Assets earmarked for children, especially from a prior marriage

Lakewood Paternity FAQs
What is paternity, and why does it matter?
Paternity legally defines who your child’s father is. It matters because it unlocks rights, like custody, visitation, support, and responsibilities. Confirming paternity ensures both parents can make decisions about your child’s future and secure financial stability.
How is paternity established in Lakewood?
Paternity in Lakewood is established by signing a Voluntary Acknowledgment at birth or through DNA testing and a court order via Jefferson County Family Court. We walk you through each step, from lab work to paperwork, to ensure courts recognize your parental status.
Can paternity be contested once signed?
Yes, it can. If you signed a voluntary acknowledgment, Colorado law allows rescission within 60 days. After that, contesting requires solid DNA evidence and court filings. We support both mothers and fathers in seeking correction, clarity, or challenge when needed.
Will I need support or custody orders afterward?
Almost always. Once paternity is set, parents usually need child support and parenting time or custody orders. We help Lakewood families establish fair financial obligations and visitation schedules that reflect your child’s needs and your family’s unique situation.

Golden Family Law Attorney FAQs
How can a Golden family law attorney help me with divorce or custody?
A Golden family law attorney assists clients with legal matters that affect their families, including divorce, child custody, parenting plans, child support, and dividing property. At The Drake Law Firm, we work closely with clients to understand their goals and take practical steps to protect their future. Whether you’re starting a divorce, adjusting custody arrangements, or handling support issues, a family lawyer guides you through your rights, paperwork, and agreements.
Will I need to appear in court for a family law case in Golden?
Not every family law case in Golden requires an in-person court appearance. Most cases start with a virtual Initial Status Conference. Many matters, such as custody schedules, support agreements, or property division, can often be resolved through negotiation or mediation. If both parties cooperate, your Golden family law attorney can help create legally binding agreements without stepping into a courtroom. If disputes arise, your lawyer is ready to represent you at hearings to protect your interests.
What is the timeline for getting a divorce in Colorado?
Colorado requires a 91-day waiting period before a divorce can be finalized, beginning after your spouse is served or immediately if you file jointly. Beyond this mandatory period, the divorce timeline depends on how quickly you and your spouse reach agreements on issues like child custody, support, and property division. A Golden family lawyer can help ensure your case moves efficiently and all legal requirements are handled correctly.
What if my spouse and I already agree on all divorce terms?
If both spouses agree on parenting schedules, asset division, and support, you can submit your settlement to the court for approval. This is called an uncontested divorce. Uncontested divorces in Golden are generally faster and more affordable than contested cases. A Golden family law attorney will review your financial disclosures, parenting plan, and agreements to ensure everything meets Colorado law, then file the necessary documents to finalize your divorce smoothly.
Can child custody or support orders be changed in later?
Yes. Custody and child support orders can be modified in Golden if circumstances change, such as a job loss, relocation, or changes in a child’s needs. To request a modification, you must show that the new situation significantly affects the original order. A Golden family law attorney can help prepare and file your request and advocate for adjustments that reflect your current reality.

## Prenup Lawyer – Arvada CO
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/prenup-lawyer-arvada-co/

Prenuptial Agreement Lawyers in Arvada, CO
The Drake Law Firm, P.C. empowers individuals, both men and women, to seek prenuptial agreements in order to strengthen their bonds and protect their futures.
Prenups in Arvada & Colorado
Marriage is often one of life’s most significant milestones, marked by hope, love, and promises for the future. No one embarks on this journey envisioning its end, which is why conversations about prenuptial agreements can feel uncomfortable. However, contrary to common belief, prenups aren’t about casting doubt on the union but rather about fostering open communication, understanding, and security.
Our Arvada, CO prenup lawyers can guide you and your future spouse in creating a fair and enforceable prenuptial agreement that will protect your property and interests, allowing you to feel more secure about your future together.
What is a Prenuptial Agreement?
A prenuptial agreement, or prenup, is a legal document created by couples before marriage to outline property division and responsibilities in the event of divorce or death. While it may seem unromantic to discuss such matters before tying the knot, a prenup can offer clarity, protection, and peace of mind for both parties.
How Can a Prenup Help Your Marriage?
Contrary to popular belief, prenuptial agreements can actually strengthen a marriage by facilitating honest conversations about finances, expectations, and goals. By openly discussing financial matters and potential scenarios, couples can build trust, understanding, and a solid foundation for their future together. In the event of divorce, a prenup can simplify proceedings, reduce conflict, and protect both parties’ interests.
Who Should Get a Prenuptial Agreement?
Prenuptial agreements aren’t just for the wealthy or those with substantial assets. They can benefit anyone who wants to safeguard their financial future, protect assets acquired before marriage, or ensure fair treatment in the event of divorce. Whether you have significant wealth, own a business, have children from a previous relationship, or simply want to clarify financial expectations, a prenup can provide invaluable protection and peace of mind.
What Can a Prenuptial Agreement Cover in Colorado?
In Colorado, a premarital agreement can address various financial and personal matters, including the division of assets (separate property) and debts, spousal support (alimony), property rights, and inheritance issues. However, they cannot include provisions related to child custody, visitation, or support, as these matters are determined based on the child’s best interests at the time of divorce. It also cannot outright deny alimony (spousal support).
Why You Need an Arvada Prenup Lawyer
Some couples consider creating their prenuptial agreement on their own, without the help of an attorney. However, this approach can be risky and problematic.
Prenuptial agreements are complex legal documents that require adherence to specific rules and guidelines to be legally binding. If the document fails to meet all legal requirements, it may not offer protection to either party or safeguard the marital assets it intends to protect. Without legal validity, couples may face complications during divorce proceedings, potential legal disputes, or significant financial liabilities.
It’s essential to seek legal guidance from an experienced prenup attorney when drafting a prenuptial agreement to ensure compliance with the law and protect your interests effectively. An experienced Arvada prenup lawyer can help you understand your rights, draft a comprehensive agreement tailored to your unique needs, and ensure its enforceability under Colorado law. With our guidance, you can enter into marriage with confidence, knowing that your future is protected, whatever may come your way.

## Prenup – Lakewood, CO
URL: https://thedrakelawfirm.com/prenup-lawyer-lakewood-co/

Lakewood, CO, Prenup Lawyers
At the Drake Law Firm, P.C., we assist both men and women in filing for prenuptial agreements.
Prenuptial Agreement in Lakewood, CO
Entering into a marriage is a beautiful journey, yet the uncertainties of life demand careful consideration. A well-crafted prenuptial agreement can offer both partners peace of mind by providing a clear roadmap in case the unexpected occurs. It’s about protecting your assets and ensuring a smoother transition should your paths diverge. Connect with our Lakewood, CO, prenup lawyer today to initiate this essential legal process.
Understanding Prenuptial Agreements
A prenuptial agreement, often referred to as a “prenup,” is a legal document that couples create before entering into marriage. Think of it as a personalized contract that establishes clear guidelines for various financial and property matters in the event of divorce, separation, or the death of one spouse.
What a Prenuptial Agreement Can Cover in Colorado
Our Lakewood, CO, prenup lawyer can assist you in tailoring a prenuptial agreement that suits your specific needs. In Colorado, a prenup can cover:
Property Division: Clearly outline how your assets and debts will be divided in the event of a divorce.
Alimony/Spousal Maintenance: Determine whether spousal maintenance will be paid, the amount, and the duration.
Business Ownership: Safeguard business interests and clarify the division of business assets.
Inheritance Rights: Specify how inheritances will be handled, ensuring clarity and protection.
Retirement Accounts: Address the division of retirement accounts and benefits.
Debt Responsibility: Clearly state which debts belong to each spouse, shielding one another from potential financial burdens.
Customized Clauses: Include personalized provisions that address unique aspects of your relationship.
By engaging our Lakewood, CO, prenup lawyer, you gain the expertise needed to draft a comprehensive prenuptial agreement that reflects your intentions and protects your interests.
When to Consider a Prenuptial Agreement
While every couple can benefit from a prenuptial agreement, there are specific scenarios where this legal document becomes especially crucial. Our experienced Lakewood, CO, prenup lawyer suggests considering a prenup if:
Either partner owns significant assets
There’s a desire to keep certain assets private
Business ownership is involved
Children from previous marriages are part of the equation
Either partner is anticipating a substantial inheritance
Securing the Legality of Your Prenuptial Agreement
Making sure your prenuptial agreement holds up in court is crucial. When you choose our Lakewood, CO, prenup lawyer, we provide clear and expert assistance on key components. The agreement needs to be in writing, with both parties willingly putting pen to paper. Exchanging complete financial disclosures is part of the process, ensuring that decisions are well-informed.
We are dedicated to preventing any form of coercion, which could jeopardize the validity of the agreement, and work diligently to steer clear of such issues.
Marital Agreements for Every Situation
Contrary to common misconceptions, marital agreements aren’t exclusive to the wealthy. Business owners and individuals seeking to safeguard their assets and mitigate potential debts can greatly benefit. Unsure if it’s right for you? Consult our Lakewood, CO, prenup lawyer for personalized legal guidance based on your unique circumstances.
Child Support and Prenuptial Agreements
While a prenuptial agreement can address various matters, it’s crucial to note that child support isn’t among them. Child support arrangements must prioritize the child’s best interests, evolving as circumstances change.
If you need legal assistance regarding child support in Colorado, our family law attorneys are equipped to guide you through this distinct legal process.
Why Hire a Colorado Prenuptial Agreement Lawyer?
Some couples may consider drafting a prenuptial agreement without seeking legal advice, thinking they can manage it themselves. However, this is not only risky but can also be extremely problematic.
Prenuptial agreements involve complex details for proper creation and enforcement. The person drafting the document must adhere to specific rules and guidelines to ensure its legal validity. Failure to comply with all laws and regulations can render the document ineffective, leaving both parties and the intended protected assets vulnerable. Without a legally sound prenuptial agreement, couples might face complex divorce proceedings, legal complications, or substantial financial liabilities.
At The Drake Law Firm, we simplify the process of creating your prenuptial agreement. Our expertise in this area enables us to craft a document that not only stands up in court but also effectively safeguards your assets in case of a divorce.
Embrace your future with confidence – contact The Drake Law Firm, P.C. Our seasoned Lakewood, CO, prenup lawyer is here to make legal complexities more manageable and ensure your assets and family’s well-being are protected.
